## A Comprehensive Mobile Platform for Fostering Communication, Literacy, Numeracy, and Emotion Understanding in Children with ASD

Bandara T.W.M.I.P.S

Department of Software Engineering Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka it20647582@my.sliit.lk

Nadeera M.S.

Department of Information Technology Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology

Colombo, Sri Lanka it20656188@my.sliit.lk

Deshan M.A.D.

Department of Information Technology Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka it20642532@my.sliit.lk

Jenny Krishara Department of Information Technology Sri Lanka Institute of Information Technology Colombo, Sri Lanka jenny.k@my.sliit.lk

Abstract -This  study  presents  SIPNENA,  a  novel  mobile application  designed  to  aid  the  learning  and  communication development  of  Sinhala-speaking  autistic  children  aged  six, particularly  in  rural  areas  of  Sri  Lanka.  It  offers  a  unique approach  to  teaching  challenging  subjects  like  English  and Mathematics,  tailored  to  the  specific  needs  of  children  with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). The application integrates interactive methodologies and gamification elements to facilitate better communication, understanding, and engagement. Additionally,  it  incorporates  real-time  emotion  recognition features to monitor and respond to children's emotional states during learning activities. This research evaluates SIPNENA's effectiveness  in  improving  communication  abilities,  academic skills, and emotion understanding among autistic children. The findings  indicate  promising  results  in  catering  to  the  unique educational  needs  of  this  target  population,  particularly  in under-resourced rural regions, where specialized interventions are often scarce.

Keywords -SIPNENA,  Autism  Spectrum  Disorder,  Mobile Learning, Rural education, Child development, Educational Technology

Communication difficulties and challenges in understanding emotions  are  common  among  children  with  ASD.  Several research papers have discussed communication interventions [3], but 'SIPNENA'  goes beyond that by incorporating activities  designed  to  improve  communication  skills  and develop  emotional  understanding. These tools often have unfriendly interfaces, bugs, and steep learning curves. Autism Spectrum  Disorder  (ASD)  is  a neurological condition characterized by social interaction, communication, and repetitive activities. Individuals with ASD face educational  challenges,  especially  in  rural  areas  [1],  where specialized  services  and  interventions  are  often  scarce.  The research  on  'SIPNENA'  aims  to  address  these  issues  by focusing on communication abilities, which are often challenging  for  children  with  ASD.  This  research  aims  to provide tailored  care  and  support  for  these  individuals.  The linguistic and cultural divide in Sri Lanka  hinders the provision of appropriate assistance for individuals with ASD, as educational and technical resources are primarily available in internationally dominant languages [2], causing a divide for Sinhala-speaking autistic children. ## II. RELATED WORK

The development of effective learning and communication  systems for ASD  students is crucial to enhancing their educational experiences and facilitating effective communication. Despite numerous research studies, challenges persist, and there is a need for continued exploration  and  innovation  in  this  domain.  Each  research endeavor  has  its  own  unique  focus,  and  while  they  have significantly  contributed  to  our  understanding,  there  is  still room for  improvement and holistic  solutions.  These  studies involve extensive reviews of existing research papers related to  learning  and  communication  systems  for  ASD  students, examining the  progress  made  and  achievements  attained  by researchers in this critical area.

The paper [6], explains a system that includes a Research based, graded Vocabulary, Symbols and Images, Measure the child's  progress  with  Avaz  analytics,  presented  as  easy  to understand graphs, Seamless Integrated Text and Keyboard Mode, and zoom and animation. is the first Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) app launched in Sinhalese [5]. Zoom  and animation features are provided using reinforcement learning. Word prediction is done using images and  text.  Children  can  say  words  and  create  sentences  by touching a picture  symbol  that can  speak  with  a  voice.  For example,  if  the  child  is  hungry  and  cannot  say  the  word "biscuit", he/she can touch the picture of a biscuit in the Avaz SL app and it will speak the word aloud. This app targets a dearth in resources of this nature in Sri Lanka especially in the local  languages;  there  is  no  better  opportunity  that  we  can provide  children  who  have  difficulty  speaking  and  their families than the ability to communicate better so that they too may have voice. The product fulfills several new features but does not fulfill several essential requirements such as recognizing emotions, maintaining a conversation and creating activities targeting the school curriculum.

Duolingo  is  a  2021  research  study  [7]  that  focuses  on  a language application that offers practical and systematic steps for  learning  a  foreign  language.  The  app,  which  teaches English to millions of people for free, differs from other free language learning apps by teaching through translation. This method, which was abandoned in the late 1960s due to the rise of  communicative  approaches,  is  based  on  web  and  mobile application technology, speech recognition for pronunciation training,  and  cloud-based  infrastructure  for  scalability  and personalization. Duolingo also uses text analysis, translation, speech-to-text,  and  natural  language  processing  (NLP)  for personalized  learning  paths.  However,  the  application  does not cover basic aspects such as identifying emotions, developing logical knowledge like mathematics, and improving communication skills.

In the year 2017, the paper [8] describes about 'AutiAid' mobile  application  which  is  done  for  ASD  students.  This provides  a  range  of  features,  including  interactive  games, videos,  and  social  stories,  that  can  help  children  with  ASD develop their cognitive, social, and communication skills. The app is based on scientific research and has been tested with a population in an Autism center. The app is designed to be userfriendly  and  accessible  to  children  with  ASD.  This  uses  an architectural solution that enables the interoperability between an autistic person and caregivers to contribute on the treatment and monitoring to persons with ASD.  The solution is implemented by creating a mobile application and tested with a  population  in  an  Autism  center.  The  app  made  a  positive treatment contribution to a person with ASD.

In the year 2020, the paper [9] describes a mobile application which is done for ASD kids who are in 1-8 age. This application is 'AutiSpark'. AutiSpark is an educational program made specifically for children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) with learning games tested and approved by special  educators  and  occupational  therapists.  Through  their pictures,  children  can  learn  to  associate  objects,  understand emotions,  classify,  recognize  sounds  and  words,  and  much more.  More  features  include  letters,  letter  combinations  and word  recognition,  increasing  basic  math  skills  to  recognize numbers and patterns, social videos, tracking games, memory games and puzzles, etc.

In  the  year  2019,  the  paper  [10]  proposes  a  new  multiagent architecture of an emotional  intelligent e-learning system,  it  aims  to  help  ASD  children  overcome  learning impairments. The paper describes the roles and functions of each  agent,  such  as  the  learner  agent,  the  tutor  agent,  the emotion agent, the pedagogical agent, and the interface agent. The paper also presents the communication protocols and the algorithms used to model the learner's profile, to select the appropriate content, and to evaluate the learner's performance and satisfaction. Some of the main features, algorithms, and architectures of this paper are: The system uses a multi-agent architecture,  which  is  a  distributed  system  composed  of autonomous  and  cooperative  entities  that  can  communicate and interact with each other. The system uses an emotional model,  which  is  a  representation  of  the  learner's  emotional state  based  on  facial  expressions,  voice,  and  physiological signals.  The  system  uses a learner model, which  is a representation of the learner's cognitive and affective characteristics,  such  as  learning  style,  preferences,  goals, knowledge, and emotions. The system uses a content model, which  is  a  representation  of  the  learning  material,  such  as topics,  concepts,  activities,  and  media.  The  system  uses  a pedagogical model, which is a representation of the teaching strategies, such as feedback, guidance, adaptation, and motivation. The system uses a Bayesian network, which is a probabilistic graphical model that can infer the learner 'profile and the optimal content based on the evidence and the prior knowledge.  The  system  uses  a  fuzzy  logic,  which  is  a mathematical framework that can deal with uncertainty and vagueness in the decision making process. The system uses a genetic algorithm, which is a bio-inspired optimization technique that can find the best solution among a population of possible solutions.

The  paper  [11]  describes  application  for  children  with ASD  that  uses  gamification  and  animation  techniques  to enhance  their  learning  experience.  The  paper  explains  the design  and  development  process  of  the  application,  which includes the following steps: analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation. The paper also discusses the algorithms used to generate the questions, to provide feedback,  and  to  track  the  progress  of  the  learners.  The application uses a gamification technique, which is the use of game  elements  and  mechanics  in  non-game  contexts  to increase  engagement  and  motivation.  Animation  technique use of moving images and sounds to create an interactive and immersive environment. This application uses a randomization algorithm, which is an algorithm that generates random  numbers  or  sequences  to  create  different  questions and scenarios for each learner. The application uses a scoring algorithm, which is an algorithm that assigns points or grades to the learner's answers based on the correctness and difficulty level. The application uses a tracking algorithm, which is an algorithm that records and analyzes the learner's performance and behavior over time.

When  compared  to  the  past  implementations  discussed above, 'SIPNENA'  has  existing  functionalities  and  new features  in  each  component.  Some  innovative  features  have been  added  such  as  giving  the  child  the  basic  knowledge  of mathematics  and English at an early stage  and  making arrangements  to  maintain  a  conversation  with  the  help  of  a chatbot to develop communication skills. User-Centered Interaction Design has been used throughout the entire implementation  to  make  the  application  more  convenient  to use..

## III. METHODOLOGY

The problem's solution has broken down into five sections. Each section has its solution to the challenges that the survey addresses.

## A. Developing an Augmentative and Alternative Communication System

## 1) System implementation

The Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) system facilitates communication development by integrating basic vocabulary images and words. The core board encompasses the most frequently used vocabulary, such  as  "you,"  "I,"  "get,"  "do,"  and  "where,"  which constitute a significant portion of everyday communication. The visual representation of symbols is consistent with the user's high-tech device, fostering ease of learning and generalization. Furthermore, the grid size is tailored to  accommodate  the  user's  requirements, ensuring  an  optimal  and  user-friendly  experience.  The color  scheme  employed  in  the  creation  of  this  AAC system adheres to established standards, enhancing clarity and familiarity for the users.

Fig.1. Workflow of the AAC system implementation.



The  color  selection  for  the  AAC  system  is  a  crucial consideration. Instead of arbitrary choices, standardized colors were employed, utilizing blue for adjectives, green for verbs, yellow for pronouns, orange for nouns, white for conjunctions, pink for prepositions and social words, purple for questions, brown for adverbs, red for essential function words, negation, and emergency words, and gray for determiners.[12]

## Data collection

A  speaking-assistance  system has  been  developed  to enhance the communication abilities of children with ASD, even at the young age of six years old. The system utilizes pre-trained, concise, and straightforward conversational questions to engage with users. Data was collected through a combination  of  online  and  physical methods,  with  the primary objective of identifying the set of questions required for training the chatbot.  The  chatbot  training  involved approximately 1000 questions, with 500 questions obtained from 50 individuals through physical interactions and another 500  questions  from  50  individuals  online.  The  data  was gathered from non-ASD children above the age of 18.

Fig. 2. Data collection process for training the conversational chatbot.



The study revealed that over 20% of children struggle with expressing their opinions as shown in Fig. 2. To address this challenge,  a  custom  neural  network  was  developed  using  a Keras  sequential  model.  The  model  was  optimized  using stochastic  gradient  descent  (SGD),  with  classifier  crossentropy  as  the  loss  function  and  accuracy  as  the  training measure.  Natural  Language  Processing  (NLP)  techniques were  employed,  including  pre-processing  input  sentences, encoding them into individual words, and lemmatizing them using the Natural Language Toolkit for working with human language data.

## B. Activity monitoring using  facial imotions

The focus of this component is to track the engagement of autistic children with on-screen learning activities. While the user  interacts  with  educational  activities  on  a  tablet,  the device's front camera is utilized to monitor their involvement. The  study  employs  computer  vision  and  deep  learning techniques to monitor  children with ASD  using  facial emotions.  A  ResNet50  pre-trained  Convolutional  Neural Network (CNN) model is used for face recognition, capturing real-time video frames at specific time intervals. The model is  trained  to  predict  real-time  emotions  using  a  dataset  of 11,500 sample images and tested on 2,500 images from six classes: angry, disgusted, happy, neutral, sad, and surprised.

Fig. 3. Real-time emotion detection using facial expressions.



The  system  continuously  monitors  a  child's  emotions during on-screen activities, generating reports detailing the dominant emotions and important details for analyzing children with ASD.  The conceptual  diagram  is  shown  in  Fig.  5.  Based  on  the child's  past  dominant  emotions,  the  system  suggests  the  next preferred  activity.  These  reports  are  stored  in  a  database  for reference by parents and teachers. If a child's engagement with an activity  exceeds a predetermined threshold percentage, an alert is sent to the parent's account.

Fig. 4. Emotion detection model architecture



## C. Develop Customize English language support system

In the development of an interactive mobile application tailored for children with autism, the primary goal is  to  facilitate  the  learning  of  the  English  alphabet  and common words through an innovative approach that combines technology with pedagogical strategies. This endeavor encompasses a multifaceted methodology, structured around four pivotal stages: initial alphabet instruction, comprehension testing, the integration of common  words  with  gamified  elements,  and  continuous progress monitoring. The foundation of this educational tool is bolstered by a rich collection of image datasets, comprising over 200 sets, which cater to a spectrum of lighting conditions for the letters. Furthermore, the incorporation of a Convolutional  Neural  Network  (CNN)  model  serves  to enhance  the  effectiveness  of  spoken  language  analysis, thereby  enabling  real-time  feedback,  personalized  learning experiences, and an engaging interface that caters specifically to the needs of children with autism.

## Teaching the Alphabet

The  application will teach children to write  English alphabet  letters  on  a  dotted  line,  presenting  each  letter  in context to aid comprehension. The application will provide immediate feedback on the child's writing, awarding points for  correct  responses  and  deducting  attempts  for  incorrect ones, ensuring a comprehensive learning experience.

## Testing Comprehension

Following the completion of alphabet lessons, the application incorporates  a  short  quiz  to  evaluate  the  child's  grasp  and retention of the material. This formative assessment serves as a  diagnostic  tool,  allowing  for  the  adjustment  of  future lessons based on the child's performance. It provides valuable insights into the child's strengths and areas needing improvement,  thus tailoring the learning path to meet individual needs effectively.

Teaching  common  words  and  implementing  gamification elements

The application introduces everyday words using alphabet lessons, requiring children to write them on a dotted line. Successful completion earns points, while unsuccessful attempts  result  in  no  points.  To  increase  engagement,  the application  uses  gamification  elements  like  leaderboards, badges, and rewards, encouraging competition and a sense of achievement upon reaching certain milestones.

## Assessing progress

This research focuses on developing a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model to support interactive English learning for children with autism. The model is trained on a dataset of audio samples and preprocessed into a  Mel spectrogram  for  consistent  analysis.  The  CNN  architecture, built  with  TensorFlow  and  Keras,  consists  of  convolutional and pooling layers for feature extraction and dense layers for classification. The training process employs the  Adam optimizer  and  categorical  cross-entropy  loss  function,  with early stopping to avoid overfitting. The model's performance is  evaluated  using  a  test  set,  and  once  satisfactory,  it  is deployed within a mobile application. This application offers real-time  analysis  of  the  child's  spoken  input,  providing immediate  feedback  on  pronunciation  and  comprehension, and fostering an engaging and personalized learning environment that enhances language acquisition for children with autism.

## D. Develop a numeracy skill improvement system

In this study, a novel approach is implemented to facilitate counting skills in autistic children, focusing on the numerical range from zero to nine. The intervention involves presenting numbers to the participants and assessing their ability to make accurate judgments. Points are awarded for correct pronunciation, while instances of incorrect pronunciation are utilized as opportunities for improvement and reinforcement.

## Data collection

In  this  research  endeavor,  a  cohort  comprising  1000 students, specifically enrolled in 2nd and 3rd grades, actively participated in the process of articulating numbers spanning from zero to the name of an advanced mathematical formula. The meticulous execution of this auditory task was facilitated using Audacity software, a sophisticated audio editing tool. Within  this  digital  environment,  extraneous  sounds  were methodically eradicated, ensuring the isolation and preservation  of  the  numerical  pronunciations.  The  process yielded a comprehensive dataset, a symphony of voices from 1000 children, each contributing their unique articulation of one-digit numbers. This extensive collection resulted in the curation  of  10,000  individual  sound  samples,  forming  the bedrock of our investigation into the  nuances of  numerical pronunciation proficiency among students in the early grades. This  methodology,  blending  technology  with  pedagogy, provides a robust foundation for analyzing and understanding the  intricacies  of  verbal  numerical  expression  in  a  diverse educational setting.

## E. Providing  an  optimal  end-user  experience  by  involving users

The research focuses on UI/UX engineering technologies for the user journey of a mobile application. Design thinking is an approach that uses design methodologies to re-evaluate paradigms  and  modify  existing  technology  to  create  new procedures suitable for users. User-Centered Design (UCD) is chosen as the best solution to ensure clear and uncomplicated designs. The research uses a pragmatic strategy that includes qualitative and quantitative methods to gain a deep understanding of users. The main goal is to demonstrate highfidelity prototypes of an e-learning system on portable devices that are easy to use, have a minimal learning curve, and do not require excessive time to understand, implement, and satisfy users' expectations. The research objectives include identifying the most appropriate data collection and analysis methods, real-world problems, and interaction design concepts.  The  survey-based  technique  was  chosen  for  data collection  and  analysis,  simplifying  participant  responses. Potential problems were identified, and changes to the mobile application were made using interactive design principles.

Overall  system  design  was  finalized  and  implemented after making the modifications for the interfaces by taking all the responses of the participants and the UCID methodology into account.

## IV. DISCUSION

The proposed research endeavor offers a comprehensive solution  to  address  the  challenges  faced  by  the  target  user group.  The  user  will  be  required  to  register  for  a  system account to access the full range of features and functionalities.

SIPNENA is a mobile application that performs real-time emotion  detection  while  children  with  Autism  Spectrum Disorder (ASD) engage in learning activities. Research efforts have  been  directed  toward  emotion  recognition  in  children with  ASD,  with  the  aim  of  providing  them  with  a  deeper understanding  of emotions  to enhance  their recognition abilities.  The  application  employs  six  distinct  emotional categories: angry, disgusted, happy, neutral, sad, and surprised, tailored to the children's emotional states [13].

SIPNENA is a comprehensive platform that provides an Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) system for  communication  and  speech  training,  with  the  primary objective of improving the speaking skills of young children. Unlike most AAC systems, which are typically emulated on phones  or  tablet  devices  [14],  SIPNENA  has  developed  a Sinhala version of the core board. This unique feature enables children to communicate using their voice, a departure from traditional systems that rely solely on typing [15]. SIPNENA's approach  transcends  conventional  AAC  systems,  allowing children  to  effectively  communicate  through  their  voices, fostering a more natural and engaging experience.

While  numerous  applications  have  been  developed  to enhance the communication skills of children with ASD, there is a paucity of e-learning applications designed to expand their knowledge base. Some applications focus solely on improving children's numeracy skills [16], while others are exclusively dedicated to enhancing English language proficiency. However, SIPNENA  has adopted a holistic approach, incorporating various activities to foster the development of multiple skills, including communication, English language, and mathematics.

SIPNENA is  a  user-friendly  application  tailored  for  young children,  with  a  strong  emphasis  on  functionality  and  an intuitive user interface. It offers a comprehensive solution by amalgamating features such as emotion detection, communication skill development, and subject-related activities. Unlike other applications that provide these features in  isolation,  SIPNENA  consolidates  them  into  a  unified platform,  facilitating  convenient  access  and  utilization  for children. This integrated approach distinguishes SIPNENA as a unique and valuable tool for children with ASD.

## V. CONCLUSTION

This article presents SIPNENA, an innovative e-learning and  communication  platform  designed  for  children  with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). It integrates features like a  chatbot,  emotion  recognition,  an  AAC  keyboard,  and activities for English and Math learning. Future work aims to expand language support, broaden subject-related activities, and enhance user experience and accessibility. The goal is to provide a comprehensive, inclusive, and engaging learning environment that empowers children  with  ASD to develop essential  skills,  while  contributing  to  the  field  of  assistive technology and inclusive education practices.

## Paper Source: A Deep Learning-Based Approach for Engagement Assessment of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder

## A  Deep  Learning-Based  Approach for  Engagement  Assessment  of  Students with  Autism  Spectrum  Disorder



Md.  Aminul  Islam  Shanto,  Sraboni  Ghosh  Joya ,  M.  Shamim  Kaiser, and  Md.  Sazzadur  Rahman

Abstract Engagement assessment plays a crucial role in understanding and improving  the  educational  experiences  of  students  with  autism  spectrum  disorder (ASD).  Traditional  methods  of  engagement  assessment  heavily  rely  on  subjective observations and manual coding, which can be time-consuming, prone to bias, and lack of  precision.  In  this  study,  we  propose  a  deep  learning-based  approach, specifically  convolutional  neural  networks  (CNNs)  to  automatically  analyze  multimodal  data streams, including facial  expressions  and  body  movements  collected during  classroom  activities.  The  multimodal  data  is  preprocessed  and  fed  into  CNN for  feature  extraction,  followed  by  CNN-2  for  temporal  modeling  and  engagement prediction.  The  results  demonstrate  that  the  proposed  deep  learning-based  approach achieves  significantly higher accuracy  that is 97.1%.  In the future, an Intelligent Tutor  System  (ITS)  will  be  built  to  help  children  with  ASD  study  more  effectively via the use of mobile  or online applications. Evaluating  participation from  since engagement  is  a  cognitive  trait  shared  by  humans,  visual  signals  alone  are  insufficient.  Physiological  elements  must  thus  be  present.  In  the  future,  we  will  work  on  a model  that  can  evaluate  a  student's  degree  of  involvement  by  combining  behavioral and  physiological  data.

Keywords Autism  spectrum  disorder · Students · Classroom · Video  data · CNN · Intelligent  Tutor  System

## 1 Introduction

## 1.1 Overview

A  neuro-developmental  ailment  known  as  autism  spectrum  disorder  (ASD)  is  characterized  by  ongoing  difficulties  in  social  interaction  and  communication  as  well as  the  prevalence  of  limited  and  repetitive  activities.  It  affects  persons  at  all  ages, with  symptoms  often  first  emerging  in  the  early  years  of  life.  The  intellectual  and social  growth  of  individuals  with  ASD  is  greatly  supported  by  education.  However, because  of  the  distinctive  cognitive  and  behavioral  traits  linked  to  the  illness,  it  may be  especially  difficult  to  include  these  individuals  in  educational  activities.  It  helps  to gauge  students  with  ASD's  extent  to  participation  for  a  number  of  reasons.  First,  the extent  of  participation,  focus,  and  interest  in  learning  activities  may  be  determined by  looking  at  their  level  of  engagement.  It  demonstrates  their  engagement,  operation, and  capacity  for  sustained  attention,  all  of  which  are  essential  for  creating  engaging learning  environments.  Second,  measuring  engagement  may  provide  important  information  into  how  well  instructional  techniques  and  treatments  designed  for  students with  ASD  work.  It  enables  teachers  to  keep  track  of  student progress,  spot areas for  development,  and  modify  their  pedagogical  approaches  as  necessary.  Finally, engagement  assessment  contributes  to  inclusive  education  by  ensuring  that  children with  ASD  get  the  proper  assistance  and  modifications  based  on  their  requirements.

## 1.2 Limitations  of  Existing  Works

Traditional  methods  of  engagement  assessment  in  students  with  ASD  primarily  rely on  subjective  observations,  self-reporting,  and  behavioral  checklists.  These  methods are  often  labor-intensive,  time-consuming,  and  prone  to  inter-rater  variability.  Moreover,  they  may  not  capture  the  subtle  nuances  and  context-specific  cues  associated with  engagement  in  individuals  with  ASD.  Consequently,  there  is  a  need  for  objective, reliable,  and  efficient  assessment  methods  that  can  provide  accurate  and  real-time insights  into  the  engagement  levels  of  students  with  ASD.

## 1.3 Motivation  of  This  Study

Deep  learning's  potential  to  autonomously  recognize  and  separate  significant  patterns and  characteristics  from  large  amounts  of  complicated  data  precisely  propels  its  use in  engagement  assessment.  Large  volumes  of  data,  such  as  the  heterogeneous  sensor data  and  video  recordings  that  are  frequently  employed  in  engagement  assessment, are  particularly  adequate  for  processing  by  deep  learning  algorithms.  By  using  deep learning,  we  can  create  models  that  can  identify  complex  patterns  and  nuanced  indicators  related  to  participation  in  kids  with  ASD,  resulting  in  more  precise  and  impartial evaluations.  Deep  learning  models  also  have  the  aptitude  to  make  assumptions  and respond  effectively  to  various  situations  and  individual  characteristics,  making  them especially  appropriate  for  assessing  engagement  in  a  diverse  population  like  students with  ASD.

## 1.4 Our  Contribution

The research involved was motivated by the dearth of educational resources for students  with  ASD.  In  addition,  we  need  to  make  sure  that  students  with  ASD  do not  slack  off  and  fall  behind  in  their  studies  for  no  apparent  reason.  In  this  study, we  provide  a  deep  learning-based  method  for  assessing  engagement  among  students with  autism  spectrum  disorder.  Our  goal  is  to  provide  teachers  and  researchers  with a  robust  and  practical  method  to  assess  interest  now  by  capitalizing  on  the  power of  deep  learning  algorithms.  This  strategy  has  the  potential  to  help  individuals  with ASD  succeed  in  school  by  facilitating  individualized  treatments  and  establishing welcoming  classroom  settings.  Using  the  camera  to  capture  the  children's  reactions while  the  teacher  was  talking  allowed  us  to  generate  a  dataset  that  was  then  interpreted  by  a  specialist  in  autism  spectrum  disorders.  By  using  deep  learning  algorithms,  we  have  differentiated  between  four  stages  of  student  engagement.  Highly involved,  partially  engaged,  not  engaged,  and  undetermined  are  the  four  categories of  participation.

## 2 Related  Work

With  the  advancement  of  artificial  intelligence  (AI)  through  deep  neural  networks, automated  engagement  analysis  has  gained  traction  since  the  early  2000s.  It  was made  possible  by  the  emergence  of  big  data,  which  is  now  relatively  easy  to  acquire. If  there  is  another  factor  that  must  be  addressed,  it  is  undoubtedly  the  rise  in  computational  power.  A  classroom-based  automated  engagement  monitoring  system  was first  proposed  by  Bidwell  and  Fuchs  [1].  After  that  several  methods  already  in  use have  been  examined  by  some  other  researchers.  For  the  purpose  of  assessing  engagement  among  students  with  ASD,  this  section  presents  an  overview  of  some  of  these methods,  pointing  out  their  benefits,  drawbacks,  and  remaining.

## 2.1 Overview  of  Different  Methods

Observational  Methods :  Observational  approaches  require  closely  observing  how students  behave  and  interact  while  participating  in  instructional  events.  To  classify engagement  based  on  behavioral  indicators  including  attention,  active  involvement, and  completion  of  tasks,  teachers  and  researchers  employ  conventional  classification systems.  According  to  McKenzie  et  al.,  there  are  certain  observational  approaches that  were  used  to  collect  rich  subjective  data  for  gauging  student  participation  during class,  but  they  are  time-consuming,  subject  to  bias  from  observers,  and  need  extensive  training  [2].  A  classroom  observation  procedure  was  created  by  Lane  and  Harris to  quantify  student  involvement  in  big  university  classrooms  [3].  Educators  may  get real-time  data  on  how  their  students  are  reacting  to  class  material  using  the  Behavioral Engagement  Related  to  Instruction  (BERI)  protocol  [3].  After  that  in  2015  Currey et  al.  intended  to  assess  the  attitudes  toward  and  participation  in  team-based  learning (TBL)  among  postgraduate  nursing  critical  care  students  [4].  A  comprehensive  evaluation  of  works  on  student  involvement  analysis  was  conducted  by  Thomas  and Jayagopi  [5].  A  prediction  approach  that  can  assess  whether  students  were  paying attention  or  preoccupied  based  on  captured  footage  from  the  classroom  was  also presented  [5].  These  studies  show  that  observational  approaches  include  direct  visual monitoring  of  students'  relationships  and  behavior  while  participating  in  instructional activities.

Questionnaires  and  Rating  Scales : Techniques  for personal or caregiver-report which  assess  several  facets  of  engagement,  including  interest,  focus,  and  motivation, include  questionnaires  and  rating  scales.  These  methods  may  record  the  opinions  of people  with  ASD  and  provide  arbitrary  insights  regarding  participation  levels.  To evaluate  the  usage  of  questionnaires  and  rating  scales  in  assessing  student  participation,  Fredricks  and  McColskey  suggested  a  model  [6].  Quantitative  studies  of  classroom  climate  and  student  participation  sit  beside  qualitative  assessment  systems  for general  student  conduct  [6].  Applying  the  Rasch-Andrich  rating  scale  model,  You et  al.  provided  a  method  for  examining  students'  levels  of  enthusiasm  and  validated the  Science  Motivation  Questionnaire  II  (SMQ  II)  created  by  Glynn  et  al.  (2011) [7].  Many  qualitative  studies  on  parental  engagement  have  flaws,  and  Bakker  and Denessen  focused  on  them.  On  an  evaluation  of  twelve  research  chosen  for  their  use of  quantitative  measures  of  parental  participation  [8].  The  results  of  this  research suggest,  however,  that  self-report  assessments  might  be  especially  problematic  for people  who  have  trouble  expressing  themselves  or  who  have  a  shallow  understanding of  their  own  capabilities.  There  is  a  risk  of  bias  in  caregiver  reporting.  In  addition, the  responses  to  surveys  and  rating  scales  are  generally  based  on  memory,  which may  not  be  an  accurate  representation  of  participants'  involvement  in  the  moment.

Audio  and  Video  Analysis :  Analyzing  audio  and  video  data  is  a  method  used  to discover engagement-related activities and signs including talking, smiling, and touching.  Computer  vision  and  audio  processing  methods  have  been  combined  with machine  learning  algorithms  to  automatically  extract  features  and  categorize  degrees of  involvement.  A  fresh  paradigm  for  gauging  student  interest  in  their  classroom  or online coursework  was  presented  by  Alkabbany  et  al. [9]. The  user's video was recorded,  and  the  suggested  framework  followed  the  user's  face  as  it  moved  from frame  to  frame  [9].  As  shown  by  the  student's  gestures,  glance  patterns,  and  overall achievement  during  brief  video  learning  sessions,  Yue  et  al.  suggested  a  combined structure  to  assess  engagement  with  learning  from  three  facets:  impact,  conduct,  and mental  state  [10].  A  technique  for  gauging  pupils'  degrees  of  focus  was  carried  out by  Li  et  al.,  who  used  a  photoplethysmogram  (PPG)  signal  detected  by  a  device that  is  worn  with  a  median  accuracy  of  0.69  [11].  Convolutional  neural  networks were  used  in  edge  computing  by  Umarale  et  al.  to  offer  a  deep  learning  method  for determining  the  learners'  degree  of  attention  [12].  Students'  levels  of  engagement are  divided  into  one  of  four  categories  by  the  neural  network:  extremely  attentive, attentive,  less  attentive,  and  least  attentive  [12].  An  open-source  dataset  was  used  in the  training  of  a  deep  learning  convolutional  neural  network  (CNN)  created  by  Wang et  al.  [13].  Quantitative  experiments  illustrated  the  effectiveness  of  this  model  and the  deep  learning  CNN  in  continuous  tracking  of  student  progress  and  engagement. These  methods  allow  for  instantaneous,  objective  evaluation.  However,  obstacles include  a  need  for  reliable  algorithms,  susceptibility  to  external  influences,  and  the necessity  of  sufficient  training  data.

Physiological  Measures : Heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, and eye tracking are just few of the physiological measurements  that have been investigated  for  use  in  assessing  students'  levels  of  involvement  who  have  autism  spectrum disorder.  Arousal,  focus,  and  mood  may  all  be  quantified  using  these  tests.  Physiological metrics  provide  a continual, non-invasive  evaluation  of  effort. They  are complicated  to  interpret  because  of  individual  variances  and  co-occurring  disorders, need  specialist  equipment,  and  are  susceptible  to  outside  influences.  GSR  detectors were  employed  as  a  measure  of  students'  participation  in  a  distributed  learning  environment,  as  shown  by  the  work  of  Wang  and  Cesar  [14].  A  self-report  questionnaire was  developed  to  evaluate  two  kinds  of  student  involvement  with  school:  cognitive and  psychological  engagement,  based  on  the  literature  review  conducted  by  Appleton et  al.  [15].  Based  on  answers  from  a  socioeconomically  and  racially  diverse  group  of urban  ninth  graders  in  1931,  the  student  engagement  instrument's  (SEI)  psychological  characteristics  were  evaluated  [15].  The  building  of  a  tool  that  allows  students  to self-report  to  evaluate  the  two  kinds  of  student  involvement  with  school-cognitive and  psychological  engagement-was  made  possible  by  Fredricks  et  al.'s  study  of pertinent  literature  [6].  Responses  from  an  urban  group  of  1931  ninth-grade  students from  a  variety  of  racial  and  socioeconomic  backgrounds  were  used  to  evaluate  the statistical  features  of  this  measure,  the  SEI  [6].

Sensor-Based  Approaches : Wearable sensors that capture information about a wearer's  position,  movement,  and  interactions  with  others  include  accelerometers and  proximity  sensors.  These  sensors  enable  undetectable,  impartial  evaluations  of involvement.  The  gathered  sensor  data  may  be  utilized  to  classify  the  levels  of  user interaction  using  machine  learning  algorithms.  There  are  limitations,  however,  such as  the  need  for  good  sensor  implantation,  the  requirement  to  guarantee  participant comfort,  and  the  requirement  to  handle  data  privacy  problems.  By  using  the  Emotiv EPOC  system,  Ghergulescu  and  Muntean  suggested  a  unique  EEG  sensor-based  way to  gauge  and  analyze  learners'  motivation  in  game-based  learning  environments  [16]. The  study  discussed  in  this  article  has  the  potential  to  promote  and  allow  motivationbased  adaptation  in  educational  games  by  offering  an  automated  real-time  solution  for motivation  evaluation  [16].  As  trainees  advanced  through  a  robotic  surgeon  training program  in  a  medical  facility,  Wu  et  al.  suggested  a  model  to  track  changes  in  their cognitive  and  behavioral  states  [17].

## 2.2 Limitations  and  Gaps  in  Current  Literature

It  is  important  to  recognize  the  constraints  inherent  in  each  study  before  drawing definitive conclusions  about  its reliability or validity. This is  more  than  simply  a synopsis of the frequency  and  trend of inaccuracies and other validity concerns. There  has  been  a  lot  of  focus  on  engagement  analysis  recently.  Constraints  unique to  each  project  must  be  identified  and  addressed  in  the  future.  The  limitations  of  the studies  we  looked  at  are  shown  in  Table  1.

## 3 Methodology

The  deep  learning-based  model  we  presented  in  this  part  can  be  seen  in  Fig.  1. The entire approach  has  broken  down  into  many  phases.  The  first  phase  consisted  of capturing  some  unedited  films  of  a  school  environment.  To  make  it  easier  for  the system  to  handle  those  lengthier  flicks  more  rapidly,  we  then  have  sliced  them  into shorter  flicks.  Then,  components  of  the  head  and  body  positions  have  extracted  using an  application  called  Mediapipe.  Then,  we  have  then  incorporated  the  preprocessed features  to  the  training  of  a  deep  learning  model.  After  a  deep  learning  model  has been  trained,  it  is  feasible  to  predict  how  interested  an  ASD  student  will  be.  There are  four  different  groups  in  this  categorization  since  it  has  many  classes.  The  four levels  of  engagement  are  highly  engaged,  moderately  engaged,  not  engaged,  and undefined.

## 3.1 Data  Collection  and  Preprocessing

It  is  important  to  recognize  the  constraints  inherent  in  each  study  before  drawing definitive.  The  development  and  implementation  of  a  deep  learning-based  engagement  assessment  method  for  students  with  ASD  requires  thorough  data  collection  and preparation.  These  steps  involve  gathering  relevant  data  and  preparing  it  for  further research  and modeling.  Below  is  an  overview  of  the steps involved  in collecting and  preparing  data,  and  Fig.  2  describes  the  whole  data  collection  procedure  in  a summary.

Fig.  1 Flowchart  of  proposed  model



Fig.  2 Procedure  of  collecting  raw  video  data  for  the  model



- a. Capturing  videos  from  the  classroom:  To  gauge  how  much  of  engagement  of students  with  ASD,  two  participants  were  recorded  for  a  total  of  4  h,  34  min while  they  were  receiving  instructions  from  a  teacher.  Many  of  the  students  were already  familiar  on  the  key  ideas  being  discussed  in  class.  We  were  recording  on video  at  the  precise  moment.  Back  then,  we  relied  on  our  mobile  cameras.  They were  cautioned  against  becoming  stale  in  front  of  massive  video  cameras.

- b. Video  capturing  and  making  short  clips:  In  class,  they  learned  by  repeating  a few  concepts  they were  already  acquainted  with.  That's when  we  first  began using  the  camera  to  shoot  video.  We  took  these  pictures  using  the  cameras  on  our mobile  phones.  Because  teachers  emphasized  the  need  of  avoiding  developing  an irrational  fear  of  large  video  cameras.  The  cameras  were  pointed  slightly  to  the learner's  left  rather  than  directly  at  them.  The  recording  procedure  was  carried out  in  this  way  without  arousing  any  suspicion.
- c. Video  preprocessing  and  augmentation:  To  use  the  body  and  head  movements of  students  as  indicators  of  their  mental  focus,  we  need  to  remove  the  pertinent segments  from  the  recordings.  After  that,  the  model  is  over  fit  using  augmentation techniques  that  are  utilized  to  clip  regeneration.  After  that,  it  is  necessary  for  us to  personally  examine  the  standard  of  the  films.  As  a  consequence  of  this,  we  now have  a  total  of  3332  clips,  of  which  825  have  been  evaluated  as  'highly  engaged' and  824  have  been  rated  as  'moderately  engaged.'  There  are  829  of  them  that  are categorized  as  'not  engaged,'  and  there  are  854  more  that  are  'undefined.'
- d. Video  annotation: Following  the creation of the videos, we  are conducting  a poll of educators at a school for students with autism to determine the best annotation  strategies.  They  have  some  suggestions  on  how  to  annotate  the  dataset to  identify  four  labels:  'highly  engaged,'  'moderately  engaged,'  'not  engaged,' and  'undefined'  based  on  the  visual  cues  and  our  questionnaire.

## 3.2 Feature  Extraction  and  Representation

To  create  a  deep  learning-based  solution  for  engagement  evaluation  in  kids  with  ASD, feature  extraction  and  representation  are  essential  stages.  These  procedures  include converting  the  raw  data  into  relevant  and  meaningful  characteristics  that  may  be  fed into  a  deep  learning  model.  The  feature  extraction  and  representation  procedure  are summarized  as  follows:

1. Detecting  the  subject:  After  getting  the  analyzed  motion  pictures,  we  proceeded with  these  operations.  Using  the  machine  vision  framework  Mediapipe  [18],  we have  performed  subject  detection.  We  weren't  able  to  examine  every  person  in the  room  using  the  framework  since  it  could  recognize  many  faces  at  once.  After identifying  the  individual,  we  have  employed  3D  models  to  extract  traits  like body  and  head  points.  The  distance  between  the  person  being  photographed  and the  camera  is  indicated  by  'Z'.  Since  a  person  does  not  always  stand  in  front of  the  camera  at  the  same  distance,  depth  measurement  is  necessary  to  identify the subject's posture. As  a result,  Mediapipe  is  the  best  detection  framework and  superior  to  other  frameworks.  The  model  for  predicting  postures  is  called BlazePose,  and  it  is  being  utilized  here.
2. Detecting the body points: Following the identification of features, we have continued  to  pursue  the  issue  in  reference  to  those  features.  It  would  locate  and keep  track  of  33  different  anatomical  landmarks.  We  were  only  utilizing  upper body  landmarks  as  our  key  body  point  to  extract  features  since  the  nature  of  our

Fig.  3 Extracted  features  for building  our  assessment model



- video  and  the  engagement  assessment  both  favored  using  landmarks  that  show the  position  of  the  head  and  body.  This  is  because  landmarks  that  indicate  the location  of  the  head  and  body  are  more  likely  to  be  accurate.
3. Extracting  the  body  points:  We  have  removed  11  points  from  the  head  point, including  the  nose,  left  inner  and  outer  eyes,  right  eye,  and  outer  eye,  left  and right ears, and the left and right  mouths.  We  have  extracted  an  additional  12 points  from  the  body  point,  including  the  left  and  right  mouths,  the  left  and  right shoulders,  the  left  and  right  elbows,  the  left  and  right  wrists,  the  left  and  right pinkies,  the  left  and  right  indexes,  and  the  left  and  right  thumbs.  Figure  3  indicates the  extracted  features.
4. Extracting  features  by  using  1-D  CNN:  1-D  CNN  performs  better  at  extracting features  from  time-series  data.  A  one-dimensional  CNN  was  utilized  to  extract the  feature  from  the  body  points  in  this  model.  Because  video  is  a  collection  of frames,  it  undoubtedly  contains  a  time-series  component,  and  by  applying  the convolution  layer,  it  can  detect  and  retrieve  the  feature  that  binds  the  inputs  to the  outputs  directly.

## 3.3 Deep  Learning  Architecture  for  Engagement  Assessment

In  the  present  study,  CNN-2  fared  better  than  the  other  models;  hence,  we  intend  on using  the  CNN-2  architecture  as  the  basis  for  our  deep  learning  system.  Our  system architecture  is  visualized  here  in  Fig.  4.  Raw  video  is  recorded  in  this  model  using a  resolution  of  1920  by  1080  pixels  and  a  frame  rate  of  24  frames  per  second.  After the  videos  have  been  captured,  shorter  clips  are  created  with  the  goal  to  reduce  the amount  of  computing  effort  required  for  the  process.  After  that,  the  clips  have  been cleaned  up  and  labeled  to  ensure  that  the  quality  is  maintained  throughout.  Following the annotation, a pre-trained architecture known  as  Mediapipe  is used to extract essential  information  from  both  the  head  and  the  body  of  the  document.  It  is  put  to use  in  the  process  of  separating  the  important  points  from  the  body  points  and  the head  points.  After  that,  information  is  input  into  the  convolution  layer,  which  consists of  64  neurons  and  uses  the  'Tanh'  activation  function.  After  this  stage,  it  proceeds to  the  next  one,  which  is  a  max-pooling  layer  that  halves  the  input.  Following  that,  a dropout  layer  consisting  of  25%  is  added  so  that  there  is  no  overfitting.  Following  this dropout  layer  is  a  new  convolution  layer  that  has  128  neurons  and  uses  the  'Tanh' activation function as its activation function. This is followed  by  a  max-pooling layer  and  a  dropout  layer.  A  layer  containing  256  neurons  and  an  activation  function denoted  as  'Tanh'  (hyperbolic  tangent  function)  is  added  as  the  third  convolution layer  of  the  network.  After  going  through  the  max-pooling  and  dropout  layers,  the data  is  then  flattened  before  being  fed  into  fully  linked  dense  layers.  This  function, known  as  Tanh,  is  responsible  for  activating  these  layers.  After  that,  at  the  output layer,  the  softmax  activation  function  is  employed  to  make  a  prediction  about  the kind  of  engagement.  As  a  loss  function,  categorical  cross-entropy  was  used  in  the construction  of  this  model.

## 3.4 Model  Train

The  development  of  a  deep  learning-based  strategy  for  engagement  assessment  in students  with  ASD  must  include  a  model  training  stage.  We  have  applied  four  models. They  are  artificial  neural  network  (ANN),  convolution  neural  network-1  (CNN-1), long  short-term  memory  (LSTM),  convolutional  neural  network-2  (CNN-2,  with different  architecture).

ANN:  It  consists  of  13  layers,  where  5  of  them  are  dense  layers  with  64,  128,  256, 128,  and  64  neurons  in  each  layer,  followed  by  a  dropout  layer  with  a  25%  chance of  omitting  the  neurons  to  activate  the  next  layer.  Dropout  layers  are  used  to  prevent the overfitting of the model.  In between  the  third and fourth dense  layers, batch normalization  is introduced  so that the values of  weighted  sum  operation  do  not explode,  and  all  numbers  belong  to  the  same  range.  The  activation  function  rectified linear unit (ReLU)  has  been  used. Categorical cross-entropy has been used as a loss function  as this  is  a  multi-class  classification  problem  and  adaptive  moment estimation  (Adam)  is  the  optimizer.  For  the  same  reason,  'softmax'  is  used  as  an activation  function  in  the  output  layer.  This  layer  has  four  outputs-'highly  engaged,' 'moderate  engaged,'  'not  engaged,'  and  'undefined.'

CNN-1:  There  are  two  convolution  layers,  followed  by  three  fully  connected  layers with  the  activation  function  being  'ReLU.'  In  the  first  convolution  layer,  it  has  128 neurons,  and  in  the  second,  there  are  256  neurons  with  kernel  size  3  for  both  layers. There  is  a  dropout  layer  in  both  convolution  layers,  followed  by  a  max-pooling  layer, which  reduces  the input size and extracts the essential features. After the flatten layer,  there  are  three  dense  layers  with  256,  128,  and  64  neurons.  Softmax  activation function is used in the output layer for multi-class classification, and categorical cross-entropy  is  used  as  a  loss  function  while  Adam  is  the  optimizer.

Fig.  4 System  architecture  of  our  assessment  model



LSTM:  Since LSTM  works better for time-series analysis, this architecture is proposed  for  this  study.  There  are  4  LSTM  layers  with  64,  128,  256,  and  512  neurons, respectively,  with  the  activation  function  being  'Tanh.'  After  the  fourth  LSTM  layer, a  dropout  layer  is  introduced  to  prevent  the  model  overfitting.  There  are  four  dense layers  with  512,  256,  128,  and  64  neurons,  respectively,  with  the  activation  function being  rectified  linear  unit  (ReLU)  followed  by  dropout  layers  with  25%  probability. Categorical  cross-entropy  is  being  used  as  a  loss  function.  In  the  output  layer,  softmax is  used  as  an  activation  function.  Adam  is  used  as  an  optimizer  for  this  model.

CNN-2:  This  architecture  comprises  a  total  of  16  layers.  There  are  three  convolution layers with  64, 128,  and  256  neurons  with  a  kernel  size  of  3. 'Tanh'  is  used as  an  activation  function  for  these  convolution  layers.  Each  convolution  layer  has  a dropout  layer  with  a  25%  possibility  and  a  max-pooling  layer  to  make  the  operation less  computationally  intensive  and  get  the  essential  features.  There  are  three  fully connected  layers  with  256,  128,  and  64  neurons.  'Tanh'  is  used  as  an  activation  function.  After  the  first  and  second  dense  layers,  dropout  layers  with  a  25%  possibility are  introduced  to  prevent  the  model  from  overfitting.  Softmax  is  used  as  an  activation  function  for  the  output  layer,  while  RMSprop  is  used  as  an  optimizer.  Since  it is  a  multi-class  classification  problem,  categorical  cross-entropy  is  used  as  a  loss function.  The  whole  CNN-2  model  is  illustrated  in  Fig.  5.

Fig.  5 CNN-2  model  that  outperforms  better  than  other  selected  models



## 4 Dataset

The  dataset  underlying  the  study's  engagement  evaluation  of  students  with  ASD  is described  in  this  section.  It  contains  information  on  the  procedures  used  to  acquire the  data,  participant  demographics,  and  the  inter-rater  reliability  of  the  annotation process.

Description  of  the  Dataset:  Since  the  dataset  has  split  into  a  75:25  train-test  ratio,  it has  a  total  of  833  clips  for  test  and  2499  clips  to  train  the  model.  Since  the  dataset has  4  classes,  it  is  a  multi-class  classification  problem.  The  number  of  clips  for  train and  test  dataset  split  is  in  Fig.  6.

Fig.  6 Annotated  dataset  that  has  been  used  for  our  model



Participant  Demographics:  Working  with  educational  institutions,  special  education programs,  and  pertinent  stakeholders  was  a  part  of the  data  gathering  procedure. Students  with  an  ASD  diagnosis  who  were  between  the  ages  of  6  and  12  made  up the  study's  subjects.  Before  any  data  was  collected,  the  participants'  parents  or  legal guardians  gave  their  approval.  To  guarantee  ecological  validity,  the  data  collecting sessions  were  conducted  in  environments  designed  for  learning,  such  as  schools  or therapeutic  spaces.  Several  recording  tools,  such  as  video  cameras,  wearable  physiological  sensors,  and  audio  recorders,  were  employed  to  record  several  modalities concurrently.  The  participants  took  part  in  a  variety  of  educational  assignments  that were  created  to  elicit  varying  degrees  of  involvement,  such  as  group  discussions,  oneon-one  conversations,  and  instructional  exercises.  The  data  gathering  sessions  were rigorously  watched  by  researchers  and  educators  to  guarantee  participant  comfort and  reduce  any  negative  impacts.  When  necessary,  breaks  and  downtime  were  given, and  stringent  privacy  and  confidentiality  rules  were  followed.

Annotation  Method  and  Inter-Rater  Reliability:  Professional  annotators  with  in-depth knowledge  of  ASD  research  and  engagement  evaluation  annotated  the  gathered  data. The  data  was  divided  into  smaller  segments  throughout  the  annotation  process,  such as  time  frames  or  activity-based  segments,  and  each  segment  was  given  an  engagement  label.  Multiple  annotators  individually  tagged  a  portion  of  the  data  to  assure consistency  and  dependability  in  the  annotation  process.  To  evaluate  the  agreement between  the  annotators,  inter-rater  reliability  metrics  such  as  Cohen's  kappa  coefficient  and  intraclass  correlation  coefficient  (ICC)  were  calculated.  To  rectify  any differences  or  ambiguities  in  labeling  requirements,  the  annotators  had  frequent  meetings  and  discussions.  To  reduce  subjectivity  and  improve  consistency,  the  annotation rules  gave  precise  definitions  and  criteria  for  each  type  of  engagement  level  (highly engaged,  moderately  engaged,  not  engaged,  and  undefined).  Through  consensusbased talks or the inclusion of a third expert to make  the ultimate decision, any discrepancies  or  doubts  were  addressed.  By  contrasting  the  annotations  made  by the various annotators, the inter-rater reliability was evaluated.  The  engagement labels  given  to  the  dataset  were  consistent  and  of  excellent  quality,  according  to  the reliability  assessments  that  followed,  which  showed  a  high  degree  of  agreement.

## 5 Result  and  Discussion

This  section  uses  a  variety  of  evaluation  matrices  and  graphs  to  show  and  evaluate the  experimental  data  for  the  provided  models.  Here,  we  show  the  model  accuracy as  well  as  the  validation  loss  for  each  model  that  we  implemented  and  calculated the  validation  accuracy  for  each  model.  Here,  we  also  provide  the  confusion  matrix considering CNN-2  architecture, as well as precision, recall, and F1-score for a specific  class  in  relation  to  the  suggested  models.

## 5.1 Model  Accuracy  and  Validation  Loss

We  started  by  figuring  out  the  validation  accuracy.  Four  alternative  suggested  architectures  have  achieved  validation  accuracy  after  100  complete  epochs.  Next,  we  established  the  model  accuracy  that  was  previously  employed  in  this  research.  Figures  7 and  8  indicate  the  validation  accuracy  after  100  epochs  as  well  as  the  accuracy  of used  models  and  their  area  under  the  roc  curve  (AUC).

ANN:  After  fine-tuning  the  hyperparameters  on  a  trial-and-error  basis,  it  achieved an  accuracy  of  94.4%  and  AUC  of  0.988  and  with  5  fully  connected  dense  layers, consisting of 64, 128, 256, 128, and 32 neurons, with an activation function  of rectified linear unit  (ReLU).  It  has  categorical  cross-entropy  as  loss  function  and adaptive  moment  estimation  (Adam)  is  the  optimizer.  The  output  layer  has  a  softmax activation  function  percent  function.

Fig.  7 Validation  accuracy  after  100  epochs



Fig.  8 Model  accuracy  and  AUC



CNN-1:  After  fine-tuning  the  hyperparameters  on  a  trial-and-error  basis,  it  achieved the accuracy of 94.4%  and  AUC  of  0.988, with 3 fully  connected  dense layers, and  2  convolution  layers,  consisting  of  128  and  256  with  an  activation  function  of rectified linear unit  (ReLU).  It  has  categorical  cross-entropy  as  loss  function  and adaptive  moment  estimation  (Adam)  is  the  optimizer.  The  output  layer  has  a  softmax activation  function.

LSTM:  After  fine-tuning  the  hyperparameters  on  a  trial-and-error  basis,  it  achieved the  accuracy  of  78.3%  and  AUC  of  0.852,  and,  with  3  fully  connected  dense  layers, and  3  LSTM  layers,  consisting  of  64,  128,  and  256  with  an  activation  function  of rectified linear unit  (ReLU).  It  has  categorical  cross-entropy  as  loss  function  and adaptive  moment  estimation  (Adam)  is  the  optimizer.  The  output  layer  has  a  softmax activation  function.

CNN-2:  After  fine-tuning  the  hyperparameters  on  a  trial-and-error  basis,  it  achieved the  accuracy  of  97.1%  and  AUC  of  0.992,  and,  with  3  fully  connected  dense  layers, and  3  convolution  layers,  consisting  of  64,  128,  and  256  with  an  activation  function  of hyperbolic  tangent  function  (Tanh).  It  has  categorical  cross-entropy  as  loss  function and  root-mean-squared-propagation  is  the  optimizer.  The  output  layer  has  a  softmax activation  function.

From  this  assessment,  it  can  be  stated  that  CNN-2  has  outperformed  other  models. Since  CNN-2  has  3  convolution  layers  and  3  fully  connected  dense  layers,  it  has  better accuracy  than  the  rest.  CNN-1-D  typically  works  better  in  time  series,  and  it  has  been proved  here  too.  Though  the  second  model  was  CNN-1-D  too,  it  has  suffered  from fewer  convolution  layers  and  fully  dense  layers.  LSTM  is  another  one  that  is  better

## 5.2 Precision,  Recall,  F1-Score  for  Particular  Class in  Respect  to  the  Proposed  Models

From  Fig.  10,  we  can  describe  that  in  the  'highly  engaged'  class,  CNN-2  outperforms other  neural  network  architecture.  It  has  scored  0.98  in  precision,  which  means  it  can easily  project  the  output  correctly  in  98%  time.  In  recall,  97%  of  the  time,  CNN-2 can  get  the  correct  class  from  the  predicted  class.  In  terms  of  the  F1-score,  it  works best  from  the  rest  of  the  models.  So,  it  can  be  easily  certified  that  CNN-2  is  better neural  network  architecture  among  others  in  predicting  the  'highly  engaged'  class.

In  the  'moderate  engaged'  class,  CNN-2  outperformed  others  with  a  score  of  0.97 in  precision  which  means  only  predicts  wrong  only  3  times  in  a  hundred  times.  In recall,  it  can  predict  the  true  class  99%  of  time,  while  the  F1-score  is  96%.  LSTM stands  last  in  every  criterion  whereas  CNN-1  and  ANN  belong  second  and  third  in every  matrix.  It  can  certainly  be  implied  that  CNN-2  has  predicted  a  better  outcome than  the  rest  of  the  neural  network  architectures  in  the  'moderate  engaged'  class.

Fig.  10 Precision, recall, F1-score for highly engaged, moderately  engaged,  not engaged, and undefined









In  the  'not  engaged'  class,  whether  the  student  is  engaged  or  not,  CNN-2  outperformed  others with a score of 0.95 in precision, which  means  it can predict the student  is  not  engaged  95  times  out  of  100  samples.  Since  the  recall  score  is  0.96,  it can  predict  the  actual  class  96%  of  the  time  and  0.98  in  the  F1-score.  In  this  regard, ANN  stands  second  in  recall  and  F1-score,  while  CNN-1  outperforms  ANN  in  the precision  matrix.

In the 'undefined' class, CNN-2  outperformed  others  with  a  score of 0.98 in precision,  which  means  it  can  predict  the  true  class  98  times  out  of  100  times  from the  predicted  true  class.  It  can  predict  the  'undefined'  class  as  a  true  class  96  times  out of  100  times  from  the  predicted  class,  and  0.95  in  the  F1-score.  In  this  'undefined' class,  ANN  stands  second  in  every  matrix  while  LSTM  stands  last.

## 5.3 Confusion  Matrix

A  confusion  matrix  gives  a  brief  comparison  of  the  model's  predictions  and  the  actual results.  The  matrix  comprises  four  cells:  true  positives  (instances  of  positive  outcomes predicted correctly), false positives (instances of positive outcomes predicted wrongly),  true  negatives  (instances  of  negative  outcomes  predicted  correctly),  and false  negatives  (instances  of  negative  outcomes  predicted  incorrectly).  The  confusion matrix  that  we  obtained  from  our  model  is  shown  in  Fig.  11.  It  aids  in  evaluating a  classification  model's  accuracy,  precision,  recall,  and  other  performance  indicators. Since  the dataset splits into 75:25  for train-test. In the test folder, there are 833  clips  to  evaluate  the  model.  Out  of  833  clips,  211  clips  are  'Highly  Engaged' class,  188  clips  belong  to  the  'Moderate  Engaged'  class,  193  clips  are  labeled  as

Fig.  11 Confusion  matrix  for  our  system  model



'Not  Engaged,'  and  the  rest  of  the  241  clips  are  'Undefined.'  Out  of  211  clips  in  the 'Highly  Engaged'  class,  206  clips  are  predicted  correctly  by  the  model.  183  of  188 clips  from  the  'Moderate  Engaged'  class  are  predicted  correctly,  183  of  193  clips from  the  'Not  Engaged'  are  defined  correctly  by  the  model,  and  237  of  241  clips  are correctly  predicted  by  the  model  as  'Undefined.'

## 5.4 Discussion

After  observing  results  from  validation  accuracy,  loss,  AUC,  and  class-wise  performance,  it  is  certainly  implied  that  CNN-2  has  performed  better  than  the  rest  of  the models.  It  has  3  convolution  layers  that  can  essentially  extract  the  features  and  then the  fully  connected  layers  can  identify  patterns  between  the  input  and  output.  To find specific patterns,  ANN  has  a  reputation  for  doing  a  good  job.  In  this  case,  it can  certainly  be  stated  that  it  has  done  a  better  job  by  placing  itself  in  the  second position  out  of  four  proposed  models.  LSTM  stands  last  in  every  category  while  it generally  works  better  in  time-series  components.  The  reason  could  be  that  since it  is  a  very  computationally  intensive  model,  it  needs  more  data  to  learn.  CNN-1, which  has  two  layers  of  convolution  layers  to  extract  features,  can  certainly  do  better if  it  has  more  convolution  layers.  Since,  in  this  study,  four  models  are  proposed,  we want  to  see  how  the  models  perform  if  the  layers  and  the  parameters  are  reduced  or increased.  CNN-1  could  perform  better  if  there  was  an  extra  convolution  layer.  Train accuracy  is  omitted  for  every  model  because,  in  the  four  proposed  models,  there  are different  parameters  used  so  the  train  accuracy  cannot  be  comparable  among  these four  models.

## 6 Limitations  of  This  Study

The  limited sample  size used to train and evaluate the deep learning model  is a limitation  of  this  study.  Results  would  be  more  reliable  and  generalizable  with  an increased  sample  size.  The  results  may  not  be  applicable  to  other  situations  or  populations  since  the  research  may  have  been  carried  out  in  a  particular  environment  or with  a  particular  group  of  students.  Additionally,  the  research  could  not  have  taken into  consideration  possible  confounding  factors  such  individual  variations  in  sensory processing  or  coexisting  illnesses  that  might  affect  student  participation.  To  confirm and  expand  on  the  results,  further  research  is  required  using  bigger  and  more  differed categories.

## 7 Conclusion

Consequently,  there  is  considerable  potential  for  improving  educational  treatments and  support  for  people  with  ASD.  A  deep  learning-based  approach  to  engagement evaluation  in  students  with  ASD  has  demonstrated  encouraging  outcomes.  Advanced deep  learning  algorithms  combined  with  multimodal  data  integration  have  made  it possible  to  monitor  student  involvement  in  a  way  that  is  more  accurate  and  objective,  which  has  improved  our  comprehension  of  their  learning  styles  and  demands. Scalability  is  a  benefit  of  the  deep  learning-based  technique  since  it  may  be  used in  a  variety  of  educational  contexts  and  can  handle  enormous  datasets.  This  creates opportunities  for  the  long-term  observation  of  student  participation  and  the  gathering of  copious  amounts  of  data  that  may  aid  in  continuing  research  and  the  development of  educational  strategies  for  students  with  ASD.  To  divide  the  students'  degree  of participation  into  four  groups,  we  created  a  study  project  using  CNN-based  architecture.  There  are  four  degrees  of  engagement:  highly  engaged,  moderately  engaged,  not engaged,  and  undefinable.  In  this  study,  we  built  an  annotated  dataset  using  behavioral  cues.  We  created  a  dataset  using  real  classroom  footage,  tagged  it,  and  trained  it using  clips  that  ranged  in  length  from  3  to  8  s.  The  videos  that  were  acquired  by  the camera  are  used  in  this  way  to  extract  data  about  the  body  and  head  attitude.  In  our suggested  method,  a  deep  learning  CNN  classifier  is  built  using  student  video  from the  dataset  and  then  utilized  for  monitoring  and  evaluating  the  participation  of  ASD students.  The  experimental  findings  show  that  the  model  has  a  97.1%  accuracy  rate. According  to  test  findings,  this  approach  for  determining  students'  levels  of  involvement  based  on  visible  student  behaviors  in  the  classroom  setting  yields  a  respectable identification  rate  and  favorable  outcomes.

## 8 Future  Work

In this research, we primarily concentrate on the engagement  categorization for kids  with  ASD  prediction  side.  A  collection  of  3332  annotated  video  clips  has  been created.  But  it  is  useless  in  a  classroom  setting.  Based  on  this  approach,  an  Intelligent Tutor  System  (ITS)  will  be  built  in  the  future  to  help  children  with  ASD  study  more effectively via the use of mobile  or online applications. Evaluating participation from  since  engagement  is  a  cognitive  trait  shared  by  humans,  visual  signals  alone are  insufficient.  Physiological  elements  must  thus  be  present.  In  the  future,  we  will work  on  a  model  that  can  evaluate  a  student's  degree  of  involvement  by  combining behavioral  and  physiological  data.

## 1 Introduction

Learning disability (LD) was initially described in 1963 (Kirk, S.A. (1963)). However, professionals in this field can still not agree on a precise definition of LD (Fletcher, J.M., et al., 2004). Alternately, the techniques  frequently  rely  on  scientific  study  experiments.  The  ''Discrepancy  Model"  (Schrag,  J. (2000).) indicates that there must be a considerable gap between intellectual capacity and academic accomplishment in at least one of the following areas:

- Oral and written expressions
- Normal reading skills
- Listening and reading comprehensions
- Mathematics calculation

Data mining is an interdisciplinary stage of "Knowledge Discovery in Databases" (KDD), and it identifies  patterns  in  large  data  sets  using  artificial  intelligence,  machine  learning,  and  statistical information techniques (Guidelines for Educating Students with Autism Spectrum Disorders", October 2010  Virginia  Department  of  Education,  Office  of  Special  Education  and  Student  Services.). Autism  is  prevalent  among  developing  children  (Felix D.C.C. Beacher et al., 2012). Autism affects the brain's activity and the child's social frame of mind. The categorization task is applied in this research to quantify and estimate the performance of autistic children.

## Ensemble Classifiers for ASD

Three  classifiers  were  chosen  based  on  previous  performance  (Gambino  O.J.,  et  al.,  2016).  The classifiers and their parameters are defined here:

- Multinomial NB. There are no external dependencies. It uses Bayes' theorem. Despite the naive assumption of class conditional independence, this approach produces good results equivalent to more complicated procedures such as neural networks (John G.H., et al., 1995). The classifier's additional soft factor, alpha, was set to 0.5.
- LR. Models the likelihood of events occurring as a linear function of a set of predictor factors. Using a recognition approach makes this algorithm a good classifier (Friedman J., et al., 2001). The inverse of regularisation strength, factor C, was set to 1.0.
- SVM. This approach transforms the real dataset into a higher dimension-a hyper-plane (Joachims T. et al., 1998). SVMs are used to find the best decision boundary for data classification. The class probabilities were determined using the algorithm given by  (Wu T.F., et al., 2004). The kernel coefficient (gamma) was set to 0.00001 and the error term penalty factor (C) 3500.

## Ensemble Classification

It diagnoses new cases by combining the outcome of numerous classifiers whose individual conclusions are integrated via weighted or unweighted voting (Dawson, G., et al., 2000). In this study, ensemble categorization categorizes fresh tweets, including in 𝑛 = 3 classifiers denoted by 𝐶1, 𝐶 2 , … , 𝐶 𝑛. 𝑃𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑗 = 1,2, … , 𝑚. 𝑃𝑖, 1 denotes the probability created by the classifier 𝐶𝑖 that the q -th tweet 𝑡 𝑞 belongs  to  class L1, Pi,2 the  probability  that  it  belongs  to  the  class 𝐿2 and  so  on  for the m classes

## 1 Introduction

Artificial intelligence, or AI for short, has become a particularly powerful tool in the healthcare field. It offers innovative solutions for a wide variety of medical conditions, including mental health disorders such as childhood depression. Ai-assisted treatment has received significant attention because it has the potential to provide personalized and adaptive interventions. These interventions can meet the different needs of each patient. With the help of advanced algorithms and the capabilities of machine learning, artificial intelligence can provide personalized and adaptive solutions to meet the unique needs of each individual. This is particularly crucial in the case of children with special needs, as the traditional approach of treating all children in one way often fails to meet the requirements. Autism spectrum disorder is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by obstacles in social communication and interaction, as well as some repetitive and limited behaviors [1]. When exploring the possibility of artificial intelligence addressing the special needs of children with autism, this study found that autism spectrum disorder requires specially designed educational intervention measures to meet the needs of children at different developmental stages [2]. Although traditional methods, such as applied behavior analysis and treatment and educational approaches for children with autism and related communication disorders, It has been proved to be effective, but these methods have been criticized for being inflexible enough to adapt well to the specific needs and preferences of each person [3]. However, by introducing an adaptive feedback mechanism, artificial intelligence can adjust the teaching content according to the specific circumstances of students to meet their needs [4]. Artificial intelligence can analyze a large amount of data to identify the patterns within it, and then customize intervention measures based on these to ensure that each child can receive the most effective support. ## Abstract

This article studies the application of artificial intelligence-assisted gamification therapy in children with autism spectrum disorder of different ages. The autism spectrum disorder mentioned here is what we commonly refer to as ASD children. This research combines gamification and artificial intelligence technology to provide children with personalized learning materials to improve their skills in language, social interaction and emotion. These projects will offer personalized advice to children with autism, plan learning paths suitable for them, and provide timely feedback to help them solve specific problems they encounter. This approach also designs courses based on different development stages and creates some sensory stimulating activities for children who haven't started to speak yet. Design tools that can help vocabulary development for children who are just beginning to learn languages, and design communication exercises for children with stronger learning abilities.
