## Paper Source: An Intelligent E-Learning System for Autistic Children Multi-Agent Architecture
============================================================

## An Intelligent E-Learning System for Autistic Children: Multi-Agent Architecture



Najoua Tahiri ( &amp; ) and Mohamed El Alami

National School of Applied Sciences of Tangier, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tangier, Morocco

najoua.tahiri@gmail.com, elalami-hassouni@ensat.ac.ma

Abstract. E-learning systems are the result of the new era of digitalization, which has affected many areas including education. These systems offer many bene fi ts like ease of access and time management. Therefore, the educational paradigm has been changed. Otherwise, since E-learning systems consider only the cognitive state of the learner regardless of his emotional state, they cannot instruct students effectively. Moreover, if the target learner has non-ordinary cognitive and socio-emotional abilities, such as a child with ASD (Autism Spectrum Disorder). So, the e-learning system must be able to satisfy those needs and propose a suitable content according to his learning rhythm.

This paper proposes a new multi-agent architecture of an emotional intelligent e-learning system, it aims to help ASD children overcome learning impairments. The proposed architecture is based on several agents, endowing to address emotional, cognitive and pedagogical issues intelligently. They are working in a collaborative and cooperative fashion to provide the appropriate content.

Keywords: Multi-agent architecture  E-learning  Intelligent learning system  Affective computing  Autism

## 1 Introduction

In recent years, the educational paradigm has been changed due to the arrival of E-learning concept. It stems from the ongoing incorporation of technology into learning and education environments. For Som [1]: E-learning refers to the systematic use of networked information and communications technology in teaching and learning. Also, Henry [2] de fi nes E-learning as the appropriate application of the Internet to support the delivery of learning, skills and knowledge in a holistic approach not limited to any particular courses, technologies, or infrastructures. Similarly, Jenkins et al. describe E-learning as learning facilitated and supported through the utilization of information and communication technologies (ICTs) [3]. In brief, there are several de fi nitions of E-learning but all de fi nitions overall describe the use of electronic tools in the process of learning. However, these systems adopt the one-size- fi ts-all strategy of delivering content to a passive learner. They have undergone several changes from computer-based training program until the appearance of the arti fi cial intelligence. Consequently, a new generation of Intelligent E-learning Systems (ILS) has started to overcome challenges of classical E-learning systems [4, 5].



ILS derives from an approach known as ITS (intelligent tutoring system) which has been pursued by researchers in education, psychology, and arti fi cial intelligence. The goal of ITS is to provide the bene fi ts of one-to-one instruction. It enables learners to practice their skills by carrying out tasks within highly interactive learning environments [6]. While establishing better emotional interaction with the learner through an intelligent E-learning system requires interpreting his socio-emotional reactions in order to provide a personalized instruction adapted to his knowledge, learning abilities and his needs. Existing intelligent E-learning systems support only the cognitive aspect of the learner by neglecting his emotional state.

Many research studies in neuroscience and psychology show the relevance of emotions in the learning process as a substrate that can promote a better development of cognitive functions. Damasio [7] has elucidated the neural bases of emotions as well as the strong link between emotion and certain cognitive processes such as attention, memory, perception and decision-making.

Including emotions in such computerized process require incorporation of Affective Computing. It is a fi eld of interdisciplinary research that involves studying the interaction between technology and feelings, including giving machines the ability to recognize, express, synthesize and model emotions [8].

Emotionally aware systems are regarded as a considerable and valuable educational technique particularly for children with special cognitive needs such as ASD children who do not respond naturally to linear curricular delivery, but rather need an educational model incorporating intra and interpersonal development skills.

In this perspective, the article fi rst draws up the related work to ILS based on multiagent architecture. Then, it establishes the proposed architecture of an intelligent elearning system for autistic children. Third, it describes a discussion and future work section. Conclusions are presented in the last section of this paper.

## 2 Related Work

Affective Computing is computing that relates to, arises from, or deliberately in fl uences emotion or other affective phenomena [8]. It is an interdisciplinary fi eld covering computer science, psychology and cognitive science. In its simplest form, emotional learning characterizes the emotional area of learning re fl ected in the beliefs, values, interests, and behaviors of learners [9]. Emotional learning is concerned with how learners feel while they are learning, as well as how learning experiences are internalized so that they can guide learner attitudes, opinions, and behavior [10]. The main application of affective computing includes emotional perception, emotional understanding and emotional expression.

Many research studies are related to intelligent E-learning systems, some are based on the multi-agent architecture (MAS), while others are still using the traditional software architecture. The common goal of all these systems is to foster learning by ensuring some features such as interactivity, adaptability and collaboration.

During a process of learning, more the learner is interested and attracted by the training, more his concentration increases and vice versa. Hence, the learner ' s behavior changes according to his feelings. The authors [11] propose an E-learning system model is composed of two agents: learner and teacher, it integrates a new component called affective computing module. Learner ' s emotions are collected through facial expressions and analyzed at this level. Afterward, the teacher agent change the pedagogical content based on result of emotional module in order to regulate learner emotional state.

Moreover, BOKHARI-Intelligent Multi-agent based E-learning System [12] is built on a four layers: user level, web level, system level and data level. The focus of the BOKHARI system is to incorporate many features like intelligence, accessibility, interactivity into a single system. Also, Daomin describes in his paper [13] a multiagent based E-learning system MAELITS applying the methodology of case-based reasoning. This system selects and deliver appropriate oriented object learning courseware based on SCORM and according to student ' s cognitive ability for individual student. Four agents (courseware interface, examination, courseware recommendation, and activity data collection) interact with E-learning curriculum creation model that is responsible on delivering the appropriate pedagogical content. However, these two systems (BOKHARI and MAELITS) do not include the emotional state of the learner.

About intelligent learning systems based on MAS architecture for autistic children, we quote the application of an agent-based approach proposed by Sehaba et al. [14], it aims to the rehabilitation of children with autism, where the multi-agent system represents the child ' s pro fi le, the expert ' s directives and the dynamics of their interactions analyze of child ' s behavior in order to adapt the activities execution.

Also, Barakova et al. [15] have developed an interactive multi-agent platform of 15 blocks with emergent behavior. It consists of building blocks that interact when positioned in each other ' s vicinity. These blocks can interact by detecting their neighbors through the built-in sensors, and show behavior in response to their sensory stimulation.

Despite the burgeoning need to consider new ways of providing ef fi cient educational services, which adopt one-to-one teaching techniques for ASD children, we noticed that intelligent learning systems based on multi-agent architecture are very rare.

## 3 Proposed Work

This work proposes the architecture of an intelligent learning system for ASD children. It ' s spin-off NEOCAMPUS2 [16], an agent factory that helps designing and implementing intelligent agents. It directly provides a modular agent architecture, quite complete which if required, other modules could be easily added. On the other hand, it is the only one that facilitates affective and fuzzy computation. It also offers extensive built-in possibilities for cooperation and control of agents.

Fig. 1. Proposed system architecture



NEOCAMPUS [17] is a platform for the design and implementation of intelligent agents, with an extensive history in the production of very diverse prototypes, fundamentally, in the fi eld of intelligent e-learning systems. Among them, we can quote MEDIC, FINANCE, FILTER, AFFECTION and ENT. MEDIC [18] is an intelligent elearning system simulating the functioning of a medical center: its departments, fi nance, and managerial problems. A set of junior managers can learn to solve the different problems or incidents happening in the center daily life. FINANCE [19] is another intelligent e-learning system for learning fi nancial or managerial accountant and fi rm analysis. Also, Diautis a multi-agent platform [20] that offers a wide and variable collection of tests to diagnosis ASD children, including computerized interviews with parents, using sensors to analyze the interaction of the child through the monitoring of ocular activity, the observation of movements, as well as the interpretation of vocal responses.

So, the proposed architecture bene fi ts from NEACAMPUS ' s capabilities and functionalities, including affective computing and the use of pedagogic agents.

The main objective of this work is to foster learning by taking into account the ASD learner ' s cognitive, emotional and pedagogical speci fi cations. Accordingly, we chose multi-agent based approach. The type of proposed architecture is heterogeneous communicating MAS where agents are of different models and granularity. The communication between agents stands on cooperation to break down the problems into sub problems and solve them more easily.

Several agent architectures used different representation approaches for their reasoning mechanism and propose different types of mental attitudes in order to solve a variety of problems. Particulary, the most adopted is the BDI (beliefs, desires, and intentions) architecture, originally proposed by Bratman [21] as a philosophical theory of the practical reasoning. It is a deliberative agent architecture where actions are derived from a practical reasoning process composed of two steps:

1. The deliberation (of goals), a set of desires is selected to be achieved, according to the current situation of the agent ' s beliefs.

2. The determination of how these concrete goals produced as a result of the previous step can be achieved by means of the available options for the agent [22].

Since BDI architecture provides a description of behavior at a much higher level, in terms of mental attitudes. It allows agents to be more autonomous and proactive. The straightforward connection between BDI architecture and emotional abilities constitutes an argument in favor of using BDI agents in simulations where emotional abilities are needed such as the proposed architecture.

The suggested architecture incorporates serious learning games as pedagogical activities that insure the child ' s engagement; it allows teaching pedagogical concepts implicitly through games and receiving the perception of the child in the reverse circuit.

And in order to provide the appropriate serious learning games according to the emotional, cognitive, pedagogical and sensory aspects of the child learner, the authors propose to use the KASP [23] methodology to allow a better design of the games. It is a new methodology of designing serious learning games for children with learning disabilities in order to improve their learning rhythm and improve their emotional state related to learning in a playful and interactive environment.

Figure 1 shows the general architecture of the system. It includes several agents:

- Emotional agent : It constantly analyzes the learner ' s emotional state along the proposed pedagogical activities using the information provided by the sensors. It communicates with the cognitive agents to obtain the necessary inputs for the analysis of the emotional state of the learner.
- Cognitive agent : Cooperating with emotional agents to analyze the learner ' s reactions of cognitive origin, they measure the learner ' s ability to learn a speci fi c concept.
- Pedagogic agent : Receive instructions from emotional and cognitive agents to accompany the learner in learning sessions by promoting his interest in the learning object. Following the data collected through sensors, it identi fi es pedagogical gaps of the child.
- Interface agent : It is the communication bridge between the user and the system. It proposes a personalized content considering the actual situation of the learner. It collaborates with game selector agent in order to customize game interface according orders getting from decision agent.
- Evaluation agent : Responsible for obtaining the evaluation of the learner ' s reactions using the inputs provided by the cognitive, emotional and pedagogic agents; Also responsible for updating and storing user ' s models in knowledge base.
- Decision agent : It establishes new orders for game selector agents and interface agents based on evaluation agent requests and recommendations.
- Game selector agent : It searches for nearby scenarios in the serious learning game database. For each particular situation, game selector agents may react differently by using the inputs supplied by decision agents.
- Report generator agent : It allows monitoring the child ' s progress through reports generated for parents or instructors in order to recognize behavioral, socioemotional state and offer a parallel support in his daily life.

The agents are based on BDI (beliefs, desires, and intentions) architecture. The BDI approach has been proposed in Arti fi cial Intelligence to represent the way agents can do complex reasoning. The proposed architecture is used to monitor the learning process of an ASD child through an intelligent E-learning system that takes into account three aspects: cognitive, emotional, and pedagogical.

The proposed architecture is based on MAS, and bene fi ts from the potential of cooperation, which is an effective way of communication between agents, and the capacity of learning from children ' s interactions as well. Thus, it allows to build a system for different types of people revolving around autistic children, which are parents, clinical staff that includes speech therapists, psychiatrists, pediatricians and ASD specialists (applied behavior analysts), and tutors such as teaching assistants, support assistants and educational professionals.

## 4 Future Work

The proposed architecture could be used not only for ASD children but it can also serve children with learning disabilities since autism and learning disability are co-associated. According to the NHS Information Centre, Community and Mental Health Team [24], between 31 and 35.4% of people with a learning disability are autistic. It will also improve diagnosis of ASD children through the acquisition of children ' s mental models.

As part of the continuity of this work, we attempt to develop an exhaustive platform that includes a system based on the current architecture and helps ASD children as a coach in their learning, from diagnostic stage until the progress monitoring, offering a computerized psychological tools and a personalized pedagogical activity by way of serious learning games. The future platform will also offer effective tools intended to assist pedagogical and medical team revolving around ASD children.

## 5 Conclusion

The learning environment has a signi fi cant impact on children with ASD. Careful consideration should be given to the physical, sensory and social environment when supporting them to access learning opportunities. The proposed architecture is based on the multi-agent approach and integrates affective computing as one of its main components. Each agent treats a speci fi c area of knowledge and collaborates with other agents to provide instructional content appropriate to the learning style as well as the emotional state of the ASD child. Furthermore, multi-agent architecture presents a better approach to provide a collaborative environment; it offers several advantages, among them the scalability that allows equipping the system with new capabilities by simply adding new agents.

## Paper Source: An Intelligent LEGO Tutoring System for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
============================================================



## An Intelligent LEGO Tutoring System for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder

Qiming Sun

School of Electrical and Computer Engineering Georgia Institute of Technology - Shenzhen Shenzhen, Guangdong, China qiming@gatech.edu

## ABSTRACT

Prior studies have shown  the effectiveness  of  LEGO-based activities to improve children's social skills, especially those with autism  spectrum  disorder  (ASD).  In  such  activities,  teachers  are expected to provide instructions/guidance and facilitate communication  among  children  during  their  collaborative  play. When  the  ratio  of  children  to  teacher  increases,  an  intelligent monitoring system could be very helpful to prompt the teachers of any  necessary  intervention,  or  to  provide  children  some  trivial feedback so that their teachers could focus on other tasks. In this paper,  we  propose  such  a  system  to  assist  both  teachers  and children in playing with LEGO bricks. At first, teachers may use the system to create some models. The system will then generate step-by-step  instructions  in  both  visual  and  auditory  forms.  In addition, the system can track the children's brick-building process  in  real  time  and  provide  some  feedback  when  any mistakes were made. Two cameras with a unique image recognition module are used to capture the 3D structure of LEGO bricks.

## CCS Concepts

· Human-centered  computing ➝ Accessibility  systems  and tools      ·  Computing  methodologies ➝ Visual  inspection      · Applied computing ➝ Computer-assisted instruction

## Keywords

LEGO therapy; intelligent tutoring system; autism; children

## 1. INTRODUCTION

LEGO bricks are one of the most common toys among children. In  this  paper,  we  proposed  a  prototype  of  intelligent  tutoring system  to  help  young  children  with  ASD  (aged  3  to  5)  to  play with  LEGO  bricks.  The  system  can  recognize  the  structure  of bricks using two cameras and monitor the children's work in real time.  The  teachers  may  use  a  separate  terminal  to  create  new structures (models) and the system can automatically generate the corresponding  instructions  in  both  visual  and  auditory  form  for each building step. This work extends our previous work reported in [1]. In the previous work we used a camera to recognize LEGO

At  the  current  stage,  the  system  can  recognize  and  provide feedback when a user has completed all tasks or made a mistake in the meantime. In the future, more complex brick combinations will  be  supported,  and  more  modalities  will  be  designed  for  the users, e.g. speech recognition, motion, tactile, etc.

## 2. RELATED WORK

Children  with  ASD,  as  young  as  18  months  age,  could  benefit from  early  intervention  [5,  6].  LEGO  bricks,  which  are  very popular among children, including toddlers, have been used as a therapeutic medium to enhanced children's social communication skills [2, 3, 4]. One of the reasons to use it is the predictability in constructing  an  assigned  structure,  which  could  make  children with  ASD  feel  more  comfortable  than  playing  in  a  free-play environment.  To  promote  communication,  teachers  may  assign children with various roles so that they will collaborate to build a structure following a set of clear instructions. Meanwhile, teachers may also intervene by helping and encouraging them.

Recently, technology-based intervention using LEGO play, including  LEGO  robots,  have  also  been  introduced  to  children with  ASD  [7,  8].  Using  machine  learning  technology,  some hobbyists  have  also  developed  LEGO  brick  sorting  machines which  could  recognize  and  classify  various  bricks.  However, using  LEGO in  an  intelligent  tutoring  system  for  improving  the social communication skills of children with ASD is rare, which motivates our study here. In the next section, we will describe the functionalities of our proposed system, its design, and architecture.

## 3. SYSTEM DESIGN AND CORE MODULES

Following our previous system in [1], our current system consists of two separate modules: a tutor's module and a child's module.

The  tutor's  module  allows  teachers/parents  to  design  a  new scheme/model of LEGO bricks, which consists of its construction steps.  At  this  stage,  our  design  aims  for  LEGO  Duplo®  bricks, and  the  maximum  dimension  of  the  model  is  20  20  20  cm. Indeed, a larger model or smaller pieces could be supported when better cameras with higher resolution are used.

The child's module  will load an assigned model, generate instructions  for  the  children,  and  monitor  the  building  process automatically.  Ideally,  both  visual  and  voice  instructions  will  be used to guide users in constructing the model.

1 Corresponding author

When a mistake was made by a user, the  system shall detect it, remind  the  user  (e.g.  'not  the  green  one'),  and  provide  an instruction  to  correct  it  (e.g.  'replace  it  with  a  blue  one').  At current prototype, all instructions are provided by the application designer and cannot be customized.

## 3.1 Setup and Working Environment

As shown in Fig. 1, two cameras are put at the front- and rightside of the user, facing the working area. The visual instructions for the user are shown on the screen. The user needs to complete the  assigned  LEGO  bricks  in  the  working  area.  The  computer processes the frames from two cameras, figures out the current 3D structure of the bricks, compared  them  with  the  goal, and generates instructions and feedback for the user.

Figure 1. The setup of the tutoring system.



To  achieve  the  best  accuracy  of  brick  recognition,  the  ambient light  should  be  bright  enough  and  the  cameras  should  have  a minimum resolution of 1280x720 pixels.

## 3.2 Brick Recognition Module

Currently,  our  proposed  system  can  recognize  three  different shapes  (long,  short,  curved),  and  three  colors  (red,  green,  blue) from  basic  LEGO  Duplo®  bricks,  as  shown  in  Fig.  2.  To determine the shape of a brick, we use the ratio of its length to its height. For example, the long brick has ratio approximately 3.3:1, and the short one is 1.6:1.

Figure 2. A set of bricks recognized by our system. [1]



Figure 3. A set of annotations generated from one camera's frame. [1]



At  first,  the  system  separately  annotates  the  bricks  from  2D frames  captured  by  each  camera,  then  synthesize  two  sets  of annotations together to detect the shape of bricks. For example, if one  camera  annotates  a  brick  with  'long  brick',  and  the  other camera annotates the same brick with 'short brick', then the real shape of the brick should be a long one since its planar projection shows  differently  on  the  two  sides.  Fig.  3  shows  a  set  of annotations generated from one camera only (reported in [1]).

Figure 4. The process of frames from two cameras for deciding the 3D structures.



Fig. 4 shows the flowchart of how the 3D structures of bricks are recognized.  To  annotate  the  frames,  our  proposed  system  uses several  functions  in  OpenCV  library  to  process  the  frames  and generate brick contours [9]. First, the pixels in a frame is filtered based on their RGB values, and the pixels with a color other than or not closed to red, green, and blue will be replaced with a whitecolor  pixel.  Then,  the  system  computes  the  derivatives  of  each frame on both x- and y- axis using an extended Sobel operator and subtract  them  to  make  the  contours  clearer.  Noises  are  then removed  by  using  threshold-based  filters  and  blur  functions  in OpenCV. A grayscale image will be sent to OpenCV's findContour function. For each contour from the result, a minimum  rotated  rectangle  that  contains  the  contour  will  be calculated. The system finally filters the rectangles based on their areas,  sloops,  length-width  ratios,  and  positions.  The  remaining rectangles will be considered as bricks and annotated respectively.

## 3.3 Layout Recognition Module

To represent each brick's position in a 3D space, the program uses a unique coordinate system. The coordinate system annotates the 3D  structure  of  bricks  thus  allows  the  comparison  between different  brick  layouts.  As  shown  in  Fig.  5,  the  system  fits  the bricks into three axes. The x, y values depend on the left corner's projections on each axis, and the z value is based on the number of layers. Furthermore, for non-square bricks, symbol '-' or '|' are used to represent a brick which is parallel or vertical to the x-axis, respectively. For instance, the brick structure shown in Fig. 5 can be annotated in text by (assuming the green brick is a short one):

long blue 0 0 1 |

short green 2 0 1

long red 0 0 2 -

The annotations are generated after the brick-recognition process, and the result  will  be  compared  with  the  model  assigned by  the teacher to determine the correctness of the built.

Figure 5. The coordinate system to represent bricks' positions.



## 4. CURRENT PROTOTYPES

## 4.1 The Tutor's Module

The  tutor's  module  is  designed  for  teachers  to  generate  their LEGO models. Fig. 6 shows the user interface of the software, in which teachers can select and put the supported bricks to the grid on the left part. Then they can click 'output scheme' to save the structures  as  a  completed  model  into  the  computer  and,  later, assign it as a task to the children. Since only two cameras are used, teachers are advised to put the bricks from the left-upper corner to the  right  and  bottom,  so  that  each  additional  brick  could  be recognized or seen by either or both cameras.

Figure 6. The user interface of the tutor's terminal.



## 4.2 The Child's Module

Fig.  7  shows  the  user  interface  of  the  child's  module.  The interface  is  built  using cvui library  [10].  Two  cameras  track  the bricks  in  real  time  and  their  frames  are  shown  on  the  two  left windows.  When  a  teacher  loads  a  new  task,  the  system  will automatically generate a preview window for the children and the subtasks.  At  each  subtask,  instruction  on  which  brick  should  be picked will be given in both visual and auditory form. The current subtask  is  labelled  with  a  star  on  the  preview  window  (see  the right  window  in  Fig.  7).  When  the  child  correctly  put  a  brick, voice  feedback  'Great!'  will  be  played  and  the  corresponding brick in the preview window will be ticked. The voice feedback is generated using the text to speech service provided by Baidu TM .

As shown in Fig. 7, the system asks for a red long brick, but the user picks a red short brick. In this case, the mistake is automatically marked in the front camera's view, and a notification 'check again' appears.

Figure 7. The user interface of the child's terminal.



## 5. DISCUSSIONS

In  summary,  we  have  proposed  an  intelligent  system  to  help children with ASD in playing with LEGO bricks. The system is an extension  of  our  previous  work  reported  in  [1].  The  system  can generate step-by-step guidance for a model defined by a teacher. Although  our  current  system  can  accurately  recognize  a  certain number  of  LEGO  structure,  some  combinations  may  not  be recognized  well,  even  using  two  cameras.  For  instance,  when  a center  brick  is  surrounded/covered  by  others,  then  it  may  be unseen  from  both  camera  POVs.  To  solve  it,  we  may  install additional cameras; however, they may increase the computational complexity  of  the  system.  Alternatively,  we  may  restrict  the teachers from designing a model which consists of such subtasks.

In the future, improvements  will be made  to increase the compatibility of different structures. Also, more interactive methods  and  feedback  will  be  considered  to  make  the  system more interesting to be played with.

This work has been done while the first author is with Wenzhou-Kean University. We wish to thank Tiffany Tang for her constructive comments.

## Paper Source: Audio Signal Recognition Based on Intervals' Numbers (INs) Classification Techniques
============================================================

## Audio Signal Recognition Based on Intervals' Numbers (INs) Classification Techniques

Chris Lytridis, Eleni Vrochidou, George Sidiropoulos, George Α . Papakostas, Vassilis G. Kaburlasos Human-Machines Interaction Laboratory (HUMAIN-Lab) International Hellenic University

Kavala, Greece

{ lytridic, evrochid, georsidi, gpapak, vgkabs } @teiemt.gr

Abstract -Speech  is  one  of  the  major  human-machine interaction modalities and it is especially important in the case of  special  education  using  social  robots.  Although  modern speech  recognition  engines  can  effectively  deal  with  normal human-robot  conversations,  there  are  instances  in special education where additional word detection and word comparison capabilities are needed to run in parallel with the typical conversation flow. This paper investigates the efficiency of a word detection method based on intervals' numbers.

Keywords-Speech recognition, Human-machine interaction, Intervals' numbers (IN)

## I. INTRODUCTION

Scientists in the field of socially intelligent robotics focus on developing robots capable of exhibiting natural-appearing social qualities [1]. Beyond the basic capabilities of moving and acting autonomously, social robots need to communicate with humans in a social and engaging manner. Dialogue is the main joint process of communication [2], [3]. Humans employ a variety of linguistic social cues (i.e. words or phrases that reveal sympathy, empathy, encouragement etc.) to regulate a dialogue. These cues would also be effective for controlling human-robot interaction, which is important due to the current robots' perception (e.g. speech processing) limits [4]. Thus, in order to improve the quality of human-robot interaction, it is essential for social robots to be capable of guiding a dialogue towards  specific  directions,  so  as,  for  example,  to  serve specific therapeutic intervention purposes.

Towards this end, the methodology presented in this paper is intended to serve the latter purpose; contribute towards the design of therapeutic interventions for children with learning disabilities or Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) where speech is the basic communication channel of child-robot interaction. More  specifically,  in  this  work  trigger  words  to  regulate  a conversation and guide the therapeutic activities are represented by Interval Numbers (INs). An IN is an established  mathematical  object  [5],  [6]  that  may  represent either  a  fuzzy  interval  or  a  distribution  of  numbers.  A proposed k nearest neighbor (kNN) classification scheme is adopted  to  recognize  the  trigger  words.  This  method  is especially designed to be a computationally inexpensive tool used in conjunction with the robots' build-in speech recognition engine.

The proposed technique falls into Lattice Computing (LC) paradigm.  LC  techniques  are  expected  to  be  beneficial  to human-robot interaction applications, since they can deal with both numerical and non-numerical data (e.g. verbal cues) and facilitate computations with semantics. Moreover, LC techniques  can deal with fuzzy sets,  engage  logic  and reasoning and can process data fast [7], [8].

Speech  recordings  may  result  in  big  data, therefore efficient data representation and processing are essential. The

This research has been co -financed by the European Union and Greek national funds through the Operational Program Competitiveness, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, under the call RESEARCH -CREATE

The layout of the paper is as follows: Section II briefly outlines the theoretical background of LC and INs. Section III describes  the  proposed  experimental  methods.  Section  IV presents  the  experimental  results.  Section  V  concludes  by discussing  the  contribution  of  the  paper  and  the  related upcoming work.

## II. THEORETICAL BACKGROUND

In  this  section, the  hierarchy  of lattices  from  Level-0 to Level-2, resulting to the lattice of INs [5], [6], [9] is presented.

## A. Application of INs

The  application  of  INs  to  Neural  Networks  (NNs)  and Fuzzy  Inference  Systems  (FIS)  have  been  reported  in  the literature [6], [8], [10]-[12].

In  [6],  an  LC  extension  of  a  fuzzy  neural  classifies  for human  facial  expression  recognition  was  presented.  The reported advantages of working with INs are the incremental real-time  learning  and  generalization  based  on  fuzzy  lattice reasoning (FLR) techniques. The proposed classifier performs efficiently, demonstrating the capability  of  INs to represent partially ordered non-numeric and nonstationary data (i.e. data semantics). The effectiveness of INs in demonstrated in [10]; accommodation of granular data, introduction of tunable nonlinearities and induction of descriptive decision-making knowledge  from  the  data,  are  some  of  the  additionally reported  advantages  of  INs  application  in  three  different benchmark problems. In [11] INs represent a distribution of image features for the recognition of  image patterns. An FLR classifier is developed to learn distributions of INs, and four well-known benchmark image pattern recognition applications  are  demonstrated.  In  [12]  novel  schemes  for tunable fuzzy rule interpolation and extrapolation are presented, based on INs. Preliminary application involves the reconstruction of partially occluded human facial expressions based on a NN.

In all aforementioned applications of INs, the algorithm CALCIN  is  used  for  inducing  an  IN  from  a  distribution. Despite its proven performance, CALCIN has been met with criticism because of the fact that the induced IN does not retain a  clear  statistical  interpretation.  An  extension  of  CALCIN, namely algorithm distrIN, was proposed in response, in order to provide a straightforward, statistical interpretation [8]. The pilot  application  of  distrIN  that  was  presented  in  [8],  uses electroencephalography  (EEG)  signals  with  significant  data reduction  without  losing  the  statistical  features  of  the  data. The kNN classification scheme was used to demonstrate the effectiveness  of  the  newly  proposed  technique,  resulting  in good  classification  performances  compared  to  alternative state-of-the-art methods in the literature.

## B. Lattice Hierarchy

This section presents a  hierarchy of lattices,  resulting in the lattice of INs. The analytic theory of FLR is presented in [5], [6], [11].

A lattice is a partially ordered set ( L , ⊑ ) with the property that any  two elements x,  y ∈ L have  both  a greatest lower bound (infimum) represented by x ⊓ y and a least upper bound (supremum) represented by x ⊔ y .  If  in a  lattice  ( L , ⊑ ) every pair ( x, y ) satisfies either x ⊑ y or x ⊐ y then the lattice ( L , ⊑ ) is totally-ordered. A lattice ( L , ⊑ ) is called complete if each of its  subsets X has  both an infimum and a supremum in L .  A non-void complete lattice contains both a least element and a greatest element symbolized by o and i , respectively [5].

- 1) Level-0; the lattice ( 𝑅 &amp; , ≤ ) of Real Numbers: Consider the  totally-ordered  complete  lattice  ( 𝑅 &amp; , ≤ ),  where 𝑅 &amp; = 𝑅 ∪ {-∞,+∞} with  least  and  greatest  elements -∞ and +∞ , respectively.  The  corresponding  infimum  and  supremum operations are symbolized by ˄ and ˅ , respectively.
- 2) Level-1; the lattice ( 𝐼, ⊆ ) of Type-1 intervals: Considering a1,a2 ∈ 𝑅 &amp; such that a1 ≤ a2 , a Type-1 interval A = [ a1, a2 ] is defined as [ a1, a2 ] = { x : x ∈ 𝑅 &amp; and a1 ≤ x ≤ a2 }.  The  set  of  Type-1  intervals  in 𝑅 &amp; (including  the  empty interval) is symbolized by I1. The lattice ( 𝐼 1 , ⊆ ) is a complete lattice, where ⊆ is  the  set  theoretic inclusion.  Considering two intervals A = [ a1, a2 ] and B = [ b1,b2 ] in I1 , their infimum ( ∩ ) is given by 𝐴 ∩ 𝐵 = 𝑎 1 ∨ 𝑏 1 , 𝑎 8 ∧ 𝑏 8 , if and only if 𝑎1 ∨ 𝑏1 ≤	𝑎8 ∧ 𝑏 8 , and their supremum ( ∪ ̇ ) is given by 𝐴 ∪ ̇ 𝐵 = 𝑎1 ∧ 𝑏 1 , 𝑎 8 ∨ 𝑏 8 .

Given of (1) a positive valuation function v : L à 𝑅= &gt; , and (2) a dual isomorphic function θ : L à L in lattice ( L , ≤ ), results a  positive  valuation  function v 1: L ´ L à 𝑅= &gt; in  lattice  ( L ´ L , ≥ ´ ≤ ) of generalized intervals , is given by v1 ([ a,b ])= v ( θ ( a ))+ v ( b ).  Therefore, both a metric  function 𝑑1 (. , . ) and two  fuzzy  order  functions 𝜎⊓ (. , . ) and 𝜎⊔ (. , . ) ,  can  be defined. The following three functions are available in ( Ι 1 , ⊑ ).

The two fuzzy order functions are introduced as 𝜎⊓ (𝑥, 𝑦) = F(G⊓H) F(G) ,  namely σ -meet,  and 𝜎⊔ (𝑥, 𝑦) = F(H) F(G⊔H) , namely σ -join.

Parametric functions ν (.)  and θ (.)  can  be  selected  with various ways  and  may  introduce  tunable  nonlinearities towards optimal classification schemes.

- 3) Level-2;  The  lattice  (F1, ≤ )  of  INs: A  Generalized Intervals' Number (GIN) is defined as a function f : [0,1] à ( 𝑅 &amp; ´ 𝑅 &amp; , ≥ ´ ≤ )  where  ( 𝑅 &amp; ´ 𝑅 &amp; , ≥ ´ ≤ ) is a lattice  of generalized intervals. Assume G the set of GINs. Then, the ( G , ⊑ )  is  a  complete lattice. The interest  is  focused  to the sublattice of IN. An IN, is defined as a function F : [0,1] à I 1, which satisfies the following:

- ∀𝑋 ⊆ [0,1] : ⋂ L∈X 𝐹L = 𝐹 ∨Y

The set F1 of INs is a partially ordered, complete lattice, which is denoted as (F1, ≼ ). An IN is interpreted as a grain of information [5]. It has been shown that the set F1 is a metric lattice with cardinality equal to the infinity ℵ 1 of set R of the real numbers. In other words, there are so many ΙΝ s, as real numbers.

The  proposed  distrIN  algorithm  is  presented  in  Fig.1. Assume a speech signal recording as shown in Fig.1(a). All the different speech signal values of Fig.1(a) can form a set of n +1 sorted real numbers x0 &lt; x1 &lt;…&lt; xn .  i.e.  a  distribution function. An IN, equivalently, can be represented as a set of intervals Fh , h ∈ [0,1],  which  is  the  interval-representation, shown in Fig.1(b), or as a function F(x) = ∨ 𝒉∈[𝟎,𝟏] {𝒉:𝒙 ∈ 𝑭 𝒉 } ,

which is the membership-function-representation, shown in Fig.1(c).  As  expected,  audio  signals  representing  the  same spoken  word  produce  very  similar  distributions,  even  for different  speaker  voices.  However,  different  spoken  words produce audio signals which result in more varied distribution shapes,  and  are  therefore  distinguishable.  Note  that  the membership-function-representation  of  the  induced  IN  is identical to the corresponding distribution function. This is a straightforward representation with a clear statistical interpretation. An IN is represented by L intervals all having the  same end,  where only one of the intervals is trivial  by construction.  In  conclusion,  it  takes  L  real  numbers  to represent  an  IN.  An  IN  also  represents  a  distribution,  i.e. orders of magnitude more than L.

## III. EXPERIMENTAL METHODS

The word classification experiments were conducted using the  spoken  digits  open  dataset  found  in  [13].  The  dataset contains 2000 recordings of English utterances of digits 'zero' to 'nine' by four speakers. The audio signals were extracted from the audio files and were converted to INs, each described by 32 cuts, as described in the previous section. This resulted in the creation of 2000 INs, i.e. 200 INs per class.

## A. Classification

For the classification tasks, the kNN classification method was employed with a 'leave-one-out' approach. This approach was selected because of its reliability, given that the amount of our training data was not prohibitively large. Table I shows how the INs are arranged for a classification task.

TABLE I. ARRANGEMENT OF INS FOR THE CLASSIFICATION TASK

|             | List of INs   | List of INs   | Label   |
|-------------|---------------|---------------|---------|
| Subject1    | IN 1,1        | IN 1,32       | ZERO    |
| ⋮           | ⋮             | ⋮             | ⋮       |
| Subject200  | IN 200,1      | IN 200,32     | ZERO    |
| ⋮           | ⋮             | ⋮             | ⋮       |
| Subject1801 | IN 1801,1     | IN 1801,32    | NINE    |
| ⋮           | ⋮             | ⋮             | ⋮       |
| Subject2000 | IN 2000,1     | IN 2000,32    | NINE    |

Initially, a subject IN is selected as the test datum, and the rest of the subjects are marked as training data. The test subject and each of the training subjects are then compared using the distance  metric  or  one  of  the  two  fuzzy  order  functions presented in the previous section. Having selected one of the three metrics, it is used to compare all of the corresponding cuts of the two INs. The mean of these per-cut comparisons, is a representation of the overall relationship between the two INs. The relationships between the test subject and the training subjects are then sorted in order to find the k INs most related to the  test  subject. The  sorting order depends on the  metric used; Training INs that are most related to the test subject are those with the shortest distance (closest to zero) but the highest fuzzy order value (closest to 1). The overall nearest neighbour is then determined using majority voting and the classes of the nearest  neighbour  and  the  test  subject  are  compared  to determine  if  classification  was  successful.  The  process  is repeated until all INs have been classified.

## B. Optimization

The classification rate depends on the parameters chosen for the parametric functions ν ( x ) and θ ( x ). For this purpose, a genetic  algorithm  has  been  implemented.  In  this  GA,  each individual is a set of ν ( x ) and θ ( x ) parameters, as well as the k value used in the kNN classifier.

An initial population of 100 individuals (sets of parameters) is generated. In each generation, every individual's set of parameters are used in a classification task as  described  above,  in  order  to  evaluate  the  parameters' performance. The performance of each individual is described by a vector D ,  which  contains the diagonal elements  of  the resulting  confusion  matrix.  The  cost C of  an  individual  is calculated  using  the  mean  of  vector D ,  subtracted  by  the optimal  performance  of  100%,  i.e. C  =  100-mean(D) .  To improve the speed of evaluation of the individuals, parallel processing techniques were employed.

Evaluation of all  individuals  results  in  a  l  ist  of  costs, used  to rank the individuals'  performance  and  genetic operations are applied. Crossover is applied in every generation  by  exchanging  random  sets  of  genes  between randomly selected individuals. Mutation is applied every five generations  by  modifying  the  values  of  randomly  selected parameters of a predefined number of individuals.

## IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

The  experiments  that  were  carried  out  investigated  the classification  performance  of  the  proposed  method  for  the following sets of classes: a) three classes (spoken digits '0', '5' and '9'), b) five classes (spoken digits '0', '3', '5', '7' and '9') and c) ten classes for all spoken digits. In each case, the distance  metric  and  the  two  fuzzy  order  functions  were evaluated. In addition, the effect in performance of employing the linear and sigmoid functions, with and without parameters, as the ν ( x ) and θ ( x ) parametric functions for the calculation of the relationship between pairs of INs was also investigated.

Initially,  the  classification  experiments  were  carried  out with no parameters for the linear ( v ( x ) = x and θ ( x ) = -x ) and sigmoid ( v (x) = 1/(1 + e -x ) and θ (x) = -1/(1 + e -x )) functions.

For the kNN classifier, an arbitrary value of 4 for k was selected. The classification results for the distance metric and the  two  fuzzy  order  functions  using  the  linear  and  sigmoid functions with default parameters are presented in Table II.

TABLE II. CLASSIFICATION RESULTS WITH NO PARAMETERS

| Metric   | Parametric function   | 3 classes   | 5 classes   | 10 classes   |
|----------|-----------------------|-------------|-------------|--------------|
| Distance | Linear                | 70.5%       | 51.3%       | 34.45%       |
|          | Sigmoid               | 54.5%       | 38.8%       | 24.05%       |
| Join     | Linear                | 64.5%       | 52.7%       | 39.8%        |
| Join     | Sigmoid               | 41.83%      | 23.4%       | 16.85%       |
| Meet     | Linear                | 67.33%      | 55%         | 41.5%        |
| Meet     | Sigmoid               | 41.83%      | 23.4$       | 16.1%        |

Following  the classification results with the default parameters,  the  parameter  optimization  process  took  place. Parameters were then introduced to the parametric equations in order to create tunable distance and fuzzy order functions, which  would  alter  the  comparisons  between  the  INs,  and would in turn lead to different classification accuracies. The positions  of  the  parameters  in  the  parametric  equations  are shown in (3) and (4) for the linear type and in in (5) and (6) for the sigmoid.









For each of the six conditions (the three sets of classes and the two types of parametric functions), a GA was executed. The conditions for the GA was an initial population of 100 individuals and the duration of the algorithm was 10 generations. The classification rate for the best individual and the corresponding parameters were recorded. The classification results are shown in Table III.

| Metric   | Parametric function   | 3 classes   | 5 classes   | 10 classes   |
|----------|-----------------------|-------------|-------------|--------------|
| Distance | Linear                | 81%         | 70.7%       | 54%          |
|          | Sigmoid               | 59.66%      | 40.2%       | 25.7%        |
| Join     | Linear                | 70.16%      | 58.4%       | 43.1%        |
| Join     | Sigmoid               | 60.83%      | 36.9%       | 16.85%       |
| Meet     | Linear                | 70%         | 56.9%       | 41.7%        |
| Meet     | Sigmoid               | 53.66%      | 34%         | 18.85%       |

It can be seen from the experimental results that the use of linear  parametric  functions  is  significantly  better  than  the sigmoid for the particular classification problem. In this case the  nature  of  the  audio  signals,  is  such  that  this  type  of parametric function is more suitable for INs' comparison.

It is also evident that the GA improves the classification performance considerably. It appears that appropriate parameter selection is vital to the effectiveness of the proposed method. These results are a clear indication that more work is needed on the selection of appropriate parametric functions according to the characteristics of the original signal.

## V. DISCUSSION

The experimental results presented in this paper demonstrate the potential of the proposed methodology. The observed classification rates illustrate that spoken words can be distinguished from each other, even though there is no preprocessing  of  the  audio  signals  and  no  feature  extraction techniques are employed, which implies a reduced computational burden and a less complex algorithm. Also, the introduction of tunable non-linearities through the parametric functions v (.) and θ (.) and the subsequent use of a GA for their optimization,  leads  to  significantly  improved  performance. Another major advantage of the method is the compression achieved without the loss of data statistics.  The  main disadvantage of INs is the loss of the time dimension. Future work will consider the preservation of the time dimension by computing INs per time-windows for a time series, as well as and the use of other classification schemes.

The  methodology  presented  in  this  paper  is  intended  to contribute towards the design of therapeutic interventions for children with certain types of learning disabilities and children with ASD as part of the national project titled 'Social Robots as Tools in Special Education', where speech will be a vital component of child-robot interaction. This method is aimed to be  a  computationally  inexpensive  tool  used  in  conjunction with the robots' built-in speech recognition engine to recognize trigger words, as well as a detection mechanism for speech  sound  errors  observed  in  children  with  learning disabilities. The generalization properties of the method allow the investigation of such varied tasks that will be pursued for the purposes of the project.

## Paper Source: CHAT (Child Helper and Assistant Tool) : An AI-Based Educational Tool for Supporting Neurodiverse Children with Autism, Dyscalculia, and DSA
============================================================

## CHAT (Child Helper and Assistant Tool): An AI-Based Educational Tool for Supporting Neurodiverse Children with Autism, Dyscalculia, and DSA

Fabio Angeli 1 ,

∗

1 Divitech S.p.A., Technical Leader, Leinì, Province of Turin, Italy

## Abstract

This article explores how artificial intelligence, like ChatGPT, can help children with special needs, including autism, dyscalculia, and Specific Learning Disorders (SLD). It introduces the CHAT system ( Child Helper and Assistant Tool ), which uses personalized conversations to support learning, confidence, and social skills. A study compares virtual assistants with human assistants, showing that ChatGPT can adapt to each child's needs and provide valuable educational and therapeutic help. The article also suggests simple ways to improve how artificial intelligence can be used in schools and therapy.

## Keywords

ChatGPT, artificial intelligence, special needs, education, therapy, autism, dyscalculia, learning support, inclusive education, personalized help

## 1. Introduction to Children with Specific Needs

## 1.1. Autism

Autism, or Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), is a condition that changes how people see the world and talk to others. Children with autism may find it hard to speak, make friends, or try new things. They might also repeat actions or focus on a few interests.

Doctors usually notice autism when a child is young by watching how they act. There is no cure, but early help, like special teaching and therapies, can make life better. Families and children can get support to improve communication and everyday skills.

## 1.2. Dyscalculia

Dyscalculia is a learning problem that makes it hard to understand numbers and math. Children with dyscalculia might have trouble counting, adding, or remembering math facts.

Teachers and psychologists can find dyscalculia by testing the child's learning. With special lessons, tools, and support, children can learn math in ways that work for them.

## 1.3. Neurodiversity

Neurodiversity is the idea that everyone's brain works differently. Some people may think and learn in ways that are not 'typical,' like those with autism, ADHD, or dyslexia. These differences are not problems; they are natural.

People who are neurodiverse may need extra help in school or daily life, but they also have special talents and ideas. Helping them means focusing on their strengths and giving them the right support to grow and succeed.

## 1.4. Specific Learning Disorders (SLD)

Specific Learning Disorders (SLD) are problems with skills like reading, writing, or math, even when a child is smart and healthy. These include:

1. Dyslexia : difficulty reading words;
2. Dysorthographia : difficulty writing correctly;
3. Dysgraphia : difficulty writing neatly;
4. Dyscalculia : difficulty with numbers and math.

Teachers and psychologists can test for these problems and offer special help. Tools and lessons made for the child can help them learn better and feel more confident at school.

## 2. Artificial Intelligence and GPT

## 2.1. Introduction to Artificial Intelligence

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a field of computer science focused on creating systems that can perform tasks requiring human intelligence. These tasks include understanding natural language, recognizing images, planning, and learning.

In recent decades, AI has made significant progress and is now an essential tool in many areas, such as medicine, education, industry, and entertainment. Using machine learning algorithms and large amounts of data, AI systems can analyze, predict, and respond to complex situations more accurately and naturally than ever before.

## 2.2. GPT: An Advanced Language Model

GPT ( Generative Pre-trained Transformer ) is an advanced language model developed by OpenAI. It is designed to understand and generate natural language text. Thanks to its transformer-based architecture, GPT can process complex contexts, answer questions, give suggestions, and create coherent written content.

The main features of GPT include:

1. Context Understanding : GPT analyzes and responds to text by considering the overall context of the conversation.
2. Natural Text Generation : The model produces responses that feel human-like and natural.
3. Adaptability : GPT can be used in many applications, from customer support to educational content creation.

This combination of abilities makes GPT a powerful and flexible tool that can address challenges in education, therapy, and professional environments.

## 2.3. AI Supporting Children with Special Needs

AI offers new opportunities in education and therapy to help children with specific learning disorders (SLD), autism, dyscalculia, and other forms of neurodiversity. GPT, in particular, can be used to:

1. Personalization : Create tailored interactions that meet each child's unique needs.
2. Educational Stimulation : Turn learning activities into engaging and interactive experiences.
3. Continuous Support : Provide constant and immediate assistance, reducing the workload on teachers and parents.
4. Encouraging Independence : Help children think and respond on their own.

With its ability to interact naturally and adaptively, GPT is an innovative tool to improve education and support for children with difficulties. However, it is essential to note its limitations, such as the lack of genuine emotional understanding and its reliance on pre-existing data.

This chapter highlights how artificial intelligence and advanced models like GPT can become valuable resources for improving education and well-being for children with special needs, complementing traditional teaching methods.

## 3. Comparison with Existing Research

## 3.1. AI in Education Studies

In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied and used a lot in education. Researchers focus on how AI can improve learning and inclusion. Many studies have explored the use of chatbots and AI systems to:

1. Help students with learning difficulties : providing personalized explanations and practice. For example, Holmes et al. (2019) studied how smart tutors can support personalized learning [1].
2. Provide instant feedback : helping students fix mistakes quickly. Wang et al. (2018) showed how automated feedback can improve language skills [2].
3. Promote inclusion : adapting educational content to individual needs. Aljarrah et al. (2020) discussed how AI can create inclusive learning environments [4].

These studies show that AI can have a positive effect in education. However, most of them focus on general applications and do not look deeply at children with specific needs like autism, dyscalculia, or learning disorders.

## 3.2. Previous Approaches for Neurodiverse Children

Research on using AI to help neurodiverse children, such as those with learning disorders or autism, has focused on:

1. Adaptive learning systems : platforms that adjust content based on student performance. For example, the 'Dybuster' system supports children with dyslexia and dyscalculia using a multisensory approach [3].
2. Social simulations : tools that help children with autism practice social interactions in a safe environment. Tartaro and Cassell (2008) studied virtual agents to improve social skills in children with autism [5].
3. Educational games : designed to make learning easier and less stressful. Grynszpan et al. (2014) conducted a meta-analysis on the effectiveness of computer-based games for children with autism [6].

However, many of these approaches have important limitations:

1. Lack of natural interaction : Many systems rely on fixed responses, reducing flexibility and adaptability.
2. No comparison with human assistance : Few studies compare AI effectiveness with human helpers.
3. Low personalization : Systems often fail to fully adjust to the emotional and cognitive needs of children.

## 3.3. Contributions of This Study

This study differs from previous research in several ways:

1. Natural interaction with GPT : Using an advanced language model like GPT, the proposed system provides smoother and more personalized interaction.
2. Real-world application : The system has been tested in extbfComparison between human and virtual assistants: The CHAT ( Child Helper and Assistant Tool ) program evaluates conversations to compare the effectiveness of virtual and human assistants.
3. Real-world application : The system has been tested in real-life scenarios where the assistant was a human, but the children were always virtual, designed to simulate characteristics of children with learning disorders, autism, or dyscalculia.

This study represents progress compared to earlier research. It addresses previous limitations and offers new ideas on how AI can support children with special educational needs.

## 4. Our Approach

## 4.1. Motivation and Starting Point

Our work began with a personal observation of ChatGPT's potential, first tested in software development. ChatGPT proved to be not only a useful tool for technical solutions but also a system that supports and motivates users. While solving software problems, ChatGPT provided answers that adapted to emotional contexts, encouraging and showing understanding. Here are some examples of its responses:

- I understand. You want to change the function so the data comes from the database instead of a JSON file. Here's how:
- Sure! We can move the query to an external SQL file and load it in Python. Here's how:
- You raised an important point, and your question makes sense.
- I'm sorry for the confusion. Thanks for clarifying.
- Your idea looks solid and could work well.
- Perfect. I'm ready! Let me know if it works or if you need more help!
- To achieve your goal, here's one way to proceed.

This protective and adaptive behavior shows ChatGPT's ability to understand both technical problems and the user's needs. This led us to an important question: Can ChatGPT, with its natural interaction and contextual understanding, support children with specific needs like autism, dyscalculia, or Specific Learning Disorders (SLD)?

## 4.2. Preliminary Simulations

To explore this question, we simulated conversations with ChatGPT, imagining it interacting with virtual children who were designed to represent the following characteristics:

1. Autism : testing ChatGPT's ability to manage social situations and provide empathetic support.
2. Dyscalculia : checking if ChatGPT can help solve math problems through fun and personalized exercises.
3. SLD : exploring how ChatGPT can simplify complex ideas and adapt to the child's cognitive challenges.
4. Neurodiversity : testing how ChatGPT encourages creativity and imagination through openended questions and free interactions.

The conversations were positive and engaging , showing that ChatGPT can adapt to educational and supportive roles. The model encouraged the virtual child, built confidence, and motivated active participation.

## 4.3. The CHAT Program

Based on these observations, we developed CHAT ( Child Helper and Assistant Tool ), a program designed to simulate a virtual assistant that interacts with children who have specific needs. CHAT has two main goals:

1. Direct interaction : Allow children to communicate directly with a virtual assistant that offers educational and social support.
2. Support for human assistants : Provide teachers or parents with a tool to facilitate interactions with neurodiverse children by offering adaptive responses and suggestions.

## 4.4. Comparison Between Human and Virtual Assistants

To evaluate CHAT's effectiveness, we conducted a comparative study:

1. Human-child interactions : where a human educator interacted with a virtual child.
2. Virtual assistant-child interactions : where CHAT acted as the assistant.

The conversations were recorded and rated on a scale from 0 to 10, with 10 being highly protective and educational. Results showed that CHAT could provide support on a level equal to or even better than human assistants in specific situations.

## 4.5. Final Goals

Our approach aims to demonstrate that a virtual assistant like CHAT, powered by GPT, can:

1. Be an educational ally : improving learning and social integration for children.
2. Support educators : reducing workload and providing personalized and continuous help.

With this program, we hope to offer an innovative and accessible tool to address the educational and social challenges faced by children with specific needs.

## 5. Description of the CHAT Application

## 5.1. System Overview

CHAT ( Child Helper and Assistant Tool ) is an application designed to simulate conversations with virtual children who have specific needs (autism, dyscalculia, SLD, and neurodiversity). The main goal is to create a safe, inclusive, and stimulating learning environment.

The system consists of two main components:

- Frontend : Developed in React, it allows users to interact with virtual children through a simple and intuitive interface.
- Backend : Built with Python, it manages the virtual assistant's responses using GPT and analyzes the conversations to provide quality evaluations.

## 5.2. User Interface

The user interface lets users select a virtual child profile they wish to interact with. Each profile is tailored to the specific needs of the selected condition, ensuring a customized experience.

Figure 2c shows the start screen for a conversation with a child who has dyscalculia. The virtual assistant (Hermes) introduces a topic, and the child responds with their choice. The interface clearly highlights the roles of the assistant and the child, making the interaction straightforward and wellorganized.



Figure 1: How the program works in both human-to-virtual-child and virtual-assistant-to-virtual-child modes.



- (a) Human assistant mode: supporting the child with empathy and clarity to guide the conversation.
- (b) Virtual assistant mode: handling all responses automatically while adapting to the child's needs.
- (c) Example of a chat: the assistant begins a conversation with a child who has dyscalculia, fostering engagement.
- (d) Final evaluation screen: providing quality analysis of the interaction with detailed scores and feedback.







Figure 2: Screenshots from the CHAT application showcasing its modes, conversations, and interaction analysis.

## 5.3. Conversation Analysis

At the end of each conversation, the CHAT system provides a detailed analysis of the interaction quality. As shown in Figure 2, the system assigns an overall score based on three main criteria:

- Protectiveness : Measures how well the interaction ensured a safe and respectful environment for the child.
- Educational Value : Assesses the assistant's ability to encourage learning and curiosity.
- Constructiveness : Analyzes how the conversation contributed to the child's personal growth and confidence.

For example, in the conversation 'The Great Adventure of Lampo' (Figure 3), the system gave a score of 9.3/10, highlighting a respectful, educational, and creative interaction.

## 5.4. Interaction Evaluation

Each conversation is recorded and analyzed by the system to identify strengths and areas for improvement. This evaluation helps monitor the virtual assistant's effectiveness and serves as a useful tool for educators and parents aiming to enhance their interactions with children.

## 5.5. Practical Implications

CHAT is an innovative application for educational and therapeutic purposes, showing how AI can support children with specific needs and assist educators and parents. By combining qualitative analysis and personalized profiles, CHAT becomes a versatile and accessible tool.

## 6. Analysis of Results

## 6.1. Statistical Data

In this study, a total of 116 conversations were analyzed, divided as follows:

- Conversations between human assistants and virtual children : 75, with an average score of 7.799.
- Conversations between virtual assistants and virtual children : 41, with an average score of 8.584.

Figure 3: Comparison of the average scores for interactions mediated by human assistants and virtual assistants with virtual children. The graph shows higher scores for virtual assistant-mediated interactions.



These results suggest that conversations mediated by virtual assistants achieved higher average scores compared to those involving human assistants. The overall scores were calculated using a GPT-based algorithm that analyzed the quality of interactions based on predefined criteria.

## 6.2. Evaluation Methodology

Each conversation was assessed based on the following criteria:

- Protectiveness : Measures how well the interaction provided a safe and respectful environment for the child.
- Educational Value : Evaluates the assistant's ability to encourage learning and curiosity in the child.
- Constructiveness : Analyzes how the conversation contributed to the child's personal growth and confidence.

The system used key phrases and simulated behaviors to personalize the interaction. For example, the virtual assistant showed empathy with phrases such as:

- 'It's okay, we can handle this together.'
- 'Great job! You focused really well on this problem.'
- 'Would you like to explore a topic that interests you?'

These phrases reflect a protective and positive approach that proved crucial for successful interactions.

## 6.3. Comparison Between Human and Virtual Assistants

The data reveals that virtual assistants provided a more consistent and predictable level of support compared to human assistants. Specifically:

- Virtual assistants maintained an empathetic and patient tone in every interaction.
- Conversations with virtual assistants were more consistent, thanks to the AI's ability to adapt continuously to the child's profile.
- Human assistants, while demonstrating good skills, showed greater variability in scores, highlighting the challenge of maintaining uniform standards.

## 6.4. Key Conclusions

The results demonstrate that:

1. Empathy and Adaptability : Virtual assistants showed a high level of empathy and adaptability to the children's needs.
2. Educational Efficiency : Virtual interactions were perceived as more constructive and engaging.
3. Practical Implications : AI systems like CHAT can support children with specific needs and help educators by reducing workload and improving the quality of interactions.

## 6.5. Future Prospects

While the results are encouraging, further study is needed to:

- Conduct tests in real settings to evaluate the virtual assistant's effectiveness in educational and therapeutic environments.
- Improve emotional recognition and contextual understanding to make interactions even more natural.
- Extend the system to cover additional categories of children with special needs.

CHAT represents a significant innovation in inclusive education, offering new opportunities to improve the quality of life for neurodiverse children.

## 7. Conclusions and Future Perspectives

The CHAT ( Child Helper and Assistant Tool ) project has shown that artificial intelligence, through advanced models like GPT, can provide meaningful support to children with special educational needs, such as those with autism, dyscalculia, and Specific Learning Disorders (SLD). Simulations have demonstrated that a virtual assistant can deliver empathetic, personalized, and engaging interactions while maintaining a high-quality standard compared to human assistants.

The key findings of our study indicate that:

1. Virtual assistants can adapt to the specific needs of children, creating a protective and inclusive environment.
2. CHAT effectively promotes learning and active participation while maintaining a constructive and motivating approach.
3. The average scores of virtual interactions were higher than those of human-assisted conversations, highlighting significant potential for use in educational and therapeutic contexts.

Despite the promising results, certain limitations should be noted. While advanced, CHAT cannot fully replicate the emotional intelligence and intuition of human educators. Additionally, the system relies on pre-existing data and could benefit from further improvements, such as recognizing non-verbal emotional cues.

## Future Perspectives and Practical Applications

Looking ahead, the system can evolve in several directions:

- Integration in schools and therapy centers : CHAT could be implemented as a support tool for educators and therapists, offering personalized interactions and adaptive learning materials.
- Development of specific modules : Additional features could be introduced to address particular needs, such as managing anxiety or improving social skills.
- Advanced emotional recognition : Integrating facial or vocal analysis technologies to better understand children's emotions and tailor responses accordingly.
- Collaboration with educators and families : Engaging parents and teachers in the development process to enhance the system's usability and effectiveness.

User feedback has played a critical role in identifying areas for improvement. Teachers and parents emphasized the need for greater personalization, while therapists appreciated the system's ability to maintain a reassuring and motivating tone.

## Implications and Final Conclusions

CHAT represents a significant step forward in using artificial intelligence to address the educational and social challenges of neurodiverse children. While it cannot replace human interaction, it serves as a complementary support tool, reducing the burden on educators and fostering autonomy and confidence in children. With further improvements and real-world testing, CHAT has the potential to become an indispensable tool for inclusive and personalized education.

## ABSTRACT

Traditional topic-specific communication boards for Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) require manual programming of relevant symbolic vocabulary, which is time-consuming and often impractical even for experienced Speech-Language Pathologists (SLPs). While recent research has demonstrated the potential to automatically generate these boards from photographs using artificial intelligence, there has been no exploration on how to design such tools to support the specific needs of AAC-based language instruction. This paper introduces QuickPic, a mobile AAC application co-designed with SLPs and special educators, aimed at enhancing language learning for non-speaking individuals, such as autistic children. Through a 17-month design process, we uncover the unique design features required to provide timely language support in therapy and special education contexts. We present emerging evidence on the overall satisfaction of SLPs using QuickPic, and on the advantages of large language model-based generation compared to the existing technique for automated vocabulary from photographs for AAC.

## 1 INTRODUCTION

Speech-Language Pathologists (SLPs) and special education teachers play a pivotal role in enhancing the expressive communication abilities of autistic children and other individuals with complex communication needs, often using Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) as a tool within therapy sessions and classrooms. A typical approach relies on providing communication boards with vocabulary symbols relevant to a specific topic grouped in a single display. These boards are then used by the professionals in activities that immerse learners in symbolic language, for example, by
