## 3.2.1. Testing based on threshold

The chatbot considered a response valid if its confidence score is equal to or greater than 0.75. The confidence score represents the model's estimation of how confident it is in generating the response. Based on the testing, when the 0.75 threshold was chosen, most test intent scored a confidence of more than 90%. To find the optimum threshold value for the chatbot, we fed the bot with the test that has been annotated with its correct responses or its correct ground truth value. Then the output was inspected based on the confidence threshold at different levels of 0.50, 0.75, 0.80, and 0.85. There were about 150 intents tested for each of the confidence  thresholds.  Results  for  the  average  accuracy  against  confidence  thresholds  are  presented  in Table 3. It can be observed that the highest accuracy is at a confidence threshold of 0.80 which is about 85%.

Table 3. Test cases of confidence thresholds

## 3.2.2. Chatbot usability questionnaires

A chatbot usability questionnaire is a set of questions designed to assess the user experience and usability of a chatbot. It helps gather feedback from users to understand their satisfaction, ease of use, and overall  impression  of  interacting  with  the  chatbot.  The  elements  that  are  included  in  a  chatbot  usability questionnaire as shown in Table 4. The questionnaires were ranked from strongly disagree to strongly agree, with intermediate choices in between.

Table 4. Chatbot usability questionnaire

| Questions                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Strongly disagree   | Disagree   | Neutral   | Agree   | Strongly agree   |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------|------------|-----------|---------|------------------|
| Q1 The chatbot's personality was realistic and engaging Q2 The chatbot seemed too robotic Q3 The chatbot was welcoming during the initial setup Q4 The chatbot seemed very unfriendly Q5 The chatbot explained its scope and purpose well Q6 The chatbot gave no indication as to its purpose Q7 The chatbot was easy to navigate Q8 It would be easy to get confused when using the chatbot Q9 The chatbot understood me well Q10 The chatbot failed to recognize a lot of my input Q11 Chatbot responses were useful, appropriate, and informative Q12 Chatbot responses were not relevant Q13 The chatbot coped well with any errors or mistakes Q14 The chatbot seemed unable to handle any errors Q15 The chatbot was very easy to use Q16 The chatbot was very complex |                     |            |           |         |                  |

| 0-25        | Worst Imaginable        |
| >84.1       | Best Imaginable         |

A  group  of  50  people  who  satisfied  the  requirements  for  being  healthy  adults  were  recruited  as volunteers  to  assess  the  usefulness  of  the  chatbot.  Figure  8  illustrates  a  boxplot  that  portrays  the  SUS outcomes acquired from the assessment of the chatbot. The chatbot has achieved a mean SUS score of 80.48 ± 13.03 with a median score of 85.95. The highest achieved score was 100.0, and the lowest recorded score was 50. The chatbot's average score places it inside the top 93rd to 100th percentile range. Hence, it can be inferred  that  the  chatbot  has  a  commendable  degree  of  usability  as  determined  by  the  conventional  SUS values.

Figure 8. Chatbot usability questionnaire scores



## 4. CONCLUSION

In this study, a chatbot is proposed as a solution to the problem of educational system management for autistic children. The  research focuses on how  to  assist teachers in  managing  their  everyday responsibilities while working with autistic students. It is an interactive system that provides pre-programmed responses in response to questions posed by users. It frees customers from the constraints of time limits and makes it possible for them to obtain responses quickly, making it an excellent substitute for conventional live chat. The Python programming language will be utilized throughout the construction of the chatbot, which will  take  place  in  the  system  gateway  of  the  school.  Users  will  have  the  ability  to  have  a  more  natural dialogue with the chatbot thanks to the implementation of deep learning, which has also been demonstrated to have a greater level of accuracy when replying to user inquiries. In the not-too-distant future, the chatbot will  be  incorporated  into  Telegram,  an  instant  messaging  service,  and  users  can  speak  with  one  another regarding autistic school management via Telegram. Users may also benefit from the chatbot system, notably reducing the time necessary to conduct a physical consultation between teachers, physiotherapists, and the upper management team.

## Paper Source: Creating a Dataset of Autistic Individuals to Recommend Evidence-Based Practices through Generative Artificial Intelligen

## Creating a Dataset of Autistic Individuals to Recommend Evidence-Based Practices through Generative Artificial Intelligence

Jennifer Kouo School of Education Johns Hopkins University Baltimore, USA jennifer.kouo@jhu.edu

Jinjuan Heidi Feng Computer and Information Sciences Department Towson University Baltimore, USA jfeng@towson.edu

Abstract -Autism is the fastest-growing developmental condition,  and  as  a  spectrum  disorder,  individuals  vary  in severity in communication and behavior. The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)  presents  opportunities  to  leverage  such  technology  to support  autistic  individuals  in  multiple  contexts,  including education,  healthcare,  and  disability  research.  However,  very limited  research  has  focused  on  developing  AI  or  ML-based solutions for autistic individuals largely due to the scarcity of autism-related datasets. In order for autistic people to equally benefit from the breakthroughs in AI, the data representation gap in AI and ML must be addressed. The project proposes an innovative human  expert and AI combined  approach  to generate synthetic data about autistic individuals. Through this approach, we are developing the first dataset of case studies of autistic individuals to effectively identify evidence-based practices (EBPs)  to address the unique  needs  of autistic individuals. The  project improves  the representation  and inclusion of autistic individuals in the rapidly evolving field of ML and AI through both methodological innovations (i.e., the expert/AI  combined  data  generation  approach)  and  practical contributions (i.e., the EBP dataset that will be made publicly accessible). The innovative data generation method and supporting materials developed in this project can be generalized to individuals with other disabilities.

Keywords- autism, artificial intelligence, machine learning, evidence-based practice

## I. INTRODUCTION AND RELATED RESEARCH

Autism is the fastest-growing neurodevelopmental condition, with 1 in 36 children diagnosed in the United States [1].  A  heterogeneous  population,  autistic  individuals  are impacted differently and with varying severity in the areas of communication, behavior, and interests [2]. Evidence-based practices  (EBPs),  such  as  those  identified  by  the  National Clearinghouse  on  Autism  Evidence  and  Practice  (NCAEP) and the National Autism Center (NAC) are critical for autistic individuals, their families, educators and practitioners, community members, researchers, advocacy groups, policymakers,  and  healthcare  providers  to  better  support autistic individuals in many contexts and situations [3, 4, 5]

Artificial intelligence in education (AIEd) has the potential to leverage novel technology to impact the learning environment and support teachers and students in teaching and learning [6]. Furthermore, the role of machine learning (ML), a subset of artificial intelligence (AI), is becoming increasingly more  present and important in educational settings  [6,  7].  ML  is  a  novel  technology  that  can  rapidly analyze vast amounts of data for pattern recognition, Enric Jiao Department of Computer Science University of Maryland, College Park College Park, USA enricjiao3@gmail.com classification, and  cluster  identification within  a  diverse population.

ML has been applied successfully in a variety of domains including self-driving cars, marketing, and early diagnosis of cancer  [8].  However,  applications  of  ML  in  autism-related research and services are very limited. Early efforts involving ML have primarily focused on diagnostics to reduce the time required for manual detection and diagnosis [9, 10, 11, 12]. Wireless sensors, smartphones, and cameras have been used to detect stereotypical motor movements or predict tantruming behaviors in classrooms through ML algorithms [13, 14, 15].

ML has only preliminarily been applied to detect learning activities and predict learning outcomes in education settings [16, 17]. In addition to leveraging ML in diagnosing autism, this technology has the potential to be applied to the identification of EBPs that can be used by educators, families, healthcare  providers,  and  community  members  to  support autistic individuals. To date, no ML-based solution exists to reduce the time and efforts needed to effectively identify EBPs to address the unique, individual needs of autistic individuals [18].  The  development  of  such  applications  requires  an extensive  amount  of  data  regarding  the  characteristics  of autistic individuals, the interventions applied together with the specific context, as well as the outcome of the interventions. Such datasets about autistic individuals do not presently exist or  are  not  available  to  researchers  and  developers  due  to security or privacy concerns [19]. Overall, there is a concerning lack of representation of people with disabilities, including autistic individuals, in ML and AI [20]. According to Brandsen et al. [21], existing AI language models demonstrate  an  alarming  level  of  bias  towards  or  negative associations with terms related to neurodiversity and autism. Limited  and unrepresentative data availability makes  it impossible  to  leverage,  train,  and  evaluate  ML  models  that support autistic individuals.

Fortunately,  recent  breakthroughs  in  pre-trained  Large Language  Models  (LLMs)  such  as  Generative  Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) provide a highly effective approach for generating various forms of data ranging from text to videos [22, 23]. Since LLMs are trained on vast amounts of world knowledge  and  human  examples,  they  have  absorbed  rich commonsense that  makes  it  possible  to  propose  reasonable plans and solve problems that require mathematical, symbolic, commonsense, and knowledge reasoning [24]. New prompt techniques such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) have demonstrated  significant  enhancement  in  problem-solving abilities  on  specific  tasks  [25].    Reinforcement  Learning through Human Feedback (RLHF) has proven to be highly effective in both training LLMs and improving the quality of LLM  output [26]. Building on top of these exciting developments in LLMs, we will address the data representation gap by generating a synthetic dataset on autistic individuals  through  human  experts  and  LLM  combined approach.

Hinojo-Lucena et al. [30] and Hopcan et al. [6] state that a greater concerted effort to apply and research the application of AI and ML in special education is needed. Hopcan et al. [6] further urge researchers 'to conduct studies on the use of AI technology for the social, emotional, and behavioral development of students with special educational needs. Also, focusing on different participant groups and designing studies to  obtain  large  datasets  is  essential  because  the  existing literature is weak in terms of researching large sample sizes'. Singh et al. [7] recommend that future research explore the validation  of  ML  to  address  the  treatment  of  autism  in healthcare settings. In parallel, the identification of EBPs to support autistic individuals is equally important in all contexts. This project novelly leverages  ML  to  impact education,  healthcare,  and  disability  research  by  addressing the data representation gap. With the engagement of experts in the field of autism, we will use a Large Language Model to generate the first synthetic dataset of case studies of autistic individuals to effectively identify EBPs to address the unique needs of autistic individuals [18, 19].

## II. METHODOLOGY

## A. Autism experts

Four experts in  autism  and  EBPs  were  recruited  for the project.  All  of  the  experts  were  current  or  former  special education teachers, had worked closely with autistic individuals, and had completed coursework on EBPs specifically for the autism population. Additional information about each of the experts is detailed in Table 1.

The phases of the project are presented in Figure 1 and detailed in the subsequent sections.

## B. Phase 1. Workshop with Autism Experts

Prior to the 2-hour workshop, autism experts were asked to view portions of a video entitled 'State of GPT' [31] and read portions of the articles published by Hartvigsen et al. [23] and Wei et al. [25] to gain basic knowledge about LLMs and related techniques. The experts then independently identified and shared detailed, exemplary case studies accurately presenting the heterogeneity and complexity of autistic individuals.  The  experts  were  encouraged  to  search  the literature for case studies, as well as other resources, including training modules and textbooks. The experts then reflected on and listed key components or descriptors of high-quality case studies (e.g., specific types of data that should be included to effectively  describe  a  student  with  autism).  Finally,  the experts  had  the  option  of  completing  any  Autism  Focused Intervention  Resources  and  Modules  (AFIRM)  modules  to review any EBPs for autistic individuals [32].

Guided by the co-authors, the autism experts engaged in the workshop. The workshop provided an introduction to ML and LLMs, the overall project, and a brief demonstration of the capabilities of LLMs in developing case studies. A large component of the workshop involved reviewing and reflecting on the activities related to high-quality case studies with the goal of co-constructing a template or framework with prompts to develop multiple case studies of various lengths during the workshop. Discussions on the activities completed before the workshop centered around concerns regarding the availability of  detailed  and  comprehensive  case  studies.  The  experts expressed  that  the  case  studies  identified  were  oftentimes broad, or focused narrowly on areas of need that were being targeted  with  a  specific  intervention.  One  expert  noted  that neuropsychological testing reports may be the most comprehensive in providing a full picture of an individual with autism.

The components of the case study template developed at the end of the workshop are detailed in Table 2. The experts and  the  co-authors  engaged  in  rich  conversations  as  the template was developed. Experts sought clarification on the perspective  of  the  case  study.  For  example,  a  case  study written from the perspective of an educator may include an increased  amount  of  quantitative  assessment  data  and  be written  in  a  manner  similar  to  a  formal,  evaluative  report. However,  a  case  study  from  the  perspective  of  a  family member or guardian may include more anecdotal observations and therefore be more qualitative. The co-authors and experts discussed that  the different perspectives  would  still provide valuable information when teaching the LLM model. Future expectations  of  the  project  will  include  both  educators  and family members providing information to support the automatic  generation  of  individualized  EBPs  used  in  an educational or healthcare context. Additionally, the co-authors emphasized  the  importance  of  teaching  the  LLM  model commonly utilized acronyms, the names of assessment tools, and clarifying the meaning or interpretation of the assessment data scores to help the LLM model make meaning of those scores and provide a comparison to a baseline of neurotypical individuals. The co-authors and experts agreed that detail in the case studies was vital to ensure that the data provided was substantive  and  informative.  Ultimately,  experts  found  the development of case studies to be in alignment with their dayto-day work as educators, especially with regard to developing Individualized Education Plans (IEP) and reports of student progress.

As part  of  the  project  aims,  experts  were  asked  to  identify three  priority  EBPs  that  would  be  responsive  to  the  needs identified  in  each  case  study  they  would  be  developing. Additionally, experts were required to provide a rationale or justification for selecting each EBP by referring directly back to the case study information. Providing a clear justification would further teach the ML model to connect the case study content with the selection of specific EBPs, as suggested by the  'chain-of-thought'  prompting  technique  [25]. ## C. Phase 2.  Development of Case Studies with Justified Evidence-based Practices

Following the workshop, each expert was asked to develop one  case  study,  including  recommended  EBPs  and  their justification. The co-authors reviewed the four generated case studies and provided feedback for the following case studies that would be developed. The feedback included the removal of identifying information including a city and state. Experts were asked to provide the full term of an acronym when first mentioned, followed by the acronym itself written in capital letters and enclosed by parentheses. References to assessment tools  in  the  case  studies  required  at  least  one  sentence describing the tool. Concerning recommending EBPs, the coauthors  asked  experts  to  refer  to  the  EBPs  and  definitions indicated  in  Steinbrenner  et  al.  [5]  when  recommending EBP(s).  After  identifying  the  EBP  from  that  table,  experts were  encouraged  to  provide  more  detail  about  the  EBP,  if applicable.  For  example,  the  recommendation  of  the  EBP prompting  could  contain  additional  detail  about  the  type, including gestural, visual, or physical prompting. To make it obvious to the LLM model, the authors asked experts to cite or quote directly from the case study what the recommended EBP would address. This change was expected to help make a clearer connection between the case study and the EBP being recommended. Applying the additional feedback, the experts each generated an additional four case studies with accompanying EBP recommendations and their justification.

Since the proposed approach is highly innovative, there is no previous work that may provide guidance on the process or insight  into  the  possible  quality  of  the  LLM  output.  An iterative approach to data generation was undertaken to ensure that the AI-generated data was continually evaluated by the co-authors and autism experts to inform the next stage of data generation. Within Phase 2 and as presented in Figure 1, the autism experts generated additional case studies and recommended  EBPs  in  increments.  The  increments  were

## AdditionalInstructionsandConsiderations

- All evidence-based practices identified and accompanying justifications should be no more than 300 words in total.

followed  by  the  development  of  AI-generated  case  studies, which are organized by rounds and further described in the next section on Phase 3.

## D. Phase 3

Round 1. Utilizing the initial four case studies developed by the autism experts in Phase 2, a total of 20 case studies were generated using the GPT-3.5 Turbo model with the following prompt:

'You  are  an  ASD  researcher.  For  the  purpose  of  ASD research,  we  would  like  you  to  generate  several  young student  or  patient  examples  based  on  the  following examples. 1. Please vary the demographics such as name, gender  and  age.  2.  Please  do  not  repeat  the  patient background. 3. Please generate information that is often observed in ASD students or patients. 4. Please keep each case to be between 500 to 1000 tokens.'

The number of cases generated during each cycle was set at two or three. The length of the generated case was set to 500 to  1000  tokens  (approximately  375  to  750  words).  These ranges were selected considering the input and output limits of the GPT-3.5 Turbo model.

After the 20 cases were generated the experts were asked to read all 20 case studies and to consider whether or not the cases were diverse. The experts provided their responses in a shared document. Then each expert was assigned five of the 20 case studies to read thoroughly. Experts provided a simple rating (Yes, No, Maybe) for each case study for the following questions:  (1)  Is  the  case  realistic  (i.e.,  does  not  contain contradictory information)?; (2) Is the case representative of an autistic individual?; and (3) Does the case contain sufficient information to provide an EBP recommendation? The experts were encouraged to provide a rationale for their ratings. The expert rating suggested that the overall quality of the 20 cases was satisfactory.

Round 2. After the first round of quality checks in Round 1,  the  autism  experts  each  developed  four  additional  case studies. The GPT-3.5 Turbo model was used to generate 300 cases using the 16 total cases created by the autism experts using the same prompt and length ranges used in Round 1. The co-authors reviewed the 300 cases and agreed that the general quality of the cases was satisfactory.

Round 3. In the final round, using all 60 cases created by the  experts  as  examples,  the  GPT-3.5  turbo  model  will  be utilized to generate approximately 3,000 to 4000 cases.

## E. Phase 4 AI-Generated Evidence-based Practices and Rating

After the quality check conducted by the co-authors on the 300 AI-generated cases, the GPT-3.5 Turbo model was used to generate EBP recommendations for the 300 AI-generated cases. The following prompt was used as instructions for the model:

'You  are  an  ASD  researcher.  For  the  purpose  of  ASD research, we would like you to generate three evidencebased practices (EBP) for a scenario. You will be given a few  scenarios  with  expert-generated  EBP,  and  several other scenarios without EBP. Your role is to create three EBPs appropriate to the scenario.'

After the EBPs were generated for the 300 cases, 20 cases together  with  the  EBP  recommendation  and  justifications were randomly selected and rated by the autism experts. Each autism expert was  assigned 10 case studies to review independently,  with  each  case  study  being  reviewed  by  2 experts to explore the consistency of ratings. The experts were asked  to  respond  to  the  following  questions  with  a  simple rating (Yes, No) for each AI-generated case study: (1) Is the case realistic (i.e., does not contain contradictory information)?; (2) Is the case representative of an individual with  autism?;  and  (3)  Does  the  case  contain  sufficient information  to  provide  an  EBP  recommendation?.  Experts then provided a rationale to support the ratings. For each AIrecommended EBP, autism experts were asked to rate (Yes, No) whether the recommendation was appropriate based on the  case  study  information,  and  if  the  justification  was accurate. After experts reviewed all 10 assigned case studies, they  were  asked  to  describe  whether  all  10  cases  reviewed were diverse.

## III. RESULTS

The  proposed  data  generation  approach  requires  close collaboration between AI and experts with experience working  with  autistic  students  in  special  education  settings and  with  knowledge  of  EBPs  responsive  to  the  needs  of autistic  individuals.  Case  studies  and  recommended  EBPs were generated by autism experts to inform the development of AI-generated data.

## A. Sample expert generated case with EBP

Table 6 in the  Appendix presents an example of a case study developed by an autism expert during Phase 2 of the project.

## B. Sample AI generated case with EBP

Based on 16 expert created case studies from Phase 2, 300 case studies with EBPs were generated by the GPT 3.5 Turbo model. An example is presented in table 7 in the Appendix.

## C. Quality assessment: Case studies

In Phase 4, 20 AI-generated case studies together with the corresponding EBP recommendations and justifications were randomly  selected  among  the  300  cases  and  rated  by  the autism  experts.  In  order  to  determine  interrater  reliability, each case study was reviewed by two experts.

Table 4 provides a summary of the expert ratings for the 20 randomly selected AI generated case studies. The experts were  asked  to  provide  three  ratings  for  each  case  study: whether it is realistic; whether it is representative; and whether it  provided sufficient information for EBP recommendation. There  was  a  65%  agreement  that  the  case  studies  were realistic. The rationale for rating the case study as unrealistic centers upon the educational setting identified and contradictory assessment and descriptive data. Regarding the setting, experts indicated that the AI-generated cases identified a general education setting when areas of need in the  case  study  (e.g.,  behaviors  during  transitioning,  support with toileting) would likely require a more restrictive setting or a setting with additional adult support through a paraprofessional. Another expert noted that an AI-generated case study referenced the use of a 'versatile special education service,'  which  is  not  a  known  school  setting  or  learning environment. Autism experts also identified contradictions as it  related  to  assessment  data  reported  in  the  case  studies. Despite the AI-generated case study indicating the age range for  an  assessment,  an  expert  noted,  'This  case  uses  an assessment that is not appropriate for the age of the individual. It states that Tara is 14 years old and then describes the use of an assessment for children birth to 5 years of age.' Another autism  expert  noted  that  in  another  case  study,  an  average reading score was reported but later indicated a large gap in terms of age and grade level reading ability. There was a 85% agreement  that  the  case  studies  were  representative  of  an autistic individual. Experts reported that the AI-generated case studies did not include a definitive description of an autistic individual and that the case study could also be representative of  a  neurotypical  child  or  a  child  with  delays  only  in communication.  There  was  a  95%  agreement  that  the  AIgenerated  case  studies  contained  sufficient  information  to recommend  EBPs,  with  one  case  study  being  identified  as lacking information.

## D. Quality assessment: EBP recommendations

Experts also rated each of the three AI-generated EBPs as well as their justifications for the 20 cases (Table 5). For each EBP, experts were asked: whether the EBP recommendation was appropriate; and whether the justification for the EBP was accurate.

For  the  first  AI-recommended  EBP,  there  was  75% agreement  on  its  appropriateness.  For  the  second  and  third EBP recommendations, there was 70% and 80% agreement respectively.  Autism  experts  provided  critiques  about  the appropriate labeling of EBPs. For example, experts suggested that visual supports should first be identified before specifically  recommending  visual  schedules  or  identifying augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) prior to recommending  Picture  Exchange  Communication  Systems (PECS).  Experts  also  noted  for  another  case  study the appropriateness of the social stories if the case study indicated the  individual  struggled  with  attending  to  stories  and  had delays in receptive language.

When reviewing the accuracy of the justification generated by AI, there was 85% agreement for the first EBP recommended, followed by 80% and 85% agreement for the second and third EBP recommendations respectively. Autism experts  noted  that  the  justifications  needed  to  go  beyond providing  a  general  definition  of  the  EBP  and  identify specifically  how  the  EBP  would  address  the  needs  of  the individual  described  in  the  case  study.  Experts  identified  a lack of specific justifications for Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA),  peer-mediated  instruction  and  intervention  (PMII), and visual supports. For example, an autism expert provided the following recommendation to improve the AI-generated justifications: 'Visual Supports are an evidence-based practice that utilizes pictures, objects or images to support an individual in understanding and engaging with their environment.  Since  Clara  struggles  with  anxiety  around changes in her routine, a visual schedule could be beneficial in preparing her for changes that may occur in her day, thus lessening her anxiety.' Another recommendation to improve justifications  included,  'ABA  is  an  evidence-based practice that  uses  the  principles  of  learning  to  increase  or  decrease target behaviors or skills. This strategy could be beneficial in addressing Oliver's aggressions and self-injurious behaviors. Methods  used  with  ABA  to  address  these  behaviors  may include reinforcing the absence of these behaviors, teaching and reinforcing behaviors that interfere with the target behavior, and teaching and reinforcing alternate behaviors that are  more  appropriate  based on  the  function of  the  behavior (e.g.  asking  for  attention).'  Autism  experts  also  noted  that there  were  a  few  cases  of  inaccurate  justification,  where information in the justification did not reflect the case study information.

After each autism expert reviewed their 10 assigned case studies, experts were asked to describe whether or not all 10 cases reviewed were diverse. Experts indicated that the case studies  generated  by  AI  were  diverse  with  regard  to  ages, abilities,  and  areas  of  need.  However,  it  was  noted  that  the cases reviewed did contain more examples of individuals with higher-intensity  needs  and  that  there  was  limited  cultural diversity among the cases.

## IV. DISCUSSION

The reported work is the first proof-of-concept project that uses the recent generative AI technology to generate synthetic data about autistic individuals and make recommendations for EBPs.  The  preliminary  result  is  promising,  with  highly positive expert agreements for both case study generation and EBP recommendations and justifications.

## A. Significance

The project novelly applies generative AI technology to autism data generation and the identification of EBPs that can be  used  to  support  professionals  in  various  fields  such  as education and healthcare. It will lead to two major outcomes that will immediately impact both the fields of generative AI and autism research: (1) the first publicly available datasets regarding  EBPs  for  autistic  individuals  that  all  researchers, practitioners, and stakeholders can use for their own research and practice, such as curriculum development, training, and the  adoption  of  LLMs  related  applications;  and  (2)  a  new method  for  creating  substantial  amount  of  synthetic  data regarding  autistic  individuals  through  the  collaboration  of domain experts and AI/LLMs. The new LLM/expertcombined  data  generation  method  will  have  a  long-lasting impact on the autism community regarding data representation  and  the  adoption  of  AI/LLMs  in  the  autism domain. Researchers and practitioners can use this method to generate data at comparatively low cost and develop specialized LLM  models  and assistants for healthcare, education,  workplace,  and  other  contexts.  The  LLM/expert combined  data  generation  method  can  also  be  generalized beyond the autism community to other types of disabilities.

The practical impacts of the project on autistic individuals span multiple disciplines. In the healthcare domain. The EBP recommendation model may be leveraged to support healthcare  professionals  in  providing  patient-  and  familycentered  care  by  identifying  effective  and  responsive  EBPs during medical care visits. The findings from the project may also be translational for the education and workplace domain.

With  the  nationwide  shortage  of  educational  evaluators, special and general education teachers, and a current process that is time-intensive, the development of a tool to rapidly and effectively  identify  EBPs  for  autistic  students  is  a  game changer. Within the workplace, managers and colleagues may utilize  the  outcomes  of  this  project,  in  conjunction  with additional  education  and  training,  to  better  support  autistic employees.  In  sum,  the  project  and  future  work  generated from it will be able to improve the quality of life of autistic individuals,  increase  the  understanding  and  support  of  this disability population, and improve inclusion and acceptance across different contexts.

## B. Limitations

The project and results are in its initial stages and include limitations that are expected  to be addressed  in future research. The reported work only engaged 4 autism experts for training  data  generation  and  the  validation  of  AI-generated cases and EBPs. The co-authors recognize that a much larger number  of  diverse  stakeholders  must  be  engaged  in  the training and validation process, including autism researchers, educators, family members, caretakers, and autistic individuals themselves, to reduce potential bias in the autism expert-created sample data.

Additionally,  Recent  research  suggested  that,  without enough real data in each generation of the autophagous loop, the quality and diversity of the generated data will gradually decrease [33]. We are planning to control this risk through two approaches: 1) collecting real-life data about autistic individuals  through  an  online  platform  to  supplement  the expert-generated real data as examples to teach the LLMs in data generation, and 2) using various LLMs, such as Llama, GPT, and BERT, to generate data. In this way, the amount of data generated by each model is comparatively low, avoiding significant  deterioration  in  data  quality.  This  approach  will also help control the potential bias contributed by each of the LLMs.

Thirdly, only a small number of AI generated cases and EBPs  have  been evaluated by human  experts.  Human evaluation of a much larger number of AI-generated cases is necessary to validate the effectiveness of the data generation and EBP recommendation functions.

## C. Future directions

Generative AI technology is rapidly evolving and research will need to evolve accordingly. The proposed data generation approach  will  need  to  be  refined  to  reflect  the  continual development of generative AI. Future directions will develop the first tailored approach to fine-tuning transformer models for  identifying  EBPs for autistic  individuals  using  a limited amount of human-labeled data and incomplete data through active  learning.  In  order  to  enrich  the  training  data,  more expansive data  from  stakeholders  will  need  to  be  gathered, including case studies generated by educators, families, and autistic individuals [21]. Additionally, field studies to assess the recommendation model in both education and healthcare contexts are needed. Data collected from the field studies will be used as additional training data for model fine-tuning to further improve the accuracy of the recommendation model.

## V. CONCLUSIONS

Recent breakthroughs in ML and AI signal timeliness for the  project.  The  growing  presence  of  AI  highlights  the importance  of  leveraging  this  powerful  tool  to  positively impact the lives of autistic individuals, their families, and all who work closely with this population. This project proposed and demonstrated an innovative human  expert  and AI combined approach to generate synthetic data about autistic individuals to support the identification of responsive EBPs. The  preliminary    results  suggest  that  data  generated  had promising quality. Through this approach, we are developing the  first  dataset  of  case  studies  of  autistic  individuals  to effectively  identify  EBPs  to  address  the  unique  needs  of autistic individuals. This project has notable impacts in both the  education  and  healthcare  context.  Accurate  and  rapid identification  of  EBPs  can  lead  to  targeted  intervention implementation to support skill development in educational settings and provide more patient- and family-centered care during medical interactions.

## ACKNOWLEDGMENT

This work was supported by the Thomas Wilson Sanitarium for Children of Baltimore City Foundation and the School of Emerging Technologies of Towson University and the Faculty Development and Research Committee at Towson University. We also would like to thank all the Autism experts who contributed to the work.

## Design and Development of a 3D Social Mobile Robot with Artificial Intelligence for Teaching with Assistive Technology

Galina Ivanova University of Ruse

Department of Computing Ruse, Bulgaria https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7799-1162

Aleksandar Ivanov Department of Computing University of Ruse Ruse, Bulgaria https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1030-0352

Abstract -In recent years, artificial intelligence is increasingly  used  in  almost  every  sector  of  society  for  the analysis of large databases, pandemic forecasting, image recognition,  machine  translation,  etc.  Robots  with  artificial intelligence, for example, can assist people by performing tasks in  extreme  or  dangerous  environments  (pandemic,  in  outer space, in explosive zones, etc.). Robots can also be used in the educational process of children with special educational needs, particularly for teaching children with autism spectrum disorder who may experience difficulties communicating with people. The paper presents the design and development process of a social robot with artificial intelligence for speech and faces emotions recognition. The aim of this paper is to present design process  of  low-budget  3D  prototype  of  mobile  social  robot capable of speech recognition, as well as faces  emotions recognition. The 3D robot components are designed and printed using  3D  software  and  printing  technologies.  A  seven-step algorithm has been presented for designing and implementation of the robot, ensuring it meets the functional requirements for assistive technology in education. The robot prototype has been implemented and tested with promising results.

Keywords- robot, artificial intelligence, assistive technology, special educational needs, autism spectrum disorder

## I. INTRODUCTION

In recent years, artificial intelligence is increasingly used in  almost  all  areas  of  our  society  for  the  analysis  of  large databases, pandemic forecasting, image recognition, machine translation, etc [1]. Projects in the field of artificial intelligence  are  relevant  and  at  the  same  time  extremely important for the development of our society [2]. Robots with artificial intelligence, for example, can help people to perform actions  in  extreme  conditions,  dangerous  or  inaccessible  to human  (pandemic,  in  space,  in  explosive  zones,  etc.)  [3]. Robots are proving to be assistive and transformative in the educational  process  for  children  with  special  educational needs [4, 5, 6], for example in teaching children with autism spectrum  disorder  who  have  difficulty  communicating  with people [7, 8, 9].

The research focuses on creating a low-budget 3D printed mobile social robot [10] with artificial intelligence capabilities for speech and faces emotions recognition. The robot can be used  as  a  personal  assistant  for  teaching  with  assistive technology by facilitating communication and interaction in a friendly, engaging manner [11, 12].

'This study is financed by the European Union-NextGenerationEU, through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan of the Republic of Bulgaria, project № BG-RRP-2.013-0001"..

Assistive technologies are designed to support people with special  needs  to  overcome  barriers  in  communication  and social interaction. In education, for example, assistive technology  allows  students  to  actively  develop  new  skills. Social robots with AI assistive technology, for example, can provide a safe and friendly environment for interaction with children  with  autism  spectrum  disorders,  who  often  have difficulty communicating with people [13, 14].

## III. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS

Extensive  testing  was  conducted  to  evaluate  the  robot's capabilities in speech recognition, moving and interaction.

The  results  of  testing  the  movements  of  the  prototype proved that the robot demonstrate stable and reliable movement navigating on various terrains without falling. The results  allow  us  to  conclude  that  the  possibilities  of  robot movement can be expanded with possibility of carrying small loads  -  for  example  delivering  items  or  medicines  to  ill patients.

At this stage, the robot can recognize some  facial expressions with more accuracy on happy face. The robot has signals for the different emotions by lighting and switching off a specially mounted light indicator, shown on Fig. 17.

Fig. 17. Light indicator for face emotions recognition



The robot can move also its head left and right using a programmable electrical motor.

Fig. 18 shows a test of the movements of the robot's legs. Both  legs  are  controlled  by  two  programmable  electrical motors. The robot moves with the help of rubber chains driven by electrical motors. The legs are separated from the body to allow  "walking-type"  movement  -  sequential  movement  of one leg and the other. The rotation in place shown on Fig. 18, is done by programming the motors in reverse directions for speed.

Fig.18.  Test of the movements of the robot's legs





The results of testing the ability to recognize speech and communicate  with  the  robot  proved  that  the  robot  could accurately interpret the meaning of questions and instructions and can respond a meaningful speech answer. The robot can also  execute  simple  commands  (such  as  playing  music  and etc.).  The  robot  communicates  at  this  stage  in  English  and Bulgarian.  Fig.  19  presents  a  fragment  of  the  developed Python program code in PyCharm program for a robot control library with voice commands in Bulgarian.

Fig. 19. Python program code in PyCharm program for a robot control library with voice commands in Bulgarian



The program code is optimized for easy integration and customization, which allows for additional adaptations to the specific user needs.

## IV. METHODOLOGY FOR TESTING WITH ASD CHILDREN

The robot prototype was tested with children with autism spectrum  disorders,  who  used  a  limited  set  of  words.  The interaction was conducted in an environment that encouraged calm  communication,  which  is  especially important for children  with  sensory  sensitivities.  The  robot  successfully interpreted  the  meaning  of  words  and  communicate  by providing  meaningful  voice  responses.  In  addition,  robot performed  simple  commands,  such  as  playing  music.  This confirms its applicability as a training tool. The results showed that the robot can support the learning process by providing an interaction.

The experiment focused on two key aspects: how the robot understands spoken words and how accurately it can recognize emotions.

- -Participants and testing environment: 5 children between  the  ages  of  7  and  12  participated  in  the experiments.
- -Environment: Testing took place in a quiet room to minimize distractions.
- -Interaction Session Time: The children engaged in a 10-15 minutes interactive session with the robot.
- -Procedure for Emotion Recognition: For  emotion recognition, children were asked to make five different facial expressions. The children were presented  with  a  series  of  5  images  of  different emotions, which they had to express while the robot tried  to  recognize  them.  Each  child  was  asked  to display five different facial expressions  (neutral, happy, sad, surprised, and angry). The robot achieved 82% accuracy  in  recognizing  emotions,  with  better performance on happy expressions, Fig. 20. Children with autism often display emotions in ways that are less  typical,  making  emotion  recognition  difficult. Happiness was the most easily recognized emotion in this study. Future research and development  of emotion recognition systems should prioritize improving the detection of other emotions to better support  the  emotional  well-being  of  children  with autism.
- -Procedure for speech recognition: Voice commands, included simple instructions with simple words, were used: start, stop, say hello, say cat, say dog. Speech recognition accuracy reached 75% (Fig. 21), and the robot responded to commands in about 2,5 seconds on average (Fig. 22).

Fig. 20. Emotion Accuracy Robot Recognition Results



Fig. 21. Accuracy of Speech Recognition Results Distribution of Response Times for Word Recognition



Fig.  22.  Results  for  Distribution  of  Response  Times  for Word Recognition



## V. CONCLUSIONS

Presented  3D  printed  robot  prototype  is  a  low  budget solution build with prefabricated parts at affordable price. A low-budget 3D printer with affordable material is used to print the parts of the robot, which simplifies the process of making specific plastic parts. The use of affordable components and materials  makes  it  applicable  in  various  educational  and therapeutic  environments,  especially  when  working  with children  with  special  educational  needs,  such  as  those  with autism spectrum disorders.

Tests with children with autism spectrum disorders have shown that the robot helps improve their communication and social  skills.  Robot's design, which includes bright colours, makes it attractive and engaging for children.

The 3D robot design and programmable system architecture allow for easy customization and upgrade of the robot's functionality adding new modules.

The  created  prototype  of  a  social  robot  with  artificial intelligence  can  be  integrated  into  various  real  educational scenarios for adaptive learning and support of children with different special educational needs.

Despite the positive results, further research is needed to improve  the  emotion  and  speech  recognition  algorithms. Additionally, future tests could include a wider range of users with different needs to increase the reach of the project.

## VI. CONCLUSION

In this work, detection of ASD and method of education of patient is being attempted using various machine learning techniques.  On  case  study  over  CNN,  SVM  and  LR  we found  out  CNN  accuracy  of  prediction  and  suggestion  on protocol dominated over other two.  CNN  model  with accuracy  of  98-99%  can  be  implemented  on  model  1  and model  2  so  patient can be diagnosed  and  non-clinical education  procedure  may  start  up  under  supervision  of therapist if required.

## Paper Source: Educational Robots and Their Control Interfaces How Can We Make Them More Accessible for Special Education
============================================================

## Educational robots and their control interfaces: how can we make them more accessible for Special Education?

Maria Jose Galvez Trigo 1 , 2[0000 -0001 -6492 -0955] , Penelope Jane 2[0000 -0003 -0003 -3358] 2[0000 -0002 -4600 -

- 2 { p.standen,sue.cobb } @nottingham.ac.uk
- Standen , and Sue Valerie Gray Cobb 6235] 1 University of Lincoln, Brayford Way, Brayford Pool, Lincoln LN6 7TS, UK mgalveztrigo@lincoln.ac.uk University of Nottingham, University Park, Nottingham NG7 2RD, UK

Abstract. Existing design standards and guidelines provide guidance on what factors to consider to produce interactive systems that are not only usable, but also accessible. However, these standards are usually general, and when it comes to designing an interactive system for children with Learning Difficulties or Disabilities (LD) and/or Autism Spectrum Conditions (ASC) they are often not specific enough, leading to systems that are not fit for that purpose. If we dive into the area of educational robotics, we face even more issues, in part due to the relative novelty of these technologies. In this paper, we present an analysis of 26 existing educational robots and the interfaces used to control them. Furthermore, we present the results of running focus groups and a questionnaire with 32 educators with expertise in Special Education and parents at four different institutions, to explore potential accessibility issues of existing systems and to identify desirable characteristics. We conclude introducing an initial set of design recommendations, to complement existing design standards and guidelines, that would help with producing future more accessible control interfaces for educational robots, with an especial focus on helping pupils with LDs and/or ASC.

Keywords: Access to education and learning · Assistive Robots · Design for All best practice · Design for Children with and without disabilities · ASC · Learning difficulties · Learning disabilities · educational robots

## 1 Introduction

Current standards applying to the design and development of interactive systems, such as those created by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) [18], provide requirements and guidelines to help designers and developers produce systems that are fit for their purpose. In terms of the creation of usable and accessible new technologies, there is an increasing number of ISO publications that provide guidance on the ergonomics of human-system interaction [12, 11, 26, 10, 9, 8, 7, 10, 25]. These standards are usually complemented with others related to software ergonomics for interfaces [18] and the accessibility of user interface components [13]. However, these standards are very general, and this is because they address all systems that involve human-system interaction and user interfaces. They clearly indicate that the needs of the end-user have to be taken into account, and that depending on the user the requirements of each system will be different. Nonetheless, they also require that all systems make a provision for allowing the use to those people with accessibility needs. This again is not very strict, because they also specify that when the nature or main objective of the system is lost or altered when making adaptations to ensure its accessibility, then, it is not required to make such adaptations.

The design of interactive systems may also be informed by more specific principles or guidelines, like Nielsen's ten 'heuristics' for user interface (UI) design [23], as well as by advice given by organisations or institutions representing different user groups.

In terms of guidelines specific to accessibility, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 [20] and the more recent working draft [1] are normally the ones against which web accessibility is measured. However, these standards, principles, guidelines, and pieces of advice are usually general, covering a very wide range of uses for the system to be designed and developed. Whilst the WCGA guidelines [20, 1] address matters related specifically to accessibility, and their use could be extended to other interactive systems and not only web content, they do not look into the accessibility of more complex systems, such as those necessary for the control of robots, since these systems may involve not only a graphical user interface (GUI), but also the physical robots and any buttons or sensors that these might have. Furthermore, and although it is normally considered good practice to follow those guidelines, in many cases certain accessibility features are disregarded by designers and/or developers.

Apossible reason behind paying less attention to the integration of accessibility features in control interfaces for educational robots, is that these interfaces are usually designed and developed for them to be used by programmers, by people learning how to code, or simply as games. The complexity of those interfaces targeted at programmers is usually high, which makes integrating certain accessibility features more complex. A similar issue occurs with interfaces aimed at people learning how to code. For those interfaces designed as games, and for games in general, the results of a recently published survey targeting professional game developers [16], reveals that only 39% of games developers have implemented accessibility measures (for those with sensory impairment, motor impairment, or other impairments) into their games. The report highlights that 'Unfortunately there is still a lot of pushback in implementing accessibility features' , and most of the accessibility measures taken focus on hearing or visual impairments.

More recently, Qbilat and Iglesias have proposed accessibility guidelines specific to tactile displays in Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) [27], however, these focus on service robots, and whilst many of them can be applied to educational robots, the nature of the use of these devices varies.

As a field, Educational Robotics (ER) has been recently defined as 'a field of study that aims to improve learning experience of people through the creation, implementation, improvement and validation of pedagogical activities, tools (e.g. guidelines and templates) and technologies, where robots play an active role and pedagogical methods inform each decision.' [3], and therefore, the robots used with those aims can be considered educational robots.

Educational robots have been used from the 1980's as tools to assist with the teaching of subjects in the area of Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) [24], and from the late 1990's as rehabilitation and education tools for children with ASC [22]. Nowadays, educational robots are mainly used to help with the teaching of STEM subjects, with an emphasis on programming and the logic behind it [19, 4, 21], but there is also an increasing number of studies and initiatives successfully introducing their use to help children with LD and ASC, focusing more on the later group [29, 2, 5, 30]. However, despite the advantages that educational robots offer to children with LD and/or ASC, recent studies have highlighted the lack of uptake for this technology in schools for children with Special Educational Needs (SEN), such as LD an/or ASC, mentioning, among other issues, the non-commercial availability and inadequate design of the interactive systems used to control them [17, 14, 15].

This paper presents an exploratory study where we aimed to answer the following research questions:

1. What are the main accessibility issues present in existing educational robots and their control interfaces?
2. How can future systems be made more accessible?

## 2 Methods

This paper presents the results of the analysis of existing interactive systems along with the results of focus groups with experts and an online questionnaire. The methods for each of them are presented.

## 2.1 Analysis of existing interactive systems

Design Analysis of existing systems looking at: capabilities of the control interface, main purpose and hardware needed to operate the robot.

Eligibility criteria For the educational robot system to be considered within this study, we applied the following eligibility criteria:

1. The system should be commercially available;
2. The system should have educational capabilities;
3. The system should include a robot and offer a clear way of interacting with it, such as an app that can be used from a mobile device or a computer, a remote, or buttons on the robot (i.e., not simply a turn-on, turn-off button or an autonomous robot);

## 4 M.J. Galvez Trigo et al.

4. A throughout description of the control interface should be available (i.e., from the manufacturer website, a manual, or a third-party review) or, for those where the control interface is an app and a detailed description is not available, the control interface should be freely available for us to download and check.

Procedure An initial selection of systems was drawn from a previous study [15], in which the five main reasons for low uptake of robots in Special Education were highlighted along with a table with information about different studies that used robots for interventions with children with Special Educational Needs (SEN). From that table we identified the three systems that met the eligibility criteria.

Since we did not want to limit the analysis to robots previously reported as used in research studies, we carried out a search in various online retailers of educational robots for other systems that met the eligibility criteria, even if these did not target children with SEN.

From both sources, a total of 26 systems were identified.

Fig. 1. Robots of the 26 systems analysed. Their names can be found in the first column of Table 1 and the order to follow in the image is row by row, from left to right and from top to bottom.



Analysis A member of the research team searched for information about each of the systems on the manufacturer's website as well as on retailers' websites. The information looked at included: the advertised main purpose of the robot, the control interface/s and the capabilities that it offered in terms of different activity types or ways of interacting with the robot, and the hardware needed to be able to interact with it. The characteristics of the systems as analysed can be seen in Table 1, and a picture of the relevant robots can be seen in Figure 1.

When a manual was available this was checked to gain a better understanding of the system being analysed.

In those cases in which an app was available for controlling the robot this was downloaded and explored to gain a better understanding of its capabilities, as well as of the potential accessibility issues that could be present in them. It is important to note that several apps were available to be downloaded and explored even if the relevant physical robot was not available to the researchers.

We took into account during the analysis the five main reasons of low uptake of robots in Special Education that were found during a previous study [15] to see if there was a clear evidence of any of them being present in the analysed systems. These five issues are: price, lack of user-friendly interface, lack of appropriate alternative ways of interaction for Special Education pupils, contents not being appropriate for Special Education students, and not being able to use different robots with the same control interface. When further expertise was necessary to determine if any of the issues was present with a specific system (i.e., expertise educating or living with children with SEN) this was sought during the focus groups with experts and parents described in the next subsection.

## 2.2 Focus groups with experts and parents, and questionnaire

Design Focus groups followed by an online questionnaire.

Participants Participants had to meet the following eligibility criteria to be able to participate in the study:

1. Be 18 years old or older;
2. Be an educator or expert in Special Education, through work-experience or training, or the parent or a close family member of a child with SEN;
3. Be fluent in either English or Spanish, as these were the languages in which the content and the focus groups would be presented.

A total of 32 participants were recruited across Spain and the United Kingdom (26 from Spain, 6 from the UK). Three of the participants were parents or close family members of a child with SEN at two different institutions, with one of them being the official Parents' Representative for the institution that the child attended. The total sample belonged to four institutions: a state-funded school for children with SEN in Toledo, Spain (6 participants); a partially statefunded school for children with SEN in Toledo, Spain (5 participants); the faculty

Procedure. Before the research activities commenced, ethics approval was obtained from the Faculty of Engineering Ethics Committee of the University of Nottingham.

To proceed with the recruitment of participants, four institutions from which recruitment for a previous study had taken place were contacted. Information about the current phase was given to the main point of contact, and they put us in touch with those that were interested in participating and met the eligibility criteria.

One in-person focus group lasting for approximately two hours was held at each of four institutions, three of them with 5-6 participants and one with 15.

During the focus group sessions, and after receiving informed consent from the participants, an initial presentation of the study was followed by an introduction to the results of the analysis of the 26 systems that can be seen in Table 1. Pictures and videos of the relevant systems were also shown to them, and a live demo of three representative systems that were available to the research team and their control interfaces. These systems were NAO Robot 3 (only for the focus group held in the UK), EZ-Robot JD 4 , Wonder Workshop Dash 5 , and a Sphero 6 . Participants were given the chance to ask questions about the systems presented to them and to try and interact with the ones that were available during the live demo. They were encouraged to share their thoughts whilst interacting with the systems. During the focus groups we asked them questions about the appropriateness of the systems for their use in Special Education. Among other questions we asked them how easy they found using the systems, if they would change anything and how, and if they would use them during a learning session with pupils with SEN or if they found any particular issues with them. We obtained permission to record the audio of two of the focus groups, during the other two, detailed notes were taken to ensure that relevant themes and opinions could be identified during the analysis. The focus groups were organised close in time and were run by the same researcher, which allowed to maintain consistency and facilitated the note-taking process.

At the end of the focus groups, an online questionnaire was sent to participants to help us identify more specific requirements for the design of interactive systems used to control educational robots, paying especial attention to usability and accessibility aspects of the design.

Analysis. The analysis was performed in three stages.

3 https://www.softbankrobotics.com/emea/en/nao

4 https://www.ez-robot.com/learn-robotics-getting-started-humanoid-robot-kit.html

5 https://uk.makewonder.com/dash/

6 https://sphero.com/collections/all/products/sphero-sprk-plus

First, a researcher transcribed and analysed the audio recordings of the two focus groups that were recorded, along with the notes taken during the other two focus groups. Initial codes were assigned to then lead to the main themes that could, as described by Braun &amp; Clarke [6], capture important information about the data in relation to the research question and represent meaning within the data set. A set of themes was defined, as well as extracts from the transcripts or the notes that represented each theme.

Further to the thematic analysis of the focus groups, the answers provided to the questionnaires were analysed. Some of the questions allowed for free-text answers. In this cases we explored if these fitted within the themes identified in the previous stage or if new themes arose.

A final exercise of consolidation of the results of the two prior stages was done to ensure that a final list of design recommendations could be produced.

## 3 Results

## 3.1 Analysis of existing systems

Main purpose of the system. We observed that most systems (23 of the 26 analysed) focused on teaching coding/programming skills and the logic behind it. Of the remaining 3, 1 was aimed at teaching robotics focusing more on the hardware side of the discipline, and 2 had a focus to act as healthcare companions or to teach other activities.

Interactive system used to control the robot. The main control method offered by 14 of the 26 systems analysed was an app with a block programming interface (see Table 2), which is the representation of coding concepts as interlocking blocks similar to puzzle pieces that are combined to create larger, more complicated sequences of actions. 17 systems offered various control systems using an app for a mobile device such as a smartphone o tablet. However, upon downloading and trying the apps, these could not be successfully controlled using embedded accessibility features provided by the device's operating system (usually called Switch Control or Switch Access) and therefore required the user to be able to interact with the screen of the device via drag &amp; drop gestures.

5 systems could only be used from a computer, with limited control or functionalities when using assistive technologies, and 4 systems had to be used with a physical remote programmer.

For those systems that used a control interfaced based on block programming, these were nearly identical, however, despite this fact, in all cases, each app or control interface could only be used with the robots from the same manufacturer.

## 3.2 Focus groups with experts and parents and questionnaire

Four main themes that relate to our question on how to make educational robots and their control interfaces more accessible were identified after the consolidation of the results from the focus groups and the free-text questions in the online questionnaire. These are:

Table 2. Number of interactive systems offering each type of control system

| Type of control system                 |   No. of systems (total |
|----------------------------------------|-------------------------|
| Block-programming                      |                      14 |
| Drag & drop of pre-existing activities |                       4 |
| Coding cards                           |                       4 |
| Remote programmer not on robot         |                       3 |
| Remote programmer on robot             |                       4 |
| Remote control through app             |                      11 |

1. Assistive technologies
2. Layout of User Interface (UI)
3. Purpose/activities offered
4. Physical aspects of the robot

Further to this, the results of the questionnaire answers to more specific questions related to the requirements for a desirable system are presented.

Theme 1: Assistive technologies. Participants believed that some of their pupils could successfully interact with a mobile device using drag &amp; drop gestures without the need for assistive technologies, but that this was limited to those that had better fine motor skills. Some indicated that being able to control the robot could serve as an incentive for some pupils to work on improving them, but that limiting those interaction to drag &amp; drop was not the best approach, as it would exclude many children. Regarding this, and after discussing the case of children with limited mobility that need to attend physiotherapy sessions for cervical rehabilitation, one participant said:

'For many children it is more interesting to work on some things through play, rather than for instance working on them with the physiotherapist, it is different' .

When we asked specifically about whether or not they considered that existing interfaces were accessible enough, they highlighted that they are not accessible enough for a Special School.

The three schools taking part in the study had several pupils that could only move their eyes, and therefore thought that more should be done to make the interfaces more accessible. Participants highlighted that they were already using assistive technologies such as micro-switches, eye-trackers or devices that kept a screen on if the child maintained their head up (for those following cervical rehabilitation), and that it would be great it those devices could be used with a robot.

'In our classrooms we do have micro-switches, then, that's it, depending on the characteristics of the child, if they can use a bigger or smaller switch, or even if they can use it only with one finger or with the whole hand, then... it would be really motivating' .

Participants mentioned as well that, whilst some of the interfaces could be used by the educators to trigger certain actions on the robot even if the child could not operate it, this was not ideal:

'It is not that much that teachers used the robots to teach the children, but that the children could use the robots themselves, that they could learn with them themselves' .

Theme 2: Layout of User Interface (UI). When it came to control interfaces for the robots, participants found more interesting the use of apps than the use of buttons on the robot or on a remote, and some did not feel that it was safe for the robot to be handled/touched by some of their pupils:

'Our pupils... that, some of them interact with things with slaps and, imagine! rraass! to the floor, and the materials they are made of are so rigid...' .

Participants indicated that, in most cases, items on the screen were very small and that, even those pupils that could successfully interact with the interface without assistive technologies would likely find it too difficult.

'I don't know you, but I find those buttons too small even for me, look at all that empty space on the screen' .

They also highlighted that the icons used to depict the action that a button would trigger were in some instances confusing. Whilst testing some of the apps themselves, one participant was very vocal in that regard, asking other participants if they knew what some of the icons meant, because they didn't.

When talking more specifically about block programming, participants in general found very interesting that you could program your own activities using the interface. However, they believed that without proper training or enough time to get familiar with the interface, it could be confusing, and that it requires to dedicate time and effort to create any activities that they could later use with they pupils:

'It's not just creating the activity in the app, I'd have to, I don't know, learn how to create anything with it first, then think of an activity that I could make, and then make it, and what if after having designed the activity I see that I cannot create it with the blockly?' .

An issue highlighted relating to the layout of the UI was that participants considered that most apps had too many unnecessary distractions on screen, which could lead to attention problems for pupils.

Theme 3: Purpose/activities offered. In general, participants felt that, whilst some pupils could benefit from learning how to code or the logic behind it, for their pupils this was not appropriate at a cognitive level:

'We have pupils with a very low cognitive level, then there are children that, precisely, you can expect a really light response from them, and so it's what it is, basic responses, but these things (of the robots) catch their attention' .

They also indicated that these technologies could be used to teach them how to anticipate things that would happen during the day, and that it was not a matter of being able to create complicated activities, that sometimes simple ones can be used to teach many concepts:

'Many times, with showing them, I don't know, a plate, a child can learn that after that we are going to see the menu because it's nearly lunch time or things like that, activities as simple as that, you can adapt it a bit to the different activities that the school does' .

Participants felt as well that the ideal would be to be able to load pre-made activities onto the app and the robot:

'Having a bank of activities that you could load and use would be very useful, and that you could get and use those activities without needing to code. That would save on work or at least make that work easier... it would be quicker.'

Theme 4: Physical aspects of the robot. Participants did not limit themselves to commenting on the control interfaces for the robots. Some physical aspects of these were also considered an issue.

During the demo of one of the robots, participants observed the use of flickering lights by one of the default behaviours of a robot, and they emphasised the importance of either adding a warning or disabling any flickering light by default, as this could negatively affect people with epilepsy.

In one of the focus groups it was also mentioned that robots that use ultrasounds to communicate with a control device should likely be avoided in Special Schools:

'It's supposedly designed for a school environment. It can interfere mainly with hearing aids. Sometimes my child says: dad, that sound is very loud; and I tell him: what a hearing sense you have! I can't hear anything! With young children that must be... don't use it, that really caught my attention' .

Participants also raised privacy concerns regarding the existence of cameras in some of the robots, and one participant suggested he would tell others to 'put a piece of tape' on the camera before using it in a school. Another participant suggested the avoidance of Internet connection from the robot and to use Bluetooth connectivity to communicate with its control interface instead.

Another aspect that was already mentioned within Theme 2 is that the robots seem to be made of very rigid materials and thus are not very robust for them to trust that a child would be able to interact with it via touching its sensors or buttons without damaging it.

Other questionnaire responses. From the responses to the questionnaires that participants filled in after the interviews, we observed the following:

- -27 of the 32 participants recommend the colour combination of black and yellow for a Graphical User Interface (GUI). The other 5 participants each recommended a different colour combination different from black and yellow (see Figure 2).

- -22 participants recommended to use round-shaped buttons in the interface instead of those with other shapes.
- -There was no consensus on whether the font type to use should be upper or lower case, and normal or bold face.
- -The two font faces identified as the best to use were Comic Sans and Arial (see Figure 3).
- -There is a general consensus on the need to include characteristics such as: 1) showing circular buttons on screen; 2) allowing the user the configuration of the number of buttons to have; 3) showing pictograms, although again, there is no agreement on the type of pictograms to use; 4) offering alternative ways of interaction; 5) not requiring Internet to work; 6) being able to create user profiles for pupils; 7) Allow access to pupil's profiles to their teachers and parents; 8) being able to use the same system to control different robots; 9) offering rewards to the pupils; and 10) not requiring any coding/programming knowledge to be able to use the system effectively.
- -In Table 3 we can see the assistive technologies that participants recommended to integrate as compatible with these systems, and how many participants recommended each of them.
- -In Table 4 we can see how many participants recommended each feature to have in the pupil's profile.
- -In Table 5 the activities that participants recommended it would be desirable to have in the interactive system can be seen.
- -As last factors to be taken into account, we can see in Table 6 the types of rewards that participants recommended the robots should produce when a pupil performed well enough in an activity.
