## DISCUSSION

## Challenges and recommendations for ASD apps

The features provided by ASD apps for college students and workers are identi fi ed in this study. In fact, previous research studies ( cf. , Rehman et al., 2021 ; Gallardo-Montes, Caurcel Cara &amp; Rodríguez Fuentes, 2022 , etc .) focused on ASD apps for children, however, college students and workers with ASD might experience several communication issues, which make their daily activities challenging. ASD apps provide a great opportunity for them in improving their skills. Moreover, the environment in fl uences people with ASD behavior such as loud noises, strong smells, etc . The challenges mentioned in the previous research studies ( cf. , Sulaimani &amp; Gut, 2019 ; Bury et al., 2021 , etc .) address mainly the dif fi culty to access the several provided services, the number of individuals for each service, limited knowledge about autism, etc . In addition, recent statistics proved that around 85% of the United States college graduates with autism are unemployed ( Catalano.N, 2020 ). Autistic workers confront several challenges in their workplace such as the lack of accessibility to appropriate employment resources, dif fi culties in adjusting to the new environment, etc . In order to determine whether the ASD apps available on Google Play and Apple App stores satisfy the needs of autistic adults, we investigated the user feedback on ASD apps. This analysis will allow us to propose some lines for apps ' improvements in the near future to improve the negative features in order to better satisfy the autistic needs. Several ASD apps used AI-based techniques for speech assistant ( e.g ., speech translation, speech to text, etc .), the use of ASD apps could improve autistic ' s life especially those with communication dif fi culties.

As we mentioned previously, user reviews have been classi fi ed into positive, negative or neutral. All these categories provide user opinions towards the ASD apps or towards a speci fi c feature offered by them. By analyzing positive reviews, we noticed that ASD apps help users successfully manage their daily activities, track their tasks, and ensure appropriate communication with others. For instance, the users of the HabitRPG app considered that ' This app has definitely helped me get my life back on track ' . ASD apps are recommended for people with autism to develop their social interactions. In fact, autistic in general have deep dif fi culties to communicate with their colleagues in universities, work space, etc . Providing several ways for communication is very helpful in this situation.

By analyzing negative reviews, we noticed that usually users complained about the quality of ASD apps ( e.g ., availability, usability, etc .). For instance, users requested that the app should work of fl ine ' Can you make this Offline ' , and ' I just want to re-quest an update that would keep me tracking my habits and dailies even when I am offline ' . While others criticized the complexity of some interfaces ' It ' s a nice concept, but there ' s too much information given at once for setting it all up ' , ' Good app but it is confusing ' , and ' It looks super good but I can ' t figure it out how to use it ' . Mobile apps for ASD people should not be complex. In fact, sometimes, the quality factor of ASD apps is classi fi ed as sophisticated and advanced functionality. It is not critical or compulsory for a patient ' s health but it facilitates and attracts users. Users also revealed other quality issues such as portability issues such as ' I can ' t login to android version or register on it ' , and ' It ' s a very good app if you want build need habits ' , reliability issues ' It crashes ' , and maintainability issues ' As soon as I did the update my acct. was gone. What happened? ' In addition, other users complained about the sounds used in some ASD apps such as ' I only tried it for about 10 minutes but I hated the sounds. That ' s the main thing I wanted ' . In fact, noise may affect autistic and increase their anxiety. For these reasons, developers should work on improving the quality of ASD apps.

Besides the quality improvement, some users suggested to update existing functionality. For instance, for the ' Todoist ' app, users proposed to update the set up a task feature by allowing the user to add a task by indicating only the week and not the day ' There ' s no good way to set up a task that you want to do once a week but on any day ' , and ' Good for people who want to develop daily habits. Not so good for weekly habits ' . In fact, the calendar feature is very important for people with ASD to help them managing their daily tasks as well as their habits. This feature has been mentioned by many users of the selected apps such as ' There is no sort of calendar overview ' . In addition, daily tasks must be related to weekly habits. Users recommended to add connect the daily tasks with the habits in order to check the user performance history, ' Allows me to track dailies, but doesn ' t connect them to habits ' . Actually, people with autism have a resistance to change. Hence, having and maintaining a routine is very important for autistic. Other users revealed an issue about the noti fi cations feature in some apps such as ' Todoist ' and ' HabitRPG ' for instance ' Notifications don ' t work ' , ' I need the notifications and they have NEVER worked for me , etc . ' , ' I ' d rate 5 stars if the app didn ' t send reminders for stuff I ' ve done already ' , and ' Sure it gamifies your tasks, but it doesn ' t remind you of anything ' . In fact, noti fi cations is an important feature for tasks management, it is very important to reminder the user about his activity. In addition, users suggested to add sub-task list in the ' Todoist ' app ' Wish there is a way to add sub-lists under one task ' . On the other hand, users complained about some features that may not work correctly in their country such as registration payment for instance, ' Kindly create an MPESA payment method? ' . Moreover, users have reported some bugs such as The habit counter is always resetting itself. Which means the feature exists but it includes some mistakes that must be corrected. A habit counter should not be reset unless the user asked for it. Finally, the users were not satis fi ed by the registration feature in some apps for example ' I can ' t register ' , and ' Please help me Wanted to delete my account. There is no option to do so ' .

In summary, to answer the fi rst research question, we conclude that technologies such as smartphones and ASD apps can be bene fi cial in helping adult autistic manage their daily activities and improve their communication skills with their colleagues, supervisors, etc . In addition, ASD apps are used by ASD people to better organize their tasks. Regarding the second research question, we conclude that despite their satisfaction with ASD apps, users proposed adding some features such as statistics about daily activities and the to-do list. These features have been highly requested by ASD apps users. In addition, the use of noti fi cation is the most requested feature by users, while others are complaining about the reminder sound. Based on the negative reviews, mobile apps developers should improve the quality of ASD apps and add the requested features ( e.g ., noti fi cation, daily activities, etc .). In addition to the quality characteristics, some functionality in the selected apps should be improved as well. In fact, although several apps provide the management tasks feature, users are not really satis fi ed with it. In addition, the noti fi cations feature is missing in some apps or does not work correctly. These two features are very important for people with ASD since they help them managing their lifestyle and keeping their routine.

## Limitations

In this sub-section, we discuss the limitations of this study. In fact, the analysis of the main features provided in this study is based on the feedback of users. Although, the selected ASD apps are developed mainly for people with ASD ( e.g ., Work Autonomy, T2 Mood Tracker, etc .), there is no guarantee that all the collected reviews are written by autistic people. For this reason, it is recommended for future work to test the selected ASD apps by people with autism and get their feedback instantly. blackMoreover, some reviews such as ' great ' , ' useful ' , and ' Amazing ' , could be considered as fake feedback. In our preprocessing tasks we did not remove them, however, these reviews do not affect the results obtained in this article. In fact, in our analysis we focus on the features provided by the ASD apps and how well the user is satis fi ed with it. And since these reviews do not talk about any feature, they will not be analyzed. In addition, the features provided by ASD apps should be also identi fi ed by installing and testing them.

On the other hand, each user review has been labeled with one type (positive, negative, or neutral). But in reality, one review may include more than one type. In fact, over the process of labeling reviews, we noticed that the proportion of the reviews with multiple types is low. In addition, we used a tokenization with our intervention to separate these reviews into a fi ne-grain sentences, which can be labeled with one type before the classi fi cation experiments are conducted. Hence, we believe that this issue did not affect our experimental results. Moreover, the dataset used in this article includes a number of positive reviews more important than the negative reviews. In order to limit the problems due to the imbalanced data, as recommended by Ito et al. (2021) , we used the right evaluation metrics to evaluate the machine learning models. Hence, we were not restricted in our evaluation on the accuracy metric but also we used precision, recall, F1 score, and AUC. In fact, accuracy is not the best metric to be used in evaluating machine learning models with imbalanced datasets ( Ito et al., 2021 ). Other metrics could be better such as: the confusion matrix, which show the correct predictions and incorrect predictions; precision, which measure the classi fi er ' s exactness; recall, which measure the classi fi er ' s completeness, etc . For this reason, we can conclude that the used machine learning models have been appropriately evaluated even with an imbalanced dataset.

## CONCLUSIONS

The main issues of ASD are (1) the inability and the deviance in social communication and interaction among the world, and (2) the limit and repetitive movements, the restriction of the patterns of behavior, interests, and the presence of stereotyped activities. The existence of these symptoms leads adults (students or workers) with ASD to have several challenges when forming new meaningful relationships. An individual with Autism has a manner to communicate either verbally, non-verbally, or both. Understanding the awareness of ASD

in our community helps in improved sup-port for adults with ASD in their universities and companies.

In this article, we investigated the opinions of ASD app users to understand their perspectives on an autism-friendly environment in order to suggest possible key in-sights for the improvement of these apps. For this purpose, we applied the SLR process to select the 13 most relevant ASD apps. Then, we used ML and DL models for user feedback analysis on ASD apps, hence, the collected user reviews from the selected 13 ASD apps are classi fi ed into positive, negative, or neutral opinions. We collected 97,051 reviews including positive, negative and neutral opinions from the Google Play and Apple App stores. After that, in the process of user reviews analysis, we applied NLP techniques, ML, and DL models and we proposed to combine RNN with LSTM models fi rstly, and RNN with GRU models secondly, with some amelioration, in order to classify user reviews into negative, neutral, or positive opinions. The evaluation results proved that the RNN-LSTM model provided the best accuracy of 96.58% and best AUC of 99.41% in classifying user reviews according to sentiment polarity. In addition, by analyzing the collected reviews, we concluded that despite the satisfaction of ASD app users towards the main features provided by these apps, users still complain especially about their quality issues especially usability, reliability, etc . Developers should focus more on improving the quality of their ASD apps and adding some features such as noti fi cation and to-do-list.

For future work, we propose to classify the collected user reviews according to the quality characteristics of the ISO 25000 quality model ( e.g ., usability, reliability, portability, etc .). Moreover, we will work on prioritizing relevant user reviews, which could be helpful in identifying the quality characteristics that should be improved fi rst.

## Paper Source: Towards Automatic Engagement Recognition of Autistic Children in a Machine Learning Approach
============================================================

## Towards Automatic Engagement Recognition of Autistic Children in a Machine Learning Approach

Zihan Tan, Anjia Zhou, Xiaojun Hei, Yayu Gao and Chengwei Zhang

School of Electronic Information and Communications Hubei Provincial Key Laboratory of Smart Internet Technology Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China, 430074 Email: {tanzihan, zaj, heixj, yayugao, zhangcw}@hust.edu.cn

Abstract -Children suffering from autism have been continue rising globally and  the early intervention may  significantly improve  the  social  and  cognitive  capacity  of  them.  The  autism treatment in China is still largely based on training courses and interventions,  nevertheless,  lacking  of  professional  teachers  is  a severe problem. Traditional individual training classes are mainly based on teachers' evaluation of students' emotional feedback, and there remain prejudices. The continuous information technology advance,  such  as  ML,  have  been  inspiring  novel  diagnosis  and treatment  for  autistic  children.  Note  that  the  majority  of  the current research on emotional recognition of autistic children have not been conducted on the autistic children in China, in this paper, we  aim  to  conduct  a  emotional  recognition  study  for  them.  We study  the  one-to-one  autism  training  class,  and  propose  an automatic engagement recognition framework to track the behaviors  and  affection  of  autistic  children  by  ML.  With  the improved spatial temporal graph convolutional  neural  network, our  experiments  based  on  the  available  datasets  show  that  the behavior  recognition  accuracy  reaches  beyond  90%  and  the affection recognition achieves 99%. The result demonstrates that the proposed system can analyze the relationship among arousal, valence and expression category for the autism training class.

Keywords -autism, action recognition, facial expression recognition

## I. INTRODUCTION

Autism  Spectrum  Disorders  (ASDs)  are  a  category  of Pervasive  Developmental  Disorders  (PDDs)  that  are  often described as a kind of disease caused by genetic or other factors which  can show social communication disorders and repeated sensory movements at a early stage. As a spectrum disorder, the autism spectrum ranges from mild to severe, and sometimes it takes  a lifetime to prove that a patient has the disease [1] [2]. Although autism  is  a  physiological  disease,  the  current  major treatment options are based on education and behavioral interventions,  drugs  are  just  important  supplementary  means. But the cost   of health care, school and care-givers brought by education and behavioral interventions is  very  high  and  often imposes a huge burden on the patient's family [1]. At present, the incidence of ASDs in the world is increasing year by year [3]. According to the investigation of the diagnosis rate of children with  autism  by  Deborah  L.  Christensen  et  al.  in  2012,  the diagnosis rate of children with autism in the United States is 1.56% [4].  Although  there  is  no  official  data  in  China  currently,  the article of Yumei Wan in 2013 estimated that   the prevalence of ASDs is 24.5/10000, which is considered that there may be 0.25% of children with autism in China [5], related research is urgently needed.

At the  same  time, Matson et al.'s research  shows  that  the sooner autism  patients  are  discovered,  the  better  the  effect  of intervention  treatment  will  be  [6].  Interventions  in  childhood autism treatment are the most effective, it is of great significance to pay attention to  the treatment of this special group of children with autism. In the process of analyzing children with autism, Rudovic  et  al.  of  MIT  Media  Lab  found  that  children  with autistic backgrounds of different cultures had different performances under the same external stimulus, however, due to the small  number  of  experimental  samples  and  the  large differences in experimental individuals, they are unable to make causal explanations for behavioral differences in different cultural  backgrounds  [7].  At  the  same  time,  Chinese  autistic children  are  not  included  in  most  of  the  foreign  research institutes, so there are still many gaps in this area to explore.

We intend  to  carry  out  emotional  recognition  research  for autistic children in China, and combine the related technologies such  as  DL  to  realize  personalized  recognition  that  suits  the characteristics of Chinese children's performance. It is conducive to effectively adjust the feedback of autistic children on the teaching content of individual training classes, so as to realize the real 'personalized learning teaching', which will be helpful for autistic teaching to step towards informationization and intellectualization.

## II. PROBLEM STATEMENT

At present, researches on autism start late in China, treatments  of  autistic  children  are  mainly  based  on  educational intervention, supplemented by drug therapy [8]. Teachers and doctors  are  more  likely  to  guide  the  performance  of  autistic children. Studies have shown that the rehabilitation of autistic children  in  special  education  schools  has  achieved  certain results, but those schools have a small number of teachers and fewer high-education teachers [9]. Under this situation, how to assist teachers and ease the burden has become a researchable direction, teachers need to observe and analyze the behavior of children with autism, which provides space for the application of computer technology. Therefore, a researchable direction in the  teaching  field  of  autistic  children  is  combining  computer technology with traditional diagnosis  and  treatment  methods, using computer technology to assist teachers in observing and analyzing the behavior of autistic children, reducing the burden on  teachers  and  enabling  teachers  to  accumulate  experience quickly to help more children with autism.

Previously, there have  been  many  studies  abroad  that combine  artificial  intelligence  with  interventional  therapy  for autism [10] [11]. One of the important directions is to quantify the external performance of autistic children [7].  In 2018, this quantitative method was applied to the teaching scene of autistic children  with  robot  participation.  A  deep  learning  model  was proposed  to  analyze  the  behavioral  characteristic  of  autistic children, hoping to help robots understand children's behaviors and  emotions  [12].  In  the  same  year,  Qandeel  Tariq  et  al. proposed to apply machine learning algorithms to help doctors shorten the diagnosis time of autistic children [13].

Thus,  there  are  much  data  in  the  world  to  support  the promotion  of  autism  education.  Different  races,  cultures  and other factors have a certain impact on the establishment of autism model, so it is particularly important to establish a database based on  Chinese  children.  However,  due  to  the  problems  of  data privacy  and reliability  of  information  technology,  parents  and relevant organizations in China are skeptical about the feasibility of this scheme, which makes it difficult   to establish a database. This project aims to design a gesture and expression recognition scoring system for autistic children through the original database to assist teachers in autism classroom, which can also facilitate the establishment of the database for autistic children in China.

## III. ALGORITHM DESIGN

## A. Basic Idea

Taking the video as the carrier and the classroom teaching as the  background,  the  desig n  of  students' emotional  perception scheme is put forward to assist teachers to grasp the stu dent's emotional  performance  during  the  classroom  teaching  and present the student's situation during class with data.  The design of the program relies on the actual need of the cooperative autism rehabilitation  education  institution,  and  the  teaching  scenario, task,  and  feedback  are  modeled  according  to  real  cases.  The scenario is a one-to-one teaching session in the actual classroom, that is, a individual training session. Every teaching task is about 3 minutes and the video duration depends on the single teaching task time, which starts with the extraction of the current teaching task and ends up with the student completing the teaching task or timeout. The camera takes an unobstructed fixed-angle view of  the  sample,  the  data  sample  obtained  are  a  series  of  short videos  and  teaching  plans  corresponding  to  the  classroom teaching  content.  The  basic  idea  of  the  research  based  on individual training class is shown in Fig. 1.

In  a  typical  one-to-one  ABA  training  class  for  autistic children, several roles are involved including teachers, autistic students,  parents,  and  assistants.  The  content  arrangement  of each classroom session is selected from the activity list by the teacher,  that  is  to  say,  the  task  of  the  classroom  activity  is limited and definite,  so does the  feedback action. The list of classroom activities is shown in Table I.

## B. Design of Emotional Evaluation Index

Emotion is one of the external manifestation of students in classroom activities,  which  is  a  direct  feedback  to  the  current teaching tasks, it has its own value to study students' emotions in  classroom  learning  activities.  Therefore,  it  is  particularly important to pay attention  to the emotional change of  autistic children in class. At the same time, emotion can be reflected by the  student's  classroom  participation  and  expression information. Thus, we pick them as indicators for relevant  research.

1) Emotional  performance  score  based  on  participation: Children with autism have the most obvious behavior during the interaction  process,  and  many  of  the  literature  focus  on  the definition of participation represented by actions. The object of this project  is  the actions  and  expressions  of  autistic  children. Therefore, we choose to define participation from the perspective of action referring to Kim's definition in 2008 [14], which is shown in TABLE II, that is, responsibility of autistic students to current teaching tasks. Kim divides it into 0-6 grades according  to  the  therapist's  instruction  repetition  degree  for autistic children and the children's responses. Each grade gives different scores, and the core logic is that the fewer instruction repetitions,  the  higher  participation.  Considering  the  actual situation of the project, the picture captured by the camera does not include the teacher's actions. In addition, since the teacher's instructions  are  often  expressed  in  the  form  of  voice,  but  the current data acquisition scheme does not include the recording function, so the logic is redesigned. Considering the actual oneto-one teaching scenario, the teacher will assign teaching tasks to the student, and the student need to respond correctly. Based on  the  correct response,  the  student's  completion  degree  and completion  time  are  available.  Setting  the  action  completion time as t and the duration of a single teaching session as m, the E = t/m  can be considered as the student's participation degree in  the  current  teaching  task.  The  smaller  the  E,  the  faster  the response of the student under the same teaching task, that is, the higher the participation of the student, the higher the E, which indicates the student's response slower, when E = 1, that is the student fails to respond correctly during the task time, and the participation is the lowest.

TABLE II. K IM'S 0-5 RICHTER PARTICIPATION CODING

|   Participation Level | Meaning                        | Example                                               |
|-----------------------|--------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
|                     5 | High Participation             | Immediately responding to the content                 |
|                     4 | Medium Participation           | Needing the guidance of Teachers                      |
|                     3 | Low Participation              | Teachers are required to repeat 2-3 times             |
|                     2 | Participation Is Extremely Low | Teachers are required to repeat more than three times |
|                     1 | Non-participation              | No response                                           |
|                     0 | Escaping                       | Going away                                            |

## 2) Emotional performance score based on expression:

There  are  many  ways  of  human  emotional  expression,  physiological  signals  such  as  blood  pressure,  heart  rate,  hormone levels  and  so  on,  external  manifestations  such  as  rich  facial expressions, tone, and limb movements, etc. Taking the privacy issues and the difficulty of data acquisition in to account, it is clear  that  choosing  the  external  manifestation  is  better.  In  the collected  video  signals,  we  can  get  most  of  the  emotional characteristic from facial expressions, so facial expressions can be used as emotional expressions of autistic students. There are two types of facial expression recognition in the academic circles. The  first  one  is  the  discrete  model  which  recognizes  facial expressions as happy, sad, angry, surprised, nervous, etc [15], the other is the continuous model, such as the PAD (pleasure, arousal, dominance) model proposed by Mehrabian in 1996 [16], the  EAP  (Evaluation,  Activity,  Power)  model  proposed  by Cowie  in  2001  [17],  and  Arousal-Valence  two-dimensional continuous  model  proposed  by  Russel  in  1980  [18],  etc.  For continuous models, the expression can be scored directly from its  dimension because of the determination of   its continuous value. Taking the Arousal-Valence model as a example, its two dimensions  represent  the  degree  of  pleasure  and  intensity  of emotion, and the score is between [-1, +1], for the discrete model, when the more people are involved and the higher degree of the satisfaction,  the  more  positive  the  feeling  and  the  higher  the emotional intensity [19], so it can be scored according to the type of  emotions.  This  experiment  chooses  to  identify  expressions based on discrete models.

## C. Evaluation Algorithm

The algorithm consists of two parts, one based on actionbased engagement scores and one based on expression-based Arousal and Valence scores. The two parts also need to acquire data and extract feature points firstly, we use video information (the classroom camera recording) and corresponding teaching task  information  (teaching  activity  plan)  as  the  data  to  be processed, then feature points are extracted from video using the OpenPose,  a  open  source  framework.  The  feature points extracted are divided into two parts for action  recognition and expression  recognition, and  the scores are based  on  the recognition results.

The main research of  this  paper  is  action  and  expression recognition based on autistic children's classroom situation. So the work is mainly the model and algorithm design based on the two parts.

The main purpose of action recognition is to recognize the action matrix and score the degree of participation. Based on the information obtained from the teaching plan, we generate the correct action label, extract the feature points from the actual classroom  video  and  transform  them  into  the  feature  points matrix,  so  as  to  predict  the  action  of  autistic  children,  if  the prediction  result  is  different  from  the  label,  the  participation degree is set to the lowest directly. If they are consistent, the action completion degree of the corresponding column of the matrix is calculated according to the label of the core feature points of the correct action. Since the matrix column label is the frame label, and the OpenPose converts video to feature point data in the frame  unit,  the  frame  selection  is  uniformly distributed according to the time, so the frame number naturally indicates the time information. When an action is disassembled, there must be angular and distance information between its core feature points. This information can be used to measure whether the action is started or completed. The frame number t of the current picture is obtained. If the total number of frames is m, the participation score can be set to E = t/m.

Happy

Fig. 2 AN AROUSAL-VALENCE TWO DIMENSIONAL CONTINUOUS MODEL [18]



The algorithm of graph convolutional neural network is used for  action  recognition.  Considering  that  the  duration  of  the teaching of students in the one-to-one teaching class of autism is generally no more than 3 minutes and the actions  that students should complete are simple and clear, the teaching situation in the video can be completely converted into a matrix of actions, and  the  form  is  referencing  to  the  ST-GCN  network  model proposed by the Chinese University of Hong Kong in 2018 [20]. The model expands the graph convolutional neural network to the  spatiotemporal  graph  convolutional  neural  network,  and adds a spatial structure in the form of frame to in simple graph data.  The  spatial  feature  of  the  action  is  represented  by  the change of the joint point of the same frame, and the temporal feature during the motion is represented by the change of the same joint point between different frames. The method to score the action participation is calculating the start time of the action. When the action starts, the coordinates of the feature point will change.  Considering  the  connection  of  the  same  key  point corresponding to the two frames as a vector, the change of the motion can be judged by the vector displacement and the angle change, then the start time of the action can be obtained, thereby the participation score can     be calculated. Euclidean distance (Eq.  1)  and  vector  cosine  (Eq.  2)  are  commonly  used  to represent the difference between vectors. The former indicates the  difference  in  displacement  between  vectors,  which  can reflect  the  range  of  the  change  in  action,  the  greater  the Euclidean distance, the greater the range of action change. The latter  indicates  the  direction  difference  between  the  vectors, when the value is closer to 1, the closer the direction change of vectors  is  to  0 ◦ ,  and  the  value  is  closer  to  0,  the  closer  the direction change of vectors is to 90 ◦ .

/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3/g3



For the expression recognition part, the aim is to score the expression matrix with Arousal-Valence [18].  The  expression feature  point  information  output  by  feature  point extraction module  is  the  same  as  the  action  feature  point  information output, which is a matrix with row label as frame  sequence and column  label  as  feature  point  coordinates.  In  the  expression analysis  module,  because  the  Arousal-Valence  model  is  a continuous  model,  if  the  expression  analysis  is  done  directly, it will become a regression problem. The  expression intensity parameter A and the expression pleasure parameter V can be obtained  by  directly  inputting  the  matrix.  If  the expression recognition is regarded as a discrete model, it is a classification problem. The specific expression is obtained and then mapped.

The algorithm used for expression recognition is Random Forest.  Random  Forest  is  a  common  method of  Ensemble Learning  [21]  in  machine  learning.  The  core  idea  of  it  is to construct multiple decision trees and then vote on the classification result to produce the final result. Sampling with replacement and  sampling  randomly  of  the  features  when generating the  decision  tree,  which  cause  the  correlation between the decision tree is very low, therefore it can effectively reduce over- fitting, and the accuracy of the final classification result  is also  improved.  At  the  same  time,  the  decision  tree can  also be  used  to  score  the  importance  of  the  feature,  the higher the score, the greater the contribution of the feature to the result. The expression recognition module directly outputs the  label of  expression  when  the  sequence  of  feature  points based  on pictures is input, that is to say, uniform sampling for video tags is needed. According to the definitions of Arousal and Valence, correlate the scores of the two dimensions with the expression tags. By maintaining the score association table, the Arousal  and  the  Valence  scores  of  the  expression  can  be obtained by looking up it.

## IV. EXPERIMENT AND RESULT

## A. Dataset

In the experiment, the data of autistic children have not been obtained for some objective reasons, so the public data set is used. First, from a medical point of view, even if the movement and the  expression  of  autistic  children  are  different  from  ordinary people, from the computer point of view, the composition of the movement can be characterized by the positional displacement of  the  joint,  and  the  composition  of  the  expression  may  be characterized by the shape change and positional displacement of the facial features. That is to say, both autistic children and ordinary people belong to human beings in the field of actions and expressions, so the feature item of the sample are the same, but the feature value will be different, therefore it does not make a  fundamental  difference  between  algorithms.  Secondly,  the main difference between children and youth lies in their different degrees of physical development, but the input of this project algorithm is feature point data, action feature points are bound to  the  bone  joints, and  facial  features  are  bound  to  the  facial features  and  cheeks,  which  can  minimize  the  physical  gap between the youth and the actual sample children in open data sets.

The action data set uses NTU RGB+D [22], it is based on the single action recognition taken in the laboratory with the fixed camera, which contains 60 actions, 40 of them are daily actions, 9 of them are medical actions, and 11 require col- laboration of more than one person. The scene of NTU RGB+D is laboratory. In the video, the same action is repeated    by several people and shot  from  different  angles.  Connecting  with  the  one-to-one teaching  environment  of  autistic  children,  NTU  RGB+D  has some  similarities  in  fixed  scenes  and  single  action.  Although autistic children and normal children must have different actions, once the action is converted into joint coordinates, this difference can be reduced. Excluding the difference of action, NTURGB+D and the one-to-one teaching scenario of the partner have good consistency.  According  to the  setting  task  of  the  partner's individual  training  classroom  teaching  session,  this  project selected 12 actions from NTU RGB+D that may appear in the classroom interaction as the alternative data for the experiment, they  are  listed  in  TABLE ċ . For instance, action mimicry and clapping are common movements in the classroom, pointing to something belongs to the perceptual task category that is adapted to  any  pairing,  or  the  cognitive  task  category  such  as  finding things,  standing  up  can  be  language  understanding  and  the expression task category adapted to one-step action instructions, etc.

The expression data set is based on NVIE (Natural Visible and Infrared Facial Expression), which divides all the pictures into six emotions: happiness, surprise, fear, sadness, disgust and anger. Some pictures contain emotional intensity (Arousal) and emotional pleasure (Valence) labels, and the value is between [ -1 , 1] .

## B. Engagement based Action Recognition

1) Establishment of Action Recognition Model: As shown above, the model used in action recognition is ST-GCN and the database is NTURGB+D, when the data are input into OpenPose, the BODY\_25 model is used to extract feature parameters. The data obtained are a series of JSON files, including the ordinates and the confidence of each point. The possible error of OpenPose and the corresponding solution are as follows: 1) The number of people detected is not the same as the actual, specifically, there is only one person in the video, but two sets of coordinates are detected. Because OpenPose does not search for people one by one, it is possible to detect a part as the human body's, we choose to  calculate  the  number  of  zero  value  in  the  second  set  of coordinates, if more than half of the total, it shows that a small part of the background detection is wrong, and the second set is discarded,  the  first  one  is  chosen.  Group  coordinates,  if  the number of zero values is less than the total, it means that it is impossible to judge which group of coordinates is the correct value, both are discarded at the same time; 2) only one set of coordinates ,  but  if  the  number  of  zero  value  of  coordinates exceeds half of the total, it is discarded; 3) the corresponding coordinate value is set to zero if the confidence level is zero.

The coordinate of feature points in the video are obtained by arranging a set of frame data according to the order of the frame. After  processing  the  video  in  TABLE  III,  a  total  of  11372 coordinate sequences are obtained.  The number of the frame varies from dozens to hundreds depending on the length of the video.  For convolution, it is necessary to unify the number of frames of the video, normalize all the frame to 260, and make up zero value at the end of whose number of the frame is less than 260. Considering the integrity of the expression change, if the number of the frame is over 260, we select from them according to  uniform  distribution  in  existing  frames.  Because  OpenPose also outputs the confidence parameters, the input channels are x, y and c.   It is believed that the feature point with high confidence level have greater influence on results.

Because the data set is shot from a fixed perspective and a fixed distance, the position of the target in the video is fixed, and there is no need to search for the size of the person. Video resolution is 1980*1080. Normalized coordinates are obtained by dividing the coordinate by the resolution directly, then the value  subtract  0.5  for  centralization,  and  the  coordinate  are converted to values between (-1, 1). The final matrix is (3, 25, 25), the 3 represents the x dimension, the y dimension and the confidence level dimension of coordinates, the 25 represents 25 feature points.

Totally, 11376 groups of videos are divided into train  set, validation set and test set according to the ratio of 6:2:2, when the train set is input, we set the learning rate as 0.01, and reduce it to 10% every 10 times. The batch size is set to 48, the epoch is set to 70, we choose the SGD optimization algorithm, and the momentu is set to 0.9. The results are shown in Fig. 3.

As we can see from the graph, the loss curve can converge quickly. And when the epoch is 60, the accuracy is 90 . 9% . It shows that the space-time graph convolution neural network can satisfy the demand of current project using existing data sets.

Fig. 3 THE PERFORMANCE OF THE LOSS AND ACCURACY IN THE ITERATION PROCESS



2) Engagement: When  the  action  recognition  is  accurate, through the ST-GCN, the classification label L of action can be obtained.    Looking  up  the  key  point  sequence ݒ ௜ ( א ݅ ሾͳǡ ܸ ሿ ) corresponding  to  label  L  from  the  database,  calculating  the displacement of the same key point between different frames for א ݐ ሾͳǡ ܶ െͳሿ can be regarded as a vector, and the displacement change matrix can be synthesized. The Euclidean distance and the cosine angle are used for calculating the difference, and the obtained feature map is as shown in Fig. 4.

The abscissa of the three groups of pictures is the number of the frame in the video, and the ordinate separately from the top to  the  bottom  are  1)  The  X-frame  and  Y-frame  figure  of 25 feature points. Because there are too many broken lines (50 in total),  the  legend  distinction  is  not  considered.  2)  Euclidean Distance-Frame Number Graph of each feature point between adjacent  frames.  3)  Cosine-Frame  Number  Graph  of  each feature point between adjacent frames. Among them, the first group of original video action is 'pointing out the object', the second is 'cheering', and the third is 'waving hands', as we show in Fig. 5. The most obvious key points in the three groups of videos are hands, elbows and shoulders, so the coordinates of feature points with serial numbers of [2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7] are selected for calculation. As we can see from the graph, when a person readies to move, his limbs will change greatly in a short time, we can find the moment when the action begins referring to this. But it is noteworthy that it is not enough to judge the beginning  of  a  action  only  from  the  change  of  distance  or direction.  In  other  words,  among  the action  performance  of autistic children, there may  be  a  initial action  which  is changing  in distance  but  unchanged  in direction (The movement like raising hands, the distance changes obviously, but the direction is almost unchanged.), as well as a change FrameNumber

That is to say, the initial frame detected by the European distance and cosine angle will be different because of the different action characteristics. ## C. Arousal and Valence based Expression  Recognition

1) Establishment  of  Expression  Recognition  Model: Pictures in NVIE are taken continuously, which can be regarded as a series of frames of a video. The NVIE also provides error frames  and  error  mode  information.  There  are  103637 available  pictures  except  those  with  zero  coordinates  of feature points.

Due  to  the  difference  of  the  number  of  video  frames,  a suitable frame size is selected according to the median and   the mode. Each frame coordinate is spliced into a  matrix with X label  as  frame  and  Y  label  as  feature  points.  Finally,  1767 matrices, namely video units, are obtained.

Because of the different shooting angles of pictures in  NVIE and  the  different  face  size  of  the  target,  the  normalization method  can  not  be  dividing  the  resolution  by  coordinates  as NTURGB+D. The common  normalization  methods  are  minmax normalization and Z-score normalization. Considering the advantage of Z-score in distance measure similarity, choosing it for normalization.

For  too  few  video  units  and  the  complexity  of  sequence features based on video units, using picture as a unit, for 103637 samples,  the  results  of  several  common  linear  and  nonlinear classifiers are displayed in TABLE. IV.

As can be seen from the tab le, for the figure input,  nonlinear classifiers perform better than the linear classifier, among them, the random forest algorithm works best because of its playback sampling and the random sampling of feature points which can prevent overfitting. Using the grid tuning to adjust the random forest, the final accuracy is 0.990062 which meets the requirement.

2) Arousal  and  Valence: We  use  NVIE  for  expression recognition  training.  There  are  877  sequences  in  the  NVIE database contain Arousal and Valence tags, and the others can be  summarized  according  to  the  point  coverage  and  the similarity.  We convert label  distribution  into density  map, as shown in Fig. 6 and Fig. 7, the 0-5 area indicates that the score is  from  low  to  high,  and  according  to  its  probability  density partition,  the  score  of  emotional  intensity  and  pleasure  under different  labels  can  be  compared.  Each dimension  is  roughly ranked  from  large  to  small  according  to  the  corresponding values  of  the  area  of  the  sample  concentrate:  1)  emotional arousal:  happiness,  surprise,  disgust,  fear,  anger,  sadness;  2) emotional  valence:  happiness,  surprise,  fear,  disgust,  anger, sadness. The higher the emotional activity, the more pleasant the performance is, and the higher the student's participation, so  the  simple  mapping  is  carried  out  in  order,  as  shown  in TABLE V.

However, this kind of scoring method has a serious dependence on data. In the actual system, it is necessary to wait     for the  sufficient  data  to  verify  and  revise  the  existing  scoring method according to the professional teachers' evaluations of the student's emotion. If Fig. 8 is based on the real data, from the perspective of the autistic student, it can be explained that when students show the positive emotion to the stimulation of the outside world in the classroom, the students' state is good, the  calmer  the  student's  performance  is,  and  even  negative emotions  are  generated,  indicating  that  the  student's  state  is worse .

## V. CONCLUSION

The performance evaluation of our proposed system is divided into two categories with three aspects. The first category is the participation score based on the student's response speed to  the  classroom  instruction.  We  define  the  scoring  method based  on  the  motion  start  frame  judgment  (start  frame/total frame number). At the same time, considering the diversity of the definition and quantification of participation in academia, the emotional indicator is also used as an auxiliary parameter. The  second  category  is  the  emotional  score  based  on  the

happiness valence For  implementation,  considering  the  actual  demand,  this work is based on OpenPose which is easy to use and has many versions.  At  the  same  time,  it  contains  the  expression feature point  and  the  action  feature  point  extraction  modules.  The action scoring module is divided into two parts, the first part is the  motion  recognition  based  on  the  spatiotemporal  graph convolutional neural network, and the second is the initial frame detection  and  scoring  based  on  the  Euclidean  distance  and cosine value, the accuracy is sufficient for training  data.  The expression scoring module is also divided into two parts. First of all, the expression tag is obtained by random forest, then the expression  label  is  used  to  score  the  mapping  relationship between the activity  rating  and  the  pleasure rating,  and  good results have also been achieved.



student's emotional expression of the classroom atmosphere, namely the activity score and the pleasure score based on the Arousal-Valence model. Our experiments based on the available datasets demonstrate  the technical feasibility to automatically  recognize  the  engagement  of  autistic  children with  high  accuracy.  In  the  future,  we  plan  to  construct  an emotional representation of the autistic students ' training class based on these three parameters. Fig. 8 CHARACTERISTIC MAP OF 'C HEERING ' AND 'W AVING  HAND '

## VI. FUTURE WORK

Because of the particularity of the research-oriented group, autistic children need real information in the classroom to test the  feasibility  in  the  actual  scenario.  After  we  collect  the autistic  children's  real  data,  future  work  can  be  carried  out from these aspects:

- 1) Current  research  mainly  identifies  the  action  of  one person, but the real classroom teaching process is a one-too ne  interaction  process.  If  teachers'  behaviors  are  included in the scope of recognition, it will be more realistic and more accurate to identify the classroom interaction between teachers and students.
- 2) After recognizing the emotional performance of autistic children, we can consider quantifying the result and find out the relationship between the result and the score of classroom participation pleasure and so on, which is conducive to future behavioral statistical analysis.

## Transformer Models for Question Answering on Autism Spectrum Disorder QA Dataset

Victoria Firsanova ( B )

Saint Petersburg State University, University Embankment 7/9, St. Petersburg 199034, Russia

st085687@student.spbu.ru

https://github.com/vifirsanova

Abstract. Question answering (QA) Transformer-based models might become efficient in inclusive education. For example, one can test and tune such models with small closed-domain datasets before the implementation of a new system in an inclusive organization. However, studies in the sociomedical domain show that such models can be unpredictable. They can mislead a user or evoke aversive emotional states. The paper addresses the problem of investigating safety-first QA models that would generate user-friendly outputs. The study aims to analyze the performance of SOTA Transformer-based QA models on a custom dataset collected by the author of the paper. The dataset contains 1 134 question-answer pairs about autism spectrum disorders (ASD) in Russian. The study presents the validation and evaluation of extractive and generative QA models. The author used transfer learning techniques to investigate domain-specific QA properties and suggest solutions that might provide higher QA efficiency in the inclusion. The study shows that although generative QA models can misrepresent facts and generate false tokens, they might bring diversity in the system outputs and make the automated QA more user-friendly for younger people. Although extractive QA is more reliable, according to the metric scores presented in this study, such models might be less efficient than generative ones. The principal conclusion of the study is that a combination of generative and extractive approaches might lead to higher efficiency in building QA systems for inclusion. However, the performance of such combined systems in the inclusion is yet to be investigated.

Question answering Dialogue system Transformer

Keywords: · ·

## 1 Introduction

Closed-domain question answering (CDQA) systems might find an application in the sphere of inclusive education by providing information about inclusion and people with special needs in a user-friendly way. In general, CDQA is a challenging task due to the volume limitations of available datasets. In the past few years, much research has focused on the abilities of the Transformer-based [1] models that can achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on various NLP tasks [2], including generative [3] and extractive question answering [4], even with limited training data.

Neural approaches allow us to achieve high metric scores. Nevertheless, the evaluation of the safety level of a built model remains unclear. The safety evaluation should help us to ensure the model does not misrepresent the data or generate false facts. Understanding how to evaluate and achieve the safety of a CDQA model for inclusive education is essential. A new app must not give misleading information, cause anxiety or negative emotions. One of the possible solutions might lie in the structure of a training dataset. For example, one can use or build a dataset containing different types of questions [5] or special keywords [6].

The purpose of the study was to explore the properties of state-of-the-art (SOTA) Transformer-based CDQA models fine-tuned for the autism spectrum disorder domain by comparing results of training extractive and generative QA systems on a dataset compiled by the author of the paper with results of other open- or medical (COVID-19 question answering) domain studies. The dataset presented in the study focuses on providing objective information about autism spectrum disorder and Asperger syndrome in the form of sets of reading passages and corresponding question-answer pairs [7]. The principal findings based on the comparison of Transformer models concern the analysis of extractive and generative QA performance. The author also looks forward to combining two approaches in the context of inclusive education. The novelty of the research is that the author tries to find out if the results of the SOTA models would be similar in the autism spectrum disorder, open- or medical domains.

The author of the paper consulted with psychiatrists from Russia. They have described to her during the interview the main features of apps for autistic people. According to experts, many people with special needs find it difficult to perceive new information by ear. The perception of visual information is more comfortable for many people with autism (but this is not true for everyone). The adapted information should be clear, unambiguous, unloaded from unnecessary details. The author of the paper considered these domain-specific features during the dataset compilation described in Sect. 3.

## 2 Related Work

Applying natural language technologies to teaching, diagnostics, rehabilitation of people with autism spectrum disorder is an extensively discussed topic. For example, in the 2000s, Boris Galitsky proposed a question answering system for autistic children [9]. His model aimed to teach patients reasoning about mental states. The online agent asked a user about mental states of characters from given scenarios. Some later studies proposed using systems based on closed-domain question answering to diagnose autism spectrum disorder. For example, the Aquabot, developed in 2017, has a psychiatrist mode that asks a user questions to predict possible achluophobia or autism [10]. Another example is the Autism AI mobile app developed in 2020 that is based on a convolutional classifier and sets of questionnaires and can be used to predict possible autism spectrum disorder [11].

The research has focused on issues of building Conversational AI (ConvAI) models. ConvAI approaches are closely related to the development of natural language interfaces and human-machine interaction. Question answering, as one of the fundamental ConvAI tasks, copes with input questions within one or several domains by generating, extracting, or retrieving an answer based on the information from a data or knowledge base [8].

Closed-domain ConvAI systems have their roots in the 1960s. For instance, ELIZA [12], a closed-domain imitator of a psychotherapist session and the forerunner of modern chatbots, could generate dialogue lines by pattern matching and memory accessing. Another example is LUNAR [13], a closed-domain question answering system on moon geology and the forerunner of natural language interfaces based on syntax and semantic analyzers [14]. The parser of LUNAR was built with an augmented transition network (ATN), an automaton that changes states while moving from one word to another in a parsed piece of text.

Recent advances in natural language processing show that Transformer architecture based solely on attention mechanisms [1] allows achieving high metric scores on a wide range of tasks by transferring knowledge gained during the model training from one task to another through so-called fine-tuning [15]. For example, models based on Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [27] fine-tuned for question answering, in fact, deal with Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) task, which is to extract an answer from a given reading passage. In turn, QA models based on Generative Pretrained Transformer [16] use zero-shot learning (a model learns to predict the data it has never seen before) to memorize the data and predict possible answers to questions.

According to the empirical findings from a study on applying GPT-2 [17] and GPT-3 [18] in building medical closed-domain question answering (CDQA) models, generative Transformer-based models might become harmfully biased [19] and, as a result, misrepresent information and cause negative emotions. On the contrary, extractive and retrieval-based approaches might be more reliable. Such models have already found their practical implementation in medical natural language processing tasks. Those are safety-first tasks [20].

The author of the paper has considered these hypotheses about generative and extractive question answering. To prove or disprove them, she has built and evaluated several CDQA models based on Transformer architecture using her custom dataset [7]. She aimed to find out domain-specific features of closed-domain question answering applied to the sphere of inclusive education. Although there are many domain-specific studies on medical natural language processing, the applicability of the existing approaches in inclusive education is not well investigated. That indicates a research gap which might be closed by further studies of the abilities and interpretability of Transformer-based models.

## 3 Dataset

The Autism Spectrum Disorder Question Answering (ASD QA) [7] is a dataset compiled by the author of the paper for the present study. The dataset contains data from the online information resource for individuals with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and Asperger syndrome [21], totaling 1 134 answered questions. One can use question-answer pairs and metadata from the dataset for training or fine-tuning models for machine reading comprehension (MRC), question answering (QA), text generation, etc.

The Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) [22,23] was the source of inspiration for the ASD QA dataset [7]. Figure 1 presents a dataset sample. On the Fig. 1, Title denotes the name of a thematic cluster. The dataset includes three clusters. The first cluster comprises general information on autism spectrum disorder and Asperger syndrome. The second cluster contains facts about interaction and communication with people with special needs. The third cluster includes practical guidelines for parents. The block Paragraphs on the Fig. 1 denotes pairs of questions and answers (see qas on the Fig. 1) along with reading passages containing the corresponding information (see context on the Fig. 1). The dataset comprises 96 reading passages. The volume of the reading passages is 45 400 symbols, 6 578 words. The maximum length of a reading passage in the dataset is 512 symbols.

Each set of question-answer (QA) pairs ( qas ) includes one question and one answer . The volume of QA-sequences is 179 174 symbols, 26 269 words. Each set of answers includes their texts and metadata: (1) the numeric representation of an answer span in a corresponding context with its first symbol ( answer start )

## 4 Models and Learning Configuration

Transformer architecture chosen for the experiments was described in [1]. This architecture is based solely on attention mechanisms with a fully connected feedforward network ( FFN ). The position-wise FFN in the Transformer takes a vector x and passes it through the matrices W1 and W2 and bias vectors b1 and b2 :



The unit of a multi-head self-attention mechanism A in the Transformer takes key-value pairs ( K, V ) as input. The keys are of dimension dk , and the values are of dimension dv . The attention function is multiplied by a matrix Q , and a softmax function is applied for the computation of the scaled dot-product attention described in [1]:



The Transformer-based models were fine-tuned using PyTorch [25] and HuggingFace [26] tools. Four models chosen for the experiments were pre-trained for masked language modeling (MLM) [27]. The author used these models for extractive QA. The list of models is as follows: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers multilingual (BERT, mBERT) base model (cased) [27], distilled version of BERT base multilingual (DBERT, mDBERT) model (cased) [28], Unsupervised Cross-lingual Representation Learning at Scale (XLM-RoBERTa, XLM-R) base model [29] and BERT base model for Russian (cased) fine-tuned by Geotrend (ruBERT) [30]. One of the models chosen for the experiments was pre-trained for traditional language modeling. The author used this model for generative QA. This model was Generative Pre-trained Transformer 2 [17].

The training data and model weights were stored on Google Cloud Storage [31]. The training was performed on Google Collaborative Environment [32] with Nvidia Tesla T4 graphics processing unit (GPU) [33]. During the experiments, the training time for each model was recorded in minutes. During the hyperparameters optimization, the author tuned batch size, learning rate, and the number of epochs. Each model was retrained ten times with different parameters.

The BERT-, DistilBERT- and XLM-RoBERTa-based models were retrained for 5, 10, 15, and 20 epochs with 1e -5, 3e -5, and 5e -5 learning rate. The optimal batch size for all those models was 1. The GPT-2-based model was retrained for 15, 20, and 30 epochs with 1e -5, 3e -5, and 5e -5 learning rate. The optimal batch size for this model is 16. The optimal parameters are presented in the next section in Table 3 in the next section. Table 2 presents models' configurations.

## 5 Experiments and Results

One of the issues identified during the training is the 'weight' of the latest natural language processing models. Even a small version of GPT-2 with 117 million parameters and BERT-based models with 110 million parameters necessitate high computation power to run training sessions. The issue was solved by using smaller batch sizes and applying a Python garbage collector. The garbage collector for the automatic memory allocation management prevented the crash of sessions caused by using all Random-Access Memory.

The next issue was related to the metric scores. The models mostly showed high precision and low recall, which means that the models were outputting very few but frequently correct answers. The problem was solved by increasing the dataset volume. During the experiments, it was found that shorter reading passages lead to better results. The reduction of reading passages' maximum length from 1 024 to 512 symbols increased the average model performance (F1Score and Exact Match) by around 10%.

Table 3. Results obtained on ASD QA (extractive and generative question answering).

|--------------|------------------|--------------------|-----------------|--------------|------|------|
| mBERT        |               22 |                 10 | 3e - 5          |            1 | 0.29 | 0.40 |
| mDBERT       |               11 |                 20 | 1e - 5          |            1 | 0.32 | 0.42 |
| XLM-R        |               10 |                 10 | 3e - 5          |            1 | 0.39 | 0.48 |
| ruBERT       |               10 |                 10 | 5e - 5          |            1 | 0.30 | 0.39 |
| GPT-2        |               30 |                 30 | 3e 5            |           16 | 0.41 | 0.53 |

-

The final issue is the choice of models. The investigation of the HuggingFace Transformers repository showed that models pre-trained on masked language modeling (MLM) and traditional language modeling (LM) are more flexible than narrow models pre-trained for question answering or machine reading comprehension (MRC). Narrow models could allow achieving higher metric scores after the fine-tuning. However, such models do not have zero-shot learning capabilities and have more dataset requirements. During the experiments, it was found that with low-resource closed-domain datasets models pre-trained on a target language data do not achieve higher results than multilingual ones. Table 3 shows the models' results.

## 6 Discussion

The author has compared the achieved metric scores (see Sect. 5) with the results of some similar studies. Table 4 is a comparison table of metric scores of Transformer-based models trained on open- and medical domain datasets. The properties of the dataset used in this study should differ from the features of the medical domain because texts about autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from the dataset are not professional. Such texts are usually being adapted for parents of people with ASD, neurotypical adults, adults with special needs, etc. In turn, medical texts that address professionals include more special vocabulary. Authors of such documents usually do not adapt their texts for non-professionals. Nevertheless, these domains have a lot in common because they both cover various medical topics. That is why the author decided to compare her results with the results of similar models trained on the medical COVID-19 Open Research Dataset (CORD-19) [34].

Table 4. Results obtained on open-domain and medical COVID-19 benchmarks.

| Model name          | Dataset                       | EM   |   F1 |
|---------------------|-------------------------------|------|------|
| BERT                | CORD-19 (medical, COVID-19)   | 81.5 | 88.3 |
| DBERT               | CORD-19 (medical, COVID-19)   | 80.6 | 87.3 |
| BERT                | SQuAD 1.1 dev (open, English) | 81.3 | 88.7 |
| DBERT               | SQuAD 1.1 dev (open, English) | 80.1 | 87.5 |
| XLM-R               | MKQA (open, multilingual)     | -    | 46.0 |
| mBERT               | MKQA (open, multilingual)     | -    | 44.1 |
| mT5 (generative QA) | MKQA (open, multilingual)     | -    | 38.5 |

Table 4 includes metric scores given in a paper describing COBERT, a BERTbased COVID-19 question answering system [35]. The authors of the COBERT compared the results of BERT-[27] and DistilBERT-based [28] models obtained on CORD-19 and open-domain SQuAD 1.1 [22] datasets in English. The results of multilingual BERT- and DistilBERT-based models obtained on the ASD QA dataset presented in this study differ. BERT showed slightly better results than DistilBERT for both CORD-19 and SQuAD. In this study, a multilingual version of DistilBERT became more efficient than multilingual BERT on the ASD QA dataset (see Table 3).

The table of comparison includes F1 scores achieved by multi- and crosslingual Transformer-based models trained on Multilingual Open Domain Question Answering dataset (MKQA) [36]. The results presented in the MKQA paper allow us to compare the efficiency of generative and extractive question answering. The MKQA authors have chosen a multilingual version of T5 [37] Transformer-based model to implement the generative approach. They have also compared the efficiency of XLM-RoBERTa [29] and multilingual BERT. XLMRoBERTa became the most powerful model. That is consistent with the results obtained on the ASD QA dataset. In this study, XLM-RoBERTa showed the highest metric scores among all the models chosen for the extractive approach implementation. In the MKQA case, the generative model achieved lower metric scores, whereas the same approach allowed the author to get the best results in this study.

## 7 Conclusion

Overall, in the study, the author compares SOTA Transformer-based question answering models' performance in the autism spectrum disorder domain with their performance in the open- or medical domain. The hypothesis that extractive models would cope with the task significantly better due to their reliability did not confirm according to the metric scores of the models and the analysis of the models' outputs obtained on the test data. The traditional language model fine-tuned for generative question answering showed higher results than any other model for extractive question answering used in the study.

Among the extractive QA models, the most effective became XLMRoBERTa. Supposedly, the number of model parameters is the reason for that. The number of parameters is the highest for XLM-RoBERTa. It is also high for GPT-2. Apart from that, the number of embeddings is the highest for GPT2. Out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rate linked to the vocabulary size did not play a crucial role (for example, XLM-RoBERTa had the highest OOV rate, but this model showed the highest performance among all the extractive models from the study). The author hasn't noticed any significant advantages of ruBERT model pre-trained on Russian (target language) data over multilingual ones.

A large number of unsuccessful outputs produced by trained systems shows that generative and extractive models are both yet far from the first trials of their integration into the education processes. One of the possible reasons for some unsuccessful outputs is the vocabulary of texts about autism spectrum disorders. Texts from the dataset used in the study contain specific words from the medical domain. For example, such texts comprise designations of mental, neurodevelopmental, generic, and other disorders (Asperger's syndrome, intellectual disability, Down's syndrome). They also include other medical terms (diagnosis, hypersensitivity, etc.). Those terms are mixed in the dataset with everyday vocabulary about childhood and adolescence, for example, names of games and school-related words. Due to the topics' narrowness, the sentences in the dataset have a similar structure and are not lexically diverse.

Extractive models are considered to be more reliable than generative ones. They do not generate a new answer but extract one from a given piece of text. However, the study showed that such models could give misleading answers as often as generative models while being trained on a low-resource closed-domain dataset. The reason for that is that such models can shift the answer by extracting the right sentence from the reading passage but the wrong word or phrase due to the lexical similarities and little diversity in the dataset vocabulary. This problem can be solved by providing the dataset with shorter answers consisting of one or two words so that models would be able to learn to extract specific unique text pieces.

Generative models could generate correct information based on the knowledge from their memory not answering a user's question. The issue was caused by the large number of similar terms repeated in different reading passages and question-answer pairs. The models were so to say confused by a large amount of repeating vocabulary. Possibly, the problem can be solved by enriching the dataset with texts on different topics with a more diverse vocabulary.

In the longer term, the author decided to continue experimenting with the dataset transformations. In particular, the author plans to add more answers to each question and investigate the effect of the length of answers and questions on system performance. The author also intends to find out how various Transformer-based models deal with unanswerable questions and which techniques might lead to higher efficiency in solving this task.

## Paper Source: Using Deep Learning and Native Mobile App to Assist Autistic Students' Educational Experience
